question.text: In a pulley arrangement, a ball hangs on one side and a thin rod of length l hangs on the other, with the ball's mass equal to η times the rod's mass. Every pulley and string in the system is weightless, and there is no friction anywhere. At the start the ball sits level with the rod's bottom end, and the system is then let go from rest. Work out how long it takes for the ball to rise level with the rod's top end.
conditions: ball's mass is η times the rod's mass
rod has length l
pulleys and threads are massless
no friction anywhere
ball begins level with the rod's lower end, released from rest

figure.description: A pulley is fixed to a bracket on the ceiling. A string passes over the top of this fixed pulley. Its left end hangs straight down to a small ball. Its right end hangs straight down to the axle of a second, smaller pulley, which is not fixed to anything and hangs in the air below and to the right of the fixed pulley, held up only by this string. A second string passes over the top of this hanging pulley, and both of its segments run downward: the left segment goes straight down to the top end of a thin vertical rod of length l, which hangs freely; the right segment goes straight down to a short fixed ledge (bracket) mounted beside the rod, at about the level of the rod's top end. The ball and the rod hang side by side, the ball on the left and the rod on the right. At the moment of release the ball is level with the rod's lower end. The ball's mass is η times the rod's mass; all pulleys and strings are massless and there is no friction.

solution.approach: Link the rod's motion to the ball's motion through the two cords, apply Newton's second law to both, then time the closing of gap l from the relative acceleration.

steps.text: The ball hangs from one end of the cord over the fixed pulley; the other end goes down to the movable pulley, which is held up only by that cord.
steps.equation: cord 1: ball to fixed pulley to movable pulley

steps.text: If the ball falls a distance x, the movable pulley must rise by x (cord 1 is fixed length); then, since the rod hangs from one side of cord 2, which passes over the top of that pulley, and a fixed bracket holds the other side, the rod's top must rise or fall by twice the pulley's own motion.
steps.why_this_step: This constraint relation ties every acceleration in the system together before any force equation is written.

steps.text: The movable pulley is massless, so cord 1's single pull must balance cord 2's two pulls.
Write Newton's second law for the ball, taking downward as positive.
Write Newton's second law for the rod, taking downward as positive, using the constraint a(rod) = −2ab.
Substitute T1 = 2T2 and mb = ηmr into both equations and eliminate the tensions to solve for the ball's acceleration.
steps.equation: ab = g(η − 2)/(η + 4), downward; this is negative for η < 2, so the ball actually rises

steps.text: The ball starts a distance l below the rod's top. With both released from rest, the gap closes with constant relative acceleration, equal to the acceleration of the ball toward the rod's top.
steps.equation: gap(t) = l + ½(ab − a_rod)t² = l + (3/2)ab t²; setting gap = 0 gives t = √(2l(η + 4)/(3g(2 − η))), valid for η < 2

final_answer.value: t = √(2l(η + 4) / (3g(2 − η))), valid when η < 2 so the ball rises to meet the rod's descending top

common_mistakes.text: Missing the movable-pulley factor of 2 in the constraint and taking the rod's speed equal to the ball's instead of twice it, which changes both the acceleration formula and the resulting time.

question.text: Two pulleys are mounted side by side on the ceiling. Between and below them hangs a third, smaller pulley that is free to move, and block B hangs from this middle pulley. One continuous string starts at block A, goes up and passes over the left ceiling pulley, comes down and loops under the free middle pulley, goes back up and over the right ceiling pulley, and finally comes down to block C. Work out how the accelerations aA, aB and aC of the three blocks are related to each other.
conditions: two pulleys fixed to the ceiling, side by side
third pulley hangs freely between them, movable
one string connects block A, over the left fixed pulley, under the movable pulley, over the right fixed pulley, to block C
block B hangs from the movable middle pulley

figure.description: Two fixed pulleys hang from the ceiling next to each other. A smaller pulley hangs freely below and between them, and block B is attached to this middle pulley. A single string goes from block A up over the left fixed pulley, down under the free middle pulley, up over the right fixed pulley, and down to block C.

solution.approach: Write the one string's total length as the sum of its four segments over the two fixed pulleys and the movable pulley, and use that this length never changes.

steps.text: The single string runs from A, up and over the left fixed pulley, down and under the movable middle pulley, up and over the right fixed pulley, and down to C. Block B hangs from the movable middle pulley.
Here yA and yC are how far A and C hang below their fixed pulleys, and yB is how far the movable pulley (with B) hangs below the fixed pulleys, since both fixed pulleys sit at the same height.
Differentiate this length equation twice with respect to time; the constant term vanishes.
This is the required relation between the three accelerations, all measured with the same downward-positive convention.

final_answer.value: aA + 2aB + aC = 0 (all three accelerations measured positive in the same direction, say downward).

common_mistakes.text: Writing aA + aB + aC = 0, missing the factor of 2 on B that comes from B hanging on the movable pulley with two string segments.
Writing aA = aC without the aB term, treating the two fixed pulleys as if they were connected by one straight string with no movable pulley in between.

question.text: A straight rod AB is pivoted at end A. Three forces act on it, as described below. Determine the anticlockwise moment about the pivot produced by each of the three forces.
conditions: force 2F acts vertically upward at a point a distance a from A
force F acts vertically downward at a point a distance 2a from A
force 3F acts at end B, a distance 4a from A, directed at 30° to the rod
rod AB is pivoted at end A

figure.description: A straight horizontal rod AB is pivoted at its left end A. A force 2F acts vertically upward at a point a distance a from A. A force F acts vertically downward at a point a distance 2a from A. A force 3F acts at the right end B, a distance 4a from A, pointing up and to the left (above the rod, back toward the A side) at 30° to the rod.

solution.approach: For each force, multiply its magnitude by the perpendicular distance from A to its line of action, and use the sense of turning it produces to fix the sign.

steps.text: The force 2F acts straight up at distance a from A. Since it is already perpendicular to the rod, its moment arm is a itself.
An upward force to the right of the pivot turns the rod anticlockwise, so this moment is anticlockwise.
The force F acts straight down at distance 2a from A, again already perpendicular to the rod.
A downward force to the right of the pivot turns the rod clockwise, which is the opposite sense to the first force.
steps.why_this_step: Taking anticlockwise as positive keeps every moment on one consistent scale.

steps.text: The force 3F acts at B, distance 4a from A, at 30° to the rod. Only the component perpendicular to the rod produces a moment about A.
Multiply this perpendicular component by the full distance 4a to get the moment.
The force points up and back toward A, which turns the rod anticlockwise about A, the same sense as the first force.
steps.why_this_step: Only the part of a force at right angles to the rod turns it; the part along the rod passes through no lever arm and contributes nothing.

final_answer.value: Anticlockwise moments about A: 2F gives 2Fa anticlockwise; F gives 2Fa clockwise (i.e. −2Fa anticlockwise); 3F gives 6Fa anticlockwise.

common_mistakes.text: Multiplying the full 3F by 4a without taking the 30° component first, giving 12Fa instead of the correct 6Fa.
Treating the downward force F as anticlockwise like the other two instead of clockwise, by fixing the sense of rotation from the position of the force alone and not from its direction.

question.text: A block sits on a rough incline that rises at 30° to the horizontal. A string tied to the block is pulled at 30° above the incline surface. Draw a diagram showing every force acting on the block, and resolve each of these forces:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the horizontal and vertical components of each force.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the components of each force parallel and perpendicular to the incline surface.

conditions: incline surface rises at 30° to the horizontal
incline surface is rough
string is held at 30° to the incline surface

figure.description: An incline rises to the right at 30° to the horizontal ground, with a block resting on its surface. Four forces act on the block: N, the normal reaction, perpendicular to the incline surface and pointing away from it; T, the tension in the string, pointing up the slope and away from the surface at 30° above the incline surface (so T makes 60° with N and 60° with the horizontal); w, the weight, acting straight down; and f, friction, acting down along the incline surface (toward the lower end of the slope).

solution.approach: Draw the four forces on the block, then project each one onto horizontal/vertical axes and onto axes along/perpendicular to the incline.

steps.text: List the four forces: N perpendicular to the incline, T at 30° to the incline surface pointing up the slope, weight w straight down, and friction f down the slope.
N is perpendicular to a surface tilted 30° to the horizontal, so N itself makes 30° with the vertical.
steps.equation: N_horizontal = −N sin30° = −N/2, N_vertical = N cos30° = N√3/2

steps.text: T is 30° above the incline surface, and the incline is 30° above the horizontal, so T makes 60° with the horizontal.
steps.equation: T_horizontal = T cos60° = T/2, T_vertical = T sin60° = T√3/2

steps.text: Weight acts straight down, so it has no horizontal part.
Friction acts down the slope, 30° below the horizontal on the lower side.
steps.why_this_step: Friction opposes the tendency of the block to move up the slope under the pull of the string, so here it is drawn pointing down the slope, as the figure shows.

steps.text: Now take axes along the incline (up-slope positive) and perpendicular to it (away from the surface positive). N has no component along the slope.
T is already given at 30° to the incline surface, so its own components along and perpendicular to the plane use that 30° directly.
steps.equation: T_parallel = T cos30° = T√3/2, T_perpendicular = T sin30° = T/2

steps.text: Weight splits into a down-slope part and an into-the-surface part using the 30° incline angle; friction lies entirely along the slope.
steps.equation: w_parallel = −w sin30° = −w/2, w_perpendicular = −w cos30° = −w√3/2, f_parallel = −f, f_perpendicular = 0

final_answer.value: (a) horizontal/vertical: N → (−N/2, N√3/2); T → (T/2, T√3/2); w → (0, −w); f → (−f√3/2, −f/2). (b) parallel/perpendicular to the plane: N → (0, N); T → (T√3/2, T/2); w → (−w/2, −w√3/2); f → (−f, 0).

common_mistakes.text: Using the incline's 30° for T's horizontal and vertical split instead of the correct 60°, which swaps the pair to T cos30° and T sin30° (T√3/2 horizontal, T/2 vertical).
Drawing friction up the slope instead of down it, which flips the sign of both its horizontal and vertical parts.

question.text: In the arrangement shown, a 2 kg block rests on a horizontal table and a 1 kg block hangs over the table's edge. Both pulleys and the string are massless, and every surface is frictionless. Use g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Calculate the acceleration of the 1 kg block.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Calculate the tension in the connecting string.

conditions: pulleys and string are massless (light)
all surfaces are frictionless (smooth)

figure.description: A 2 kg block rests on a smooth horizontal table. A short link from the block's right face holds the axle of a movable pulley, so the pulley moves with the block. A fixed pulley A is mounted at the table's right-hand edge. One end of a single string is anchored at the table edge just below pulley A; the string runs left along the table, wraps around the movable pulley, runs back right above the first strand, passes over the top of pulley A, and hangs straight down to the 1 kg block. The two horizontal strands between the movable pulley and the edge are parallel; when the 1 kg block descends a distance x, the 2 kg block moves right by x/2.

solution.approach: The tension is the same throughout the string; two segments pull the table block through the movable pulley, and the given 2:1 displacement link fixes how the accelerations relate.

steps.text: Let T be the string's tension, a2 the table block's acceleration and a1 the hanging block's acceleration; the given displacement link fixes their ratio.
steps.equation: a1 = 2 a2 (1 kg block falls x while 2 kg block moves x/2)

steps.text: Two string segments run from the movable pulley to the fixed points, the anchor and pulley A, so both pull the movable pulley, and hence the 2 kg block, toward the table's edge with total force 2T.
For the hanging 1 kg block, tension T acts upward and its weight acts downward.
Substitute T = a2 = a1/2, from step 2 and the displacement link, into the hanging-block equation to leave a single equation in a1.
Solve for a1, then get a2 and T from it.

final_answer.value: (a) acceleration of the 1 kg block = 20/3 m/s² ≈ 6.67 m/s², directed downward. (b) tension in the string = 10/3 N ≈ 3.33 N.

common_mistakes.text: Using only T, not 2T, for the pulling force on the table block, while keeping a1 = 2a2, gives the 1 kg block's acceleration as 5 m/s² and the tension as 5 N.

question.text: A block of mass m sits on an inclined plane whose angle θ with the horizontal is slowly increased from 0° up to 90°. The coefficients of static and kinetic friction between the block and the plane are μₛ and μₖ. Sketch how the friction force f acting on the block varies as θ increases.
conditions: block of mass m on an incline
angle θ increased from 0° to 90°
static friction coefficient = μₛ
kinetic friction coefficient = μₖ

figure.description: A block of mass m rests on an inclined plane whose angle θ with the horizontal can be increased. The friction coefficients between the block and the plane are μₛ (static) and μₖ (kinetic).

solution.approach: Friction equals mg sinθ while the block rests; once θ passes tanθ = μₛ, it drops to the kinetic value and falls further as θ increases.

steps.text: For small θ the block does not slide, so friction balances the component of weight along the incline.
steps.equation: f = mg sinθ, for 0 ≤ θ ≤ θₛ

steps.text: Friction can rise only up to its maximum static value. The block is on the verge of sliding when the incline angle reaches θₛ.
steps.equation: tanθₛ = μₛ, f_max = μₛ mg cosθₛ

steps.text: Past θₛ the block slides, so friction switches to the kinetic value, which is smaller than the static maximum because μₖ < μₛ.
steps.equation: f = μₖ mg cosθ, for θ > θₛ
steps.why_this_step: Kinetic friction is always less than the limiting static friction, so f drops suddenly at θₛ.

steps.text: As θ increases further toward 90°, cosθ keeps falling, so the kinetic friction keeps falling with it, reaching zero at θ = 90°.
steps.why_this_step: At θ = 90° the incline is vertical, the normal force is zero, and friction is proportional to the normal force.

final_answer.value: f rises as mg sinθ from 0 at θ = 0° up to the limiting value μₛ mg cosθₛ at θₛ = tan⁻¹μₛ, drops there to the smaller kinetic value μₖ mg cosθₛ, then falls further as μₖ mg cosθ down to 0 at θ = 90°.

common_mistakes.text: Drawing friction as always increasing with θ, never dropping at θₛ, by forgetting that friction switches from static to a smaller kinetic value once sliding begins.
Drawing friction as a straight line in θ instead of following sinθ then cosθ, by treating the angle dependence as linear.

question.text: A ladder that weighs 250 N rests against a vertical wall that is smooth (frictionless). Between the ladder and the floor, the coefficient of friction is 0.3. What is the greatest friction force that can act where the ladder touches the floor?
conditions: wall is smooth (frictionless)
coefficient of friction between ladder and floor = 0.3
ladder weight = 250 N

solution.approach: Since the wall is smooth, the floor alone carries the ladder's full weight, so the maximum friction at the floor is the coefficient of friction times that weight.

steps.text: The wall is smooth, so it pushes only sideways on the ladder and supplies no vertical support. The floor must therefore carry the ladder's entire weight vertically.
steps.equation: N (floor, vertical) = weight of ladder = 250 N

steps.text: The maximum friction force the floor can supply is the coefficient of friction times this normal force.

common_mistakes.text: Misreading the ladder's weight of 250 N as a mass of 250 kg and multiplying by g again gives f_max = 0.3 × 250 × 10 = 750 N.

question.text: Assertion: For a set of forces that all pass through one common point, the total turning effect (moment) taken about any chosen point has the same value whichever point is chosen. Reason: If such concurrent forces add up to zero as vectors, their total moment about every point is zero as well.

options.1: both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
options.2: both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
options.3: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
options.4: Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

conditions: forces are concurrent (all act through one common point)

solution.approach: Test whether the moment of concurrent forces about two different points is actually the same, using a concrete numeric example, then check the zero-resultant case separately.

steps.text: For concurrent forces acting through one point P, the moment about any point O equals the vector from O to P crossed with the resultant force R.
Take two concurrent forces through P = (1,0) that do not cancel: F₁ = (1,1) N and F₂ = (2,−1) N.
Compute the moment about the origin (0,0) and about the point (0,5).
steps.equation: moment about (0,0) = 0 N·m, moment about (0,5) = 15 N·m

steps.text: These two moments are different, so the moment of concurrent forces about different points is not constant in general — the Assertion is false.
Repeat with forces that cancel instead: F₁ = (1,1) N and F₂ = (−1,−1) N, so R = 0.
With R = 0, the moment about each of the same two points, (0,0) and (0,5), comes out zero, confirming the Reason's specific claim that a zero resultant gives zero moment everywhere.

final_answer.value: Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

common_mistakes.text: Assuming that forces meeting at one point is by itself enough to make the moment the same about every point, without testing a case where the resultant is not zero.

question.text: A force F of magnitude 8 N acts at 45° above the horizontal. Split this force into its horizontal and vertical components.
conditions: force F makes an angle of 45° with the horizontal

figure.description: A force F drawn as a diagonal arrow at 45° above the horizontal from the origin. Dashed lines complete a right-angled box, with the horizontal side labelled F_H, the vertical side labelled F_V, and the 45° angle marked between F and the horizontal side.

solution.approach: Split the force into horizontal and vertical parts using the cosine and sine of the given angle.

steps.text: The force F makes 45° with the horizontal, so its horizontal part is F cos 45° and its vertical part is F sin 45°.
steps.equation: F_H = F cos 45°, F_V = F sin 45°

steps.text: Put in F = 8 N and cos 45° = sin 45° = 0.7071.
The vertical part comes out the same, since sin 45° equals cos 45°.
steps.why_this_step: At 45°, the two right-angle components of any force are always equal.

common_mistakes.text: Taking F_H = F and F_V = 0 by ignoring that the force is tilted, instead of resolving it.

question.text: Starting at the same instant from a common point O, two particles slide down two straight, frictionless wires. The first wire makes an angle of 30° with the vertical, and the second wire makes an angle of 60° with the vertical, both wires lying on the same side of the vertical line through O. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the second particle relative to the first?
conditions: both particles start together from the same point O
wires are straight and smooth (frictionless)
first wire inclined at 30° to the vertical plane
second wire inclined at 60° to the vertical plane
both wires lie on the same side of the vertical through O

solution.approach: Write each particle's acceleration along its own wire as a vector using horizontal and vertical parts, then subtract the two vectors to get the relative acceleration.

steps.text: Each particle's acceleration along its wire equals g times the cosine of the wire's angle from the vertical.
steps.equation: a₁ = g cos30°, a₂ = g cos60°

steps.text: Write these as vectors, since the two wires point in different directions on the same side of the vertical.
steps.equation: a₁ = g cos30°(sin30°, cos30°), a₂ = g cos60°(sin60°, cos60°)

steps.text: The horizontal parts of the two vectors come out equal, so they cancel when the vectors are subtracted.
Subtract the vertical parts to get the size of the relative acceleration.
steps.equation: a_rel = g cos²60° − g cos²30° = g/4 − 3g/4 = −g/2, magnitude g/2

common_mistakes.text: Taking the first particle's own acceleration along its wire, g cos30° = √3g/2, as if it were the relative acceleration.

question.text: Starting from rest, a particle is sped up to a velocity v by a force F₁. Afterwards, the same particle is slowed from that same velocity v back down to rest by a different force F₂. Which of these statements about F₁ and F₂ must be true?

options.1: F₁ and F₂ are always equal in magnitude
options.2: F₂ must be larger than F₁
options.3: F₂ could be smaller than, larger than, or equal to F₁

conditions: particle starts from rest
force F₁ speeds the particle up from rest to velocity v
force F₂ then slows the same particle from velocity v back to rest

solution.approach: Each force equals mass times the speed change divided by the time it acts over, and the question gives no relation between the two times.

steps.text: Write each force using Newton's second law, with the speed change divided by the time each force acts.
steps.equation: F₁ = m(v − 0)/t₁, F₂ = m(0 − v)/t₂ in size

steps.text: The question states only that the particle speeds up from rest to v under F₁ and slows from v to rest under F₂. It gives no information about the times t₁ and t₂, or about the distances covered.
steps.equation: no fixed relation between t₁ and t₂

steps.text: Since t₁ and t₂ can be anything, F₂ can come out smaller than, larger than, or equal to F₁, depending on the time over which each force acts.
steps.equation: F₂ ⋛ F₁, all three are possible

final_answer.value: F₂ may be smaller than, greater than or equal to F₁

common_mistakes.text: Assuming that the same change in speed must come from the same force overlooks that the time or distance over which each force acts is not given as equal.
Assuming that slowing something down always takes a bigger push than speeding it up confuses direction of motion with the size of the force needed.

question.text: A block of mass 5 kg sits on a horizontal table. A pulley is fixed at each edge of the table, one on the left and one on the right. A string from the block goes left over the left pulley and down to a hanging block of mass 15 kg; call its tension T₂. Another string from the block goes right over the right pulley and down to a hanging block of mass 5 kg; call its tension T₁. The coefficient of friction between the table and the 5 kg block on it is 0.2. What is the ratio T₁ : T₂ (tension in the right string to tension in the left string)?
conditions: coefficient of friction between the 5 kg block and the table is 0.2
5 kg block sits on the table, connected by strings over pulleys at each edge
left string (T₂) hangs a 15 kg block
right string (T₁) hangs a 5 kg block

figure.description: A block of mass 5 kg rests on a horizontal table. A pulley sits fixed at the left edge of the table and another at the right edge. The string on the left, labeled T₂, runs from the block over the left pulley and down to a hanging 15 kg block. The string on the right, labeled T₁, runs from the block over the right pulley and down to a hanging 5 kg block.

solution.approach: Write Newton's second law for all three blocks with one common acceleration, include friction on the table block, and solve the three equations together.

steps.text: The 15 kg block is heavier than the 5 kg block, so the system accelerates with the 15 kg block going down, the table block sliding toward the left pulley, and the 5 kg block on the right going up. Call this common acceleration a.
steps.equation: a is the same size for all three blocks

steps.text: Write Newton's second law for the 15 kg block (falling) and the 5 kg block (rising).
Write Newton's second law for the table block. Friction opposes its leftward slide, so it acts to the right; its size is the coefficient of friction times the block's own weight.
Substitute the first two equations into the third and solve for a, then get T₁ and T₂.
The ratio of the right tension to the left tension is T₁ to T₂.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the system as staying at rest and setting each tension equal to the weight it holds gives T₁ = 50 N and T₂ = 150 N, a ratio of 1 : 3.
Leaving out friction on the table block and solving the same three equations with μ = 0 gives T₁ = 70 N and T₂ = 90 N, a ratio of 7 : 9.

question.text: A 2 kg block lies on a rough horizontal floor with coefficient of friction μ = 0.6. A horizontal force, whose value in newtons is F = 2t with t measured in seconds, is applied on the block. Take g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Sketch how the block's acceleration changes with time.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out the friction force on the block at t = 2 s and at t = 8 s.

conditions: block mass = 2 kg
μ = 0.6 between block and floor
applied force F = 2t newtons, with t in seconds
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A 2 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor with coefficient of friction μ = 0.6. A horizontal force F = 2t (in newtons, t in seconds) pulls the block along the floor.

solution.approach: Find the time when the applied force equals the maximum static friction; before that the block stays still, after that kinetic friction acts and gives the acceleration.

steps.text: Find the maximum static friction and the time at which the applied force reaches it.
steps.equation: f(max static) = μmg = 0.6×2×10 = 12 N; F = 2t = 12 N at t = 6 s

steps.text: For t < 6 s the applied force is less than the maximum static friction, so the block stays still and friction equals the applied force.
For t > 6 s the block slides, so kinetic friction takes its constant maximum value and the net force gives the acceleration.
At t = 2 s the block is still in the static phase.
At t = 8 s the block is in the sliding phase.

final_answer.value: (a) a = 0 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6 s, then a = t − 6 for t > 6 s, a straight line through (6 s, 0) with slope 1; (b) friction = 4 N at t = 2 s, friction = 12 N at t = 8 s

common_mistakes.text: Using a = t − 6 at t = 2 s, before the block actually slides, gives friction = 12 N and a = −4 m/s², impossible for a block still at rest.
Forgetting to divide the net force by the mass gives a = 2t − 12 directly, so a = 4 m/s² at t = 8 s instead of the correct 2 m/s².

question.text: A plank called B, with mass 2m and length l, lies on a horizontal road. A block called A, with mass m, rests on top of plank B at its left-hand edge. The block and the plank are both given the same initial rightward speed v and then move together as a system. Friction acts at two surfaces: road against plank, with coefficient 1/2, and plank against block, with coefficient 1/4. Determine the following.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the time that passes before block A slides completely off plank B.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find how far block A and plank B each travel relative to the ground up to that moment.

conditions: A (mass m) sits at B's (mass 2m, length l) left end
B rests on a horizontal road
A and B start together with rightward speed v
friction coefficient road–plank = 1/2
friction coefficient plank–block = 1/4

figure.description: Block A rests on top of plank B, positioned at B's left-hand end; plank B in turn rests on the horizontal road below it. The plank's length, l, runs the full length of B, shown by a measurement arrow beneath it. Both A and B move together to the right with the same initial speed v; the road exerts friction against the plank (coefficient 1/2), and the plank exerts friction against the block (coefficient 1/4).

solution.approach: Check whether block and plank decelerate together; since they cannot, find each deceleration and use their relative motion to find when the block has moved l relative to the plank.

steps.text: If A and B moved together, deceleration would need 0.5mg of friction between them on A alone; but the maximum available is only μ₁mg = (1/4)mg, where μ₁ = 1/4 is the block-plank coefficient (μ₂ = 1/2 is the road-plank coefficient, M = 2m the plank mass), so A and B slide on each other.
steps.equation: required 0.5mg > available μ₁mg = 0.25mg  →  A and B move separately
steps.why_this_step: This confirms the block genuinely separates from the plank, matching the question.

steps.text: Block A is decelerated only by kinetic friction from the plank.
Plank B is decelerated by road friction (backward, on its total weight (M+m)g) and pushed forward by the reaction friction from A.
Since B decelerates faster than A, A keeps sliding forward relative to B at a relative acceleration equal to the difference of the two decelerations.
Both start with the same velocity v, so their relative velocity starts at zero; the block separates once it has moved a length l relative to the plank.
Use this time in each block's own equation of motion to get the two ground displacements.
steps.equation: s_A = vt − ½(g/4)t² = vt − 2l/3;  s_B = vt − ½(5g/8)t² = vt − 5l/3

final_answer.value: (a) t = 4√(l/3g) = √(16l/3g). (b) displacement of block A = vt − 2l/3, displacement of plank B = vt − 5l/3, with t as above

common_mistakes.text: Assuming A and B decelerate together without checking the friction needed against the friction available, missing that separation ever happens.
Using the plank's own deceleration 5g/8 as the relative deceleration instead of subtracting the block's deceleration g/4, gives the wrong t = 4√(l/5g).

question.text: A person of mass 50 kg stands on a platform of mass 25 kg. Holding one end of a rope that runs through a set of frictionless pulleys attached to the platform and to a fixed support, he pulls the rope. With what pulling force must he pull for the platform to rise at a constant speed?
conditions: pulleys are frictionless
platform moves upward at a steady, constant speed
person stands on the platform while pulling the rope

figure.description: Three pulleys are used. Two pulleys, ceiling pulley 1 (left) and ceiling pulley 2 (right), are fixed to an overhead support. A third pulley, the platform pulley, is fixed to the platform on a short post at its left edge, at a height below the two ceiling pulleys. One end of the rope is tied off at the overhead support next to ceiling pulley 1. From that fixed end the rope runs straight down and passes under the platform pulley, goes back up and over ceiling pulley 1, runs across and over ceiling pulley 2, and then comes straight down to the person's hand; the person stands on the platform and pulls this final end.

solution.approach: Trace the rope through the pulleys to count how many rope segments pull upward on the person-and-platform system, then balance that total pull against the total weight.

steps.text: Follow the rope: it is tied to the fixed ceiling support, runs down to the pulley mounted on the platform, wraps under it, runs back up to a ceiling pulley, across to a second ceiling pulley, and down to the person's hand.
steps.equation: one continuous rope, tension T throughout, since the pulleys are frictionless

steps.text: Two of the rope segments pull straight up on the pulley fixed to the platform, and the segment coming down to the person's hand pulls straight up on the person. All three segments carry the same tension T.
steps.equation: total upward pull on the person-and-platform system = T + T + T = 3T

steps.text: The platform moves up at a steady rate, so the system is in equilibrium: the total upward pull equals the total weight of the person and platform.

common_mistakes.text: Counting only the two rope segments on the platform's own pulley and missing the segment pulling up on the person's hand gives 2T = 750 N, so T = 375 N.

question.text: A ramp rises from level ground at 60°, the angle being marked at the bottom vertex where the ramp starts. At one point on the ramp's surface four forces act together: an unknown force F directed up along the ramp (parallel to the slope), an unknown force R directed perpendicular to the ramp's surface, away from it, a known force of 3 N pulling horizontally to the left, and a known force of 10 N pulling straight downward. These four forces balance exactly. Work out the values of R and F.
conditions: incline makes a 60° angle with the horizontal ground
horizontal force of 3 N, directed to the left
vertical force of 10 N, directed downward
force F acts along the incline's upward slope direction
force R acts up and to the left, steeper than F
the four forces are in equilibrium

figure.description: A ramp rises from a vertex at the lower left toward the upper right, making the marked angle of 60° with the horizontal ground. At one point on the ramp's surface four forces act: F points up the ramp, along the surface toward the upper right; R points perpendicular to the ramp's surface, away from it (up and to the left); a 3 N force points horizontally to the left; a 10 N force points vertically downward.

solution.approach: Resolve F, along the incline, and R, perpendicular to it, into horizontal and vertical parts, and balance them against the 3 N and 10 N forces.

steps.text: Write the directions of F and R measured from the horizontal ground; F runs along the incline and R stands perpendicular to it.
steps.equation: F at 60° above horizontal, R at 150° above horizontal

steps.text: Balance the horizontal forces at the point: the 3 N force pulls left, while F and R each contribute a horizontal part.
Balance the vertical forces at the point: the 10 N force pulls down, while F and R each contribute a vertical part.
Solve the two equations together for F and R.

common_mistakes.text: Matching F directly to the 3 N force and R directly to the 10 N force, without resolving their actual 60° and 150° directions, gives F = 3 N and R = 10 N.

question.text: Two blocks rest on a rough horizontal floor, each pulled by a horizontal force F applied to it. Case A: a 4 kg block is pulled by a horizontal force of 20 N; the coefficient of static friction between the block and the floor is 0.6 and the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.4. Case B: a 2 kg block is pulled by a horizontal force of 20 N; the coefficient of static friction is 0.6 and the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.4. For each case, determine the block's acceleration and the friction force acting on it.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the acceleration and friction force for the 4 kg block (Case A).

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the acceleration and friction force for the 2 kg block (Case B).

conditions: force is applied horizontally to a block on a horizontal rough floor
μs = 0.6 and μk = 0.4 in both cases
Case A block mass = 4 kg
Case B block mass = 2 kg
applied force F = 20 N in both cases

figure.description: Two separate cases, each a single block sitting on a horizontal rough floor. A horizontal force F pulls the block to the right (arrow drawn pointing right from the block). Case A: block mass 4 kg, F = 20 N, μs = 0.6, μk = 0.4. Case B: block mass 2 kg, F = 20 N, μs = 0.6, μk = 0.4.

solution.approach: In each case compare F to the maximum static friction; if F is smaller the block stays still and friction matches F, otherwise the block slides and kinetic friction applies.

steps.text: Case (a): find the maximum static friction the 4 kg block can have.
Compare this to the applied force. Since F = 20 N is less than 24 N, the block does not move, and friction equals F.
Case (b): find the maximum static friction the 2 kg block can have.
Compare this to the applied force. Since F = 20 N exceeds 12 N, the block slides, so kinetic friction acts instead.
Apply Newton's second law to the sliding block using kinetic friction.

final_answer.value: (a) block stays still: acceleration = 0, friction = 20 N. (b) block slides: acceleration = 6 m/s², friction = 8 N (kinetic).

common_mistakes.text: Assuming case (a) also slides and using kinetic friction anyway, giving f = 16 N and a = 1 m/s² instead of the correct rest state.
Using the static maximum 12 N as the friction force in case (b) instead of the kinetic value 8 N, giving a = 4 m/s² instead of 6 m/s².

question.text: In the arrangement shown, assume the table exerts negligible friction on both blocks. If m₁ = 300 g, m₂ = 200 g and the applied force F = 0.40 N, work out the pull (tension) that the cord connecting m₂ to the pulley carries, and the acceleration of m₂.
conditions: negligible friction between the blocks and the table

figure.description: A vertical wall stands at the left; both blocks rest on a smooth horizontal table to its right, m₁ nearer the wall and m₂ further right. One cord is anchored to the wall: it runs right, wraps around a movable pulley that sits between m₁ and m₂, and its other end comes back left to m₁. So the cord's two strands (wall to pulley, and pulley to m₁) are parallel and horizontal. A second cord joins the axle of that movable pulley to m₂. The force F pulls m₂ horizontally to the right, away from the wall. When m₂ moves right by x, the pulley moves right by x and m₁ moves right by 2x.

solution.approach: Use the string constraint from the movable pulley to relate m1's and m2's accelerations, then apply Newton's second law to m1, the pulley, and m2.

steps.text: The cord runs from the wall to the movable pulley and back to m1; a second cord runs from the pulley's axle to m2, which F pulls away from the wall.
steps.equation: cord 1: wall to pulley to m1 (tension T1); cord 2: pulley to m2 (tension T2)

steps.text: If m2 moves a distance x away from the wall, the pulley (tied to it by cord 2) also moves x; then, since cord 1 has two strands on the wall side, m1 must move 2x toward the pulley in the same time.
steps.why_this_step: This is the constraint relation, fixed by the string lengths, and it holds before any force equation is written.

steps.text: The movable pulley is massless, so cord 2's single pull must balance the two pulls of cord 1.
Write Newton's second law for m1 on the frictionless table.
Write Newton's second law for m2.
Substitute T2 = 2T1 = 4m1 a2 into m2's equation and solve for a2.
Use a2 to find the tension in the cord between m2 and the pulley.

final_answer.value: acceleration of m2 = 2/7 m/s² ≈ 0.29 m/s²; tension in the cord between m2 and the pulley = 12/35 N ≈ 0.34 N

common_mistakes.text: Missing the movable-pulley factor of 2 in the constraint and taking a1 = a2, which gives a2 = F/(m2 + 2m1) = 0.5 m/s², off the correct 2/7 m/s².

question.text: A man stands still relative to a horizontal conveyor belt, while the belt itself speeds up at 1 m/s². The man's mass is 65 kg, and the coefficient of static friction between his shoes and the belt surface is 0.2. Using g = 9.8 m/s², work out the net force acting on the man. Also work out the largest acceleration the belt can have while the man still stays in place relative to it, without slipping.
conditions: man stands stationary relative to a horizontal conveyor belt
belt accelerates at 1 m/s²
mass of the man = 65 kg
coefficient of static friction between shoes and belt = 0.2
g = 9.8 m/s²

figure.description: A man stands on the horizontal top surface of a conveyor belt loop; the top surface (where the man stands) moves in one direction while the belt's underside returns in the opposite direction, driven around two end rollers.

solution.approach: The man shares the belt's acceleration since he does not slip; the net force on him is mass times acceleration, supplied by static friction up to its limiting value.

steps.text: Since the man does not slip on the belt, his acceleration equals the belt's acceleration, so apply Newton's second law with the given acceleration.
This net force is supplied entirely by static friction between the man's shoes and the belt, since there is no other horizontal force on him.
The belt can accelerate the man only as long as the needed friction does not exceed the limiting static friction, so set the required force equal to the maximum static friction.
Solve for the maximum acceleration, using g = 9.8 m/s².
steps.why_this_step: Beyond this acceleration, the required friction would exceed the maximum the shoes can supply, so the man's feet slide on the belt.

final_answer.value: Net force on the man = 65 N (in the direction of the belt's acceleration); maximum acceleration = 1.96 m/s²

common_mistakes.text: Using g = 10 m/s² instead of the given 9.8 m/s² gives a maximum acceleration of 2.0 m/s².
Forgetting that the maximum friction force is μₛ m g = 0.2 × 65 × 9.8 = 127.4 N, and instead reporting the net force 65 N as the maximum friction the belt can supply.

question.text: A block of mass m lies at rest on a slope inclined at angle θ to the horizontal; the coefficient of friction between block and slope is μ. Find the magnitude of the resultant contact force (normal reaction and friction combined) that the slope applies to the block.
conditions: block is at rest on the incline
angle of incline is θ
coefficient of friction is μ

solution.approach: The block is in equilibrium with only two forces on it, so the incline's total push (normal plus friction combined) must be equal and opposite to gravity.

steps.text: The block is at rest, so only two forces act on it: gravity mg straight down, and everything the incline exerts on it — its normal push and its friction — combined into one net contact force.
Since these are the only two forces and the block is in equilibrium, the incline's net force must be equal and opposite to gravity.
This holds for any θ and μ as long as the block truly stays at rest; the normal and friction parts individually depend on θ and μ, but their combined vector always equals mg.

final_answer.value: mg

common_mistakes.text: Reporting only the along-incline friction component, mg sinθ, as the total force from the incline, forgetting to combine it with the perpendicular normal component.

question.text: A 1 kg block is pressed against a rough vertical wall by a horizontal force of 20 N. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the wall is ¼. At the same time a second horizontal force of 10 N, directed parallel to the wall's surface, acts on the block. Using g = 10 m/s², determine whether the block moves; if it does, state the direction of its motion; if it does not, work out the friction force the wall exerts on the block.
conditions: block pressed against a rough vertical wall
coefficient of static friction μₛ = ¼
second force acts parallel to the wall's surface
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Find the maximum static friction from the push force, then compare it with the resultant of gravity and the parallel force to see if the block can stay still.

steps.text: The wall's normal reaction equals the push force, so find the maximum static friction it can provide.
steps.equation: R = 20 N, f(max static) = μₛR = 0.25×20 = 5 N

steps.text: Gravity (10 N, downward) and the second 10 N force (horizontal, along the wall) both lie in the plane of the wall and are perpendicular to each other.
Find the resultant of these two forces, which is what friction would need to balance for the block to stay still.
Since 14.1 N is greater than the maximum available friction of 5 N, the block slides, moving along the direction of this resultant.
steps.equation: resultant direction is 45° from the vertical, toward the 10 N force

final_answer.value: The block moves, sliding along the resultant of gravity and the 10 N force, at 45° from the vertical.

common_mistakes.text: Adding the two 10 N forces (gravity and the applied force) directly instead of combining them as perpendicular vectors gives 20 N instead of 10√2 N ≈ 14.1 N.

Comparing only the applied 10 N force with the maximum friction of 5 N, ignoring gravity, still concludes the block moves but with the wrong direction, along the applied force alone rather than at 45°.

question.text: In the pulley arrangement shown, block M hangs from a fixed pulley, while a movable pulley, suspended from the other end of the same string, carries a 3 kg block on one side and a 2 kg block on the other. Both pulleys and strings are massless, and there is no friction anywhere. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the value of M for which block M stays at rest.
conditions: pulley and string are massless (light)
no friction anywhere

figure.description: A fixed pulley is attached to a rigid support at the top. A string runs over this fixed pulley: block M hangs from one end (the left side), and the other end connects to the axle of a second, movable pulley hanging below it. A second string runs over this movable pulley, with a 3 kg block hanging from its left end and a 2 kg block hanging from its right end.

solution.approach: Require the movable pulley to stay at rest so M stays at rest, then find the tensions consistent with the motion of the 3 kg and 2 kg blocks.

steps.text: For M to stay at rest, the movable pulley below it must also stay at rest.
With the movable pulley at rest, the 3 kg and 2 kg blocks move oppositely with the same acceleration size a, both pulled by the same string tension T₂. Write Newton's second law for each.
Solve the two equations together for a and T₂.
The massless movable pulley is pulled down by T₂ from each side, so the string above it, holding M, carries twice T₂.
For M to stay at rest, its weight must equal T₁.

final_answer.value: 4.8 kg

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting that the string above a movable pulley carries twice the tension of the string below it gives M = 2.4 kg, half the correct mass.

question.text: A rod OA hangs from a hinge fixed at point O on a vertical wall. Its lower end, point A, is tied by a weightless string to a fixed point B on a support to the right, at the same height as A. Draw a diagram of the rod alone showing every force acting on it.
conditions: rod is hinged to a wall at O
string AB is massless
B is fixed to a support at the same height as A

figure.description: On the left is a vertical wall. Point O is a hinge fixed on this wall, near the top. A rigid rod runs from O down and to the right to its other end, point A. From A, a horizontal massless string runs further right to point B, which is fixed to a second vertical support at the same height as A. The rod slopes downward from the upper-left hinge O to the lower-right end A, and the string AB is horizontal.

solution.approach: The rod is a rigid body in equilibrium under three forces: its own weight, the string tension, and the hinge reaction.

steps.text: Mark the weight of the rod, Mg, acting vertically downward at its centre of mass, the midpoint of OA.
steps.equation: Mg ↓ at the midpoint of OA

steps.text: Mark the string tension T at end A, directed along AB, pulling from A toward B, horizontally away from the wall.
Mark the hinge reaction at O. A hinge can push or pull in any direction, so it has two unknown components at O.
steps.why_this_step: A hinge is not a string, so its reaction is not restricted to one direction.

steps.text: The free body diagram of the rod carries three forces in total.
steps.equation: Mg at the midpoint, T at A along AB, and (Hₒ, Vₒ) at O

final_answer.value: Three forces act on the rod: weight Mg downward at its midpoint, string tension T at A along AB, and a hinge reaction at O with two unknown components Hₒ (horizontal) and Vₒ (vertical).

common_mistakes.text: Drawing the hinge reaction only along the rod's own length, as if it were a string; a hinge can push in any direction, not only along OA.
Leaving out the weight of the rod, treating it as massless like the string; the rod has mass and its weight acts at its midpoint.

question.text: A 1 kg block sits on a surface that is not smooth. A horizontal pull F acts on the block, as pictured. Taking the static-friction coefficient μₛ = 0.5, the kinetic-friction coefficient μₖ = 0.4, and g = 10 m/s², describe how the friction force f and the block's acceleration a behave as the pull F is raised steadily from zero.
conditions: block mass is 1 kg
the surface is rough, not smooth
coefficient of static friction μₛ = 0.5
coefficient of kinetic friction μₖ = 0.4
g = 10 m/s²
the horizontal force F is increased gradually from zero

figure.description: A block rests on a rough horizontal surface, drawn with hatching to show roughness. A horizontal arrow labeled F, pointing rightward, is applied to the block, pushing it along the surface.

solution.approach: Friction matches F exactly while F stays below its maximum static value, then drops to a fixed kinetic value once the block starts sliding.

steps.text: Find the maximum force of static friction, the largest value friction can reach before the block starts to move.
While F is less than or equal to this maximum, the block stays at rest, so friction exactly matches the applied force and there is no net force.
steps.equation: For 0 ≤ F ≤ 5 N: f = F, a = 0

steps.text: Once F goes past 5 N, the block starts to slide, and friction switches to the smaller kinetic value, which stays fixed however large F gets.
With friction now fixed at 4 N, the net force on the 1 kg block grows with F, giving its acceleration.
steps.why_this_step: Once sliding starts, friction no longer rises to match F — it stays at the constant kinetic value, so the net force F − 4 N produces the acceleration of the block.

final_answer.value: For 0 N ≤ F ≤ 5 N: f = F, a = 0. At F = 5 N the block is on the verge of sliding. For F > 5 N: f = 4 N (constant), a = (F − 4) m/s².

common_mistakes.text: Using the kinetic value f = μₖ mg = 4 N even before the block starts to slide, instead of f = F.
Assuming friction stays at its maximum static value f = μₛ mg = 5 N even after the block starts to slide, instead of dropping to 4 N.

question.text: A vertical wall and a horizontal ceiling meet at a right-angle corner. From a junction point somewhere below and to the right of that corner, string T₂ runs horizontally and attaches to the wall, while string T₁ runs up and to the right, making an angle of 60° with the horizontal, and attaches to the ceiling. A block of weight W = 4 × 9.8 N hangs straight down from the same junction point on a vertical string. Find the tensions T₁ and T₂.
conditions: string T₂ runs horizontally from the junction to the wall
string T₁ runs from the junction to the ceiling, making a 60° angle with the horizontal
a block of weight W = 4 × 9.8 N hangs vertically from the junction
the wall is vertical and the ceiling is horizontal, meeting at a right angle

figure.description: A vertical wall and a horizontal ceiling meet at a right-angle corner in the upper left of the picture. A junction point lies below and to the right of that corner. String T₂ goes from the junction straight left to the wall. String T₁ goes from the junction up and to the right to the ceiling, making a 60° angle with the horizontal. A block hangs from the junction on a vertical string directly below it, its weight W = 4 × 9.8 N pulling straight down.

solution.approach: The block's weight is held up by the vertical part of T1, and the horizontal part of T1 is balanced by T2 pulling toward the wall.

steps.text: The weight hangs from the junction, so the vertical part of T1 must support the full weight.
Solve for T1.
The horizontal part of T1 is balanced by T2 pulling toward the wall.

common_mistakes.text: Using cos60° in place of sin60° to find the vertical part of T1 gives T1 = 78.4 N instead of the correct 45.26 N.

question.text: Blocks m (5 kg) and M (10 kg) rest on the ground and are joined to each other by a cord that runs over a light pulley labelled B. A second cord runs from the axle of pulley B down to the ground, looping over a separate light pulley labelled A on its way. An upward pull F acts on the axle of pulley A, and both pulleys are taken to have zero mass. Taking g = 10 m/s², determine the accelerations of blocks m and M for each of the following pulls.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the acceleration of m and M when F = 100 N.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the acceleration of m and M when F = 300 N.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the acceleration of m and M when F = 500 N.

conditions: blocks m and M start resting on the ground
m and M are joined by a cord passing over pulley B
a separate cord joins pulley B's axle to the ground, passing over pulley A
F pulls upward on pulley A's axle
both pulleys are massless
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: Pulley A is held up only by the upward applied force F on its own axle (nothing above it holds it up). A cord passes over pulley A: one end is tied to the ground, the other end is tied to the axle of pulley B, which hangs below A. A separate cord passes over pulley B; its two ends go straight down to block m on the left and block M on the right, both resting on the ground. Both pulleys are frictionless and massless.

solution.approach: Both pulleys are massless, so each has zero net force; this fixes the m–M string's tension at F/4, and a block moves only if that exceeds its weight.

steps.text: The string over pulley A has one end tied to the floor and the other to pulley B's axle, so its tension T₁ is the same throughout. Pulley A is massless, so the upward force F balances the two downward pulls of this string.
Pulley B is massless too, held up by T₁ and pulled down by the two strands of the string that carries m and M, so the same balance applies to it.
steps.equation: T₁ = T₂ + T₂ = 2T₂  →  T₂ = T₁/2 = F/4
steps.why_this_step: Because both pulleys are massless, this tension T₂ holds at every instant no matter how the pulleys themselves move, so it can be found without tracking their motion.

steps.text: A block leaves the floor only once T₂ exceeds its own weight; compare T₂ to m g = 50 N and M g = 100 N for each value of F.
For F = 100 N, T₂ = 25 N is less than both 50 N and 100 N, so neither block lifts off and both accelerations are zero.
For F = 300 N, T₂ = 75 N exceeds m's weight (50 N) but not M's weight (100 N), so only m lifts off; apply Newton's second law to m alone.
steps.equation: T₂ − mg = m a_m  →  75 − 50 = 5 a_m  →  a_m = 5 m/s² (up), a_M = 0

steps.text: For F = 500 N, T₂ = 125 N exceeds both weights, so both blocks lift off; apply Newton's second law to each.

final_answer.value: (a) F=100 N: a_m = 0, a_M = 0 (both remain on the floor). (b) F=300 N: a_m = 5 m/s² upward, a_M = 0 (M remains on the floor). (c) F=500 N: a_m = 15 m/s² upward, a_M = 2.5 m/s² upward

common_mistakes.text: Taking the string tension on m and M as equal to F itself instead of F/4, by forgetting that each massless pulley halves the tension passed to the next string.
For F = 100 N, wrongly assuming a block must accelerate only because F is large, without checking that the actual tension T₂ = 25 N is below both weights.

question.text: A 2 kg block and a 1 kg block rest on a smooth horizontal surface, joined by a string AB of mass 1 kg, with end A attached to the 2 kg block and end B attached to the 1 kg block. A horizontal force F of 8 N pulls the 1 kg block away from the 2 kg block. Find the string tension at end A and the string tension at end B.
conditions: horizontal surface is smooth (frictionless)
string AB has mass 1 kg (not massless)
end A of string attached to the 2 kg block, end B attached to the 1 kg block
F = 8 N applied horizontally on the 1 kg block, pulling it away from the 2 kg block

figure.description: On a horizontal frictionless surface: a 2 kg block on the left connected by string end A to string end B on a 1 kg block to its right; the force F = 8 N acts horizontally on the 1 kg block, pointing further right (away from the 2 kg block).

solution.approach: Find the common acceleration of the whole three-part system, then apply Newton's second law to each end block to get the tension at each end of the string.

steps.text: Find the acceleration of the whole system: the two blocks plus the string.
Apply Newton's second law to the 2 kg block alone; only the tension at A pulls it.
Apply Newton's second law to the 1 kg block alone; F pulls it forward and the tension at B pulls it back.

final_answer.value: T_A = 4 N, T_B = 6 N

common_mistakes.text: Treating the string as massless makes the tension equal at both ends, giving a = 8/3 m/s² and one tension of 5.33 N instead of the two different values 4 N and 6 N.

question.text: A 1 kg block and a 2 kg block hang from the two ends of a light, smooth string that passes over a pulley clamped to a fixed support. The system starts from rest and is released. Exactly 1.0 s after release, the 2 kg block (the larger mass) is caught and stopped for an instant, then let go again at once. Find how much time passes after that instant before the string becomes taut again.
conditions: pulley is light, smooth, and clamped to a fixed support
string connects a 1 kg block and a 2 kg block over the pulley
system released from rest
the 2 kg (larger) block is stopped for a moment at t = 1.0 s after motion starts

figure.description: A fixed pulley is clamped at the top. A string over the pulley carries a 1 kg block hanging on one side and a 2 kg block hanging on the other side; the 2 kg block, being heavier, moves down while the 1 kg block moves up.

solution.approach: Find the common speed at 1 s, then track each block's free motion after the string goes slack until their positions again satisfy the fixed string length.

steps.text: Released from rest, the system accelerates at a = (m2 − m1)g/(m1 + m2), so at t = 1 s both blocks have the same speed v = a × 1.
When the 2 kg block is suddenly stopped, its speed drops to zero while the 1 kg block still moves upward at speed v, so the string cannot stay taut and goes slack.
steps.equation: string slack: both blocks now move under gravity alone

steps.text: After the stop, the 1 kg block rises then falls freely from initial upward speed v, and the 2 kg block falls freely from rest.
steps.equation: x1(t') = −v t' + ½g t'², x2(t') = ½g t'²  (downward positive)

steps.text: The string becomes tight again when the sum of the two downward displacements returns to zero, restoring the original taut length.
Solve for the nonzero root, using v = g/3.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the string stays taut so the 1 kg block also stops instantly gives 0 s; this misses that a string cannot push, so the block keeps moving and the string goes slack.
Treating only the 1 kg block's motion and ignoring that the 2 kg block also falls freely during the slack period gives t' = 2v/g = 2/3 s.

question.text: A block of mass m is pressed flat against the vertical side face of a much larger block of mass M (the wedge), as the figure shows; block m has no surface beneath it and stays in place purely because of friction against the wedge's face, with a friction coefficient μ between the two surfaces. A horizontal push F drives the wedge (and the smaller block moves along with it). What is the least value F can take so that the smaller block does not slide down relative to the wedge?
conditions: wedge has mass M, block has mass m
friction coefficient between wedge and block is μ
block m has no support underneath it, held up only by friction against the wedge's vertical face
block m must stay stationary relative to the wedge, i.e. move together with it

figure.description: A large block of mass M (the wedge) stands on the ground. A horizontal force F pushes it from the left, shown by an arrow. A smaller block of mass m touches the wedge's right-hand vertical face; this smaller block has nothing beneath it and is kept from falling only by friction against the wedge's surface. As F acts, the wedge and the smaller block accelerate together horizontally.

solution.approach: The block m is held up only by friction against the wedge's vertical face, and that friction comes from the normal force created by the sideways acceleration.

steps.text: Since M and m move together, they share one horizontal acceleration.
The wedge pushes block m sideways, so the normal force N between them equals m times that acceleration.
The block has nothing below it, so friction alone must support its weight; for the minimum F, friction is at its maximum value.
Put N = ma into this and solve for a.
steps.equation: μ m a = mg ⇒ a = g/μ
steps.why_this_step: This is the smallest sideways acceleration at which the available friction is exactly enough to hold the block up.

steps.text: Put a = g/μ into the system equation and solve for F.

final_answer.value: F = (M+m) g / μ

common_mistakes.text: Leaving block m's own mass out of the accelerating system and writing F = M g / μ instead of (M+m) g / μ.

question.text: Two setups are shown below. In each, someone must lift a block that is currently sitting on the ground up to a height h using a string that passes over one or more pulleys fixed to an overhead support. Both the pulleys and the strings are light (massless) and frictionless. In which setup must the person pull with a greater force, if any?
conditions: pulleys and strings are light (massless)
block starts resting on the ground and is raised to height h
setup (i) has one pulley fixed to an overhead bracket
setup (ii) has two pulleys, a larger one and a smaller one, both fixed to the same overhead bracket and neither attached to the block

figure.description: Setup (i): a block rests on the ground; a string tied to the block goes straight up, passes over a single pulley fixed to an overhead bracket, and comes down to a person standing beside the block, who pulls the free end. Setup (ii): the same overhead bracket carries one fixed pulley. A second pulley is mounted on a short post fixed to the top of the block, so it moves with the block. The string is tied to the bracket, runs down and passes under the block's pulley, goes back up over the fixed pulley, and comes down to the person, who pulls the free end. In both setups the person pulls the string to raise the block through the same height h.

solution.approach: Compare the two setups by the tension each strand of string must carry, since the person's pulling force always equals that tension.

steps.text: In Setup (i), the string runs from the block, over one fixed pulley, straight to the person. The block hangs from a single strand, so that one strand alone must support the block's full weight.

In Setup (ii), the string is tied to the bracket, goes down and under the block's own pulley, then back up over the fixed pulley and down to the person. The block's pulley is now held up by two strands of the same string.
The string and both pulleys are light and frictionless, so the tension is the same all along the string. The two strands under the block's pulley share its weight equally.
Solve for the tension in each strand of Setup (ii).
The person's pulling force equals the tension in the strand they hold, so Setup (i) needs Mg while Setup (ii) needs only Mg/2, half as much.
The person exerts more force in Setup (i), so the correct choice is (a): Setup (i).

final_answer.value: (a) Setup (i) — it needs Mg, twice the Mg/2 needed in Setup (ii).

common_mistakes.text: Thinking the extra pulley in Setup (ii) adds effort and picking Setup (ii) as needing more force reverses the mechanical advantage: two supporting strands there mean less force, not more.
Assuming the same weight always needs the same pulling force, no matter how many strands hold it, misses that Setup (ii) splits the load across two strands, so same in both is wrong.

question.text: A round cylinder of weight W rests inside a V-shaped groove, touching both of the groove's slanted walls. Sketch the free-body diagram for the cylinder.
conditions: cylinder rests inside a V-shaped groove
cylinder touches both slanted walls of the groove

figure.description: A V-shaped groove made of two walls slanting inward like a wedge, with a circular cylinder resting inside it and touching both slanted walls.

solution.approach: List every force that touches the cylinder: its weight, and one normal reaction from each wall of the groove.

steps.text: The cylinder has weight W. This acts at its centre, pointing straight down.
The cylinder touches two slanted walls. Each wall pushes on the cylinder with a normal reaction, perpendicular to that wall's surface at the point of contact.
Because the cylinder is circular, the line of each normal reaction passes through the cylinder's centre, so N₁, N₂ and W all act through the same point.
steps.why_this_step: A normal force on a circular surface always points along the radius, so it passes through the centre.

steps.text: The free body diagram of the cylinder shows three forces meeting at its centre: W straight down, N₁ perpendicular to the first wall pointing toward the centre, and N₂ perpendicular to the second wall pointing toward the centre. For the cylinder to be in equilibrium, N₁ + N₂ balances W.

final_answer.value: three concurrent forces act on the cylinder: weight W downward at its centre, normal reaction N₁ from wall 1 (perpendicular to wall 1, directed toward the centre), and normal reaction N₂ from wall 2 (perpendicular to wall 2, directed toward the centre)

common_mistakes.text: Drawing only one normal reaction, missing that the cylinder touches both walls of the groove.
Drawing a normal reaction that is not perpendicular to the wall it comes from.

question.text: A three-pulley chain — one pulley fixed to the ceiling, with two lighter pulleys hanging one below the other in series, strung as the figure describes — carries block 1 (mass 1 kg) at the base and block 2 (mass 2 kg) hanging from the lowest pulley's string. The string lengths tie the two accelerations together as a₂ = −7a₁ (block 2 accelerates seven times as fast as block 1, in the opposite sense). Take g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out how fast each block accelerates.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out the pulling force (tension) carried by each string segment.

conditions: the two lower (movable) pulleys are massless, so the net force on each of them is zero
the shortest string carries tension T; the other two strings carry 2T and 4T
block 1 accelerates upward with a, and block 2 accelerates downward with 7a (the constraint relation from the earlier example)
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A large pulley P₁ is fixed to the ceiling. Below it hang two smaller movable pulleys, P₂ (medium) and P₃ (small), one below the other, and at the bottom sits block 1 (a wide base block); block 2 hangs beside the chain. Three light strings are used. String S₁ passes over P₁: its left end goes straight down to block 1 and its right end goes straight down to the axle of P₂. String S₂ passes over P₂: its left end goes straight down to block 1 and its right end goes straight down to the axle of P₃. String S₃ passes over P₃: its left end goes straight down to block 1 and its right end hangs straight down to block 2. So three string ends are tied to block 1 (one from each pulley) and block 2 hangs from S₃ only. All strings are vertical; pulleys and strings are massless and frictionless. Block 1 has mass 1 kg and block 2 has mass 2 kg. If the tension in S₃ is T, the tensions in S₂ and S₁ are 2T and 4T.

solution.approach: Use the given string constraint a₂ = −7a₁ with Newton's second law on block 1 (pulled up by 4T+2T+T = 7T) and on block 2 (pulled up by T).

steps.text: Block 1 (1 kg) is pulled up by three string ends of tension 4T, 2T and T, and pulled down by its own weight, while it accelerates upward with a.
Block 2 (2 kg) is pulled up by tension T and down by its own weight, while it accelerates downward with 7a, from the given string constraint a₂ = −7a₁.
From the first equation, T = (10+a)/7. Put this into the second equation.
Multiply out and collect terms in a.
Solve for a, then find T, 2T and 4T.
steps.why_this_step: T follows from putting a back into either block's equation, and 2T, 4T are twice and four times that value.

final_answer.value: Block 1: a₁ = 1.31 m/s² upward. Block 2: a₂ = 7a₁ = 9.19 m/s² downward. T = 1.62 N, 2T = 3.23 N, 4T = 6.46 N.

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the movable-pulley chain and solving it as a plain two-mass pulley, giving a = (m₂−m₁)g/(m₁+m₂) = 3.33 m/s².

question.text: A ball weighing 100 N sits at rest on a rough slope tilted 30° from the horizontal; a horizontal cord, running from a point A on the ball to a fixed point B on the slope, keeps the ball from sliding down. Work out the following three quantities.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the tension in the cord.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the friction force acting on the ball.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the normal reaction the slope exerts on the ball.

conditions: ball's weight is 100 N
incline angle is 30° from horizontal
incline surface is rough
a horizontal cord AB (A on the ball, B fixed on the incline) holds the ball stationary

figure.description: An inclined surface rises from the ground at an angle of 30°. A ball rests on this sloped surface, its centre marked C. A horizontal cord runs from point A, the topmost point of the ball (directly above its centre C), to point B, a fixed point on the incline surface farther up the slope at the same height as A, so the cord itself is horizontal and tangent to the ball at A.

solution.approach: Weight and normal reaction pass through the sphere's centre, so balancing moments there for the tension and friction gives one relation, and force balance gives the rest.

steps.text: The string AB is horizontal and tied where it touches the sphere without cutting into it, so A is the topmost point of the sphere; there the radius to A is vertical, at height r above the centre C.
steps.equation: moment arm of T about C = r

steps.text: Friction f acts at the contact point with the incline, tangent to the sphere there, which is also always at a perpendicular distance r from the centre.
steps.equation: moment arm of f about C = r

steps.text: The weight acts at the centre and the normal reaction acts along the radius through the contact point, so both pass through C and add no moment; balancing the moments of T and f about C then requires them to be equal.
steps.why_this_step: With only T and f having a nonzero moment arm about the centre, and the sphere in equilibrium, their moments must cancel, which — since both arms equal r — makes the two forces equal.

steps.text: Resolve all forces horizontally and vertically: weight w down, normal reaction N perpendicular to the 30° incline, friction f up the incline, tension T horizontal.
steps.equation: horizontal: T − N sin30° + f cos30° = 0;  vertical: N cos30° + f sin30° = w

steps.text: Substitute f = T into both equations and solve.
steps.equation: T(1+cos30°) = N sin30°;  N cos30° + T sin30° = w

steps.text: Solve the two equations for T and N.

final_answer.value: (a) tension T = 100(2−√3) N ≈ 26.8 N. (b) friction f = 100(2−√3) N ≈ 26.8 N, acting up the incline. (c) normal reaction N = 100 N

common_mistakes.text: Treating the sphere as frictionless and solving only T − N sin30° = 0 and N cos30° = w gives the wrong N ≈ 115.5 N and T ≈ 57.7 N, missing the incline's friction.
Writing only the two force-balance equations and stopping, because T, f and N are three unknowns; the third equation is the moment balance about the centre, which gives f = T.

question.text: Assertion: A block sits motionless on a rough horizontal floor. Two forces, F₁ (pressing straight down on top of the block) and F₂ (pushing horizontally against the block), act on it at the same time. Raising the value of either force — F₁ or F₂ — will make the friction force on the block larger. Reason: Increasing F₁ makes the ground's normal reaction on the block larger.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: block is at rest
ground is rough
F₁ acts vertically downward on top of the block
F₂ acts horizontally, pushing the block

figure.description: The block sits on a horizontal rough floor, drawn as a straight ground line. F₁ is drawn as an arrow pointing straight down onto the top of the block. F₂ is drawn as an arrow pointing horizontally to the right, pushing into the block from its left side.

solution.approach: The block stays at rest, so friction must equal the horizontal push F₂ alone; check separately whether raising F₁ or raising F₂ changes that value.

steps.text: The block stays at rest, so along the ground the friction force must exactly balance the horizontal push F₂.
If F₂ increases while F₁ stays fixed, the friction needed for equilibrium increases too, since it must still equal F₂.
If F₁ increases while F₂ stays fixed, the horizontal force to balance is still F₂, so the actual friction in use does not change.

Increasing F₁ only raises the normal reaction and the maximum friction available, μN, not the friction actually being used — so the Assertion's claim that either force increases friction fails for F₁ alone, making the Assertion false.
Taken by itself, the Reason is a true statement: pressing down harder with F₁ does raise the normal reaction from the ground.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming a larger normal reaction by itself always means larger actual friction, missing that it only raises the friction limit, and picking both statements true with the Reason explaining it.

question.text: A 4 kg block sits above a 2 kg block, the two joined by a vertical light string that cannot stretch. An upward pull of F = 120 N is applied at the top of the 4 kg block, lifting both blocks straight up together. Take g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out the acceleration produced in the blocks.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out the pulling force (tension) carried by the string.

conditions: blocks connected by a light, inextensible string
the string and blocks move vertically upward together
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: The 4 kg block is on top; a 2 kg block hangs directly beneath it, joined by a vertical light inextensible string. A force F = 120 N pulls straight upward on the top (4 kg) block, lifting the whole two-block system vertically.

solution.approach: Treat both blocks as one system to find the acceleration, then apply Newton's second law to the 2 kg block alone to find the tension.

steps.text: For the whole system, the pulling force acts up and the total weight acts down.
Put in the numbers: total mass 6 kg, weight 60 N, force 120 N.
Solve for the acceleration.
For the 2 kg block alone, the string tension acts up and its own weight acts down.
Put in m₂ = 2 kg, g = 10 m/s², a = 10 m/s² and solve.
steps.why_this_step: The 2 kg block is pulled only by the string above it, so its own equation gives the tension directly.

final_answer.value: (a) a = 10 m/s², (b) T = 40 N

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the weight of the blocks and taking a = F/(m₁+m₂) = 120/6 = 20 m/s².
Splitting the 120 N force equally between the two blocks and taking T = F/2 = 60 N.

question.text: A string passes over a pulley fixed to a ceiling support. One end of this string holds a 4 kg block. The other end holds a 3 kg block, and a second string ties a 1 kg block below that 3 kg block. Work out the ratio of the tension in the string holding the 4 kg block to the tension in the string holding the 1 kg block.
conditions: pulley is fixed to the ceiling
4 kg block hangs from one end of the string over the pulley
3 kg block hangs from the other end of the string over the pulley
1 kg block hangs below the 3 kg block, tied to it by a second string

figure.description: A pulley hangs fixed from a ceiling support. A string runs over this pulley: its left end carries a 4 kg block, hanging straight down. Its right end carries a 3 kg block, also hanging straight down. A separate string then connects downward from the 3 kg block to a 1 kg block beneath it.

solution.approach: Since the total mass on each side of the pulley is equal, the system stays at rest, and each string tension equals the weight it directly supports.

steps.text: Add the masses on each side of the fixed pulley.
steps.equation: left side = 4 kg, right side = 3+1 = 4 kg

steps.text: Equal masses on each side mean the system has zero acceleration.
steps.why_this_step: With no acceleration, each string tension can be found from plain equilibrium instead of a full Atwood-machine equation.

steps.text: The tension in the string over the pulley, attached to the 4 kg block, supports the whole 4 kg block in equilibrium.
The tension in the string attached to the 1 kg block supports only the 1 kg block, since it hangs below the 3 kg block.
Take the ratio of the two tensions.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the system accelerates because the two sides look different, missing that 3 kg + 1 kg on the right equals the 4 kg on the left.
Taking the tension in the string attached to the 1 kg block as the same main tension over the pulley, instead of the smaller tension in the separate lower string.

question.text: A 2 kg block rests on top of a 1 kg block, and the 1 kg block rests on a smooth (frictionless) horizontal surface. The friction coefficient between the two blocks is μ = 0.6. The 2 kg block is given an initial velocity of 3 m/s to the right, while the 1 kg block is given an initial velocity of 18 m/s to the left. Assume the lower block is long enough that the upper block never slides off it. Taking g = 10 m/s²,

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out the time at which the relative sliding between the two blocks stops.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out the common velocity the two blocks share at that instant.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Work out how far the 1 kg block and the 2 kg block each travel up to that instant.

conditions: 2 kg block on top of a 1 kg block
1 kg block rests on a smooth horizontal surface
μ = 0.6 between the two blocks
initial velocity of the 2 kg block = 3 m/s to the right
