initial velocity of the 1 kg block = 18 m/s to the left
lower block assumed long enough that the upper block does not fall off
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A 2 kg block sits on top of a 1 kg block; the 1 kg block rests on a smooth horizontal floor. The 2 kg (upper) block moves at 3 m/s to the right, and the 1 kg (lower) block moves at 18 m/s to the left.

solution.approach: Find the kinetic friction between the blocks from the top block's weight, get each block's constant acceleration, then find when their velocities become equal.

steps.text: The friction between the blocks depends on the normal force at their interface, which equals the weight of the top block alone.
The top block moves right relative to the bottom block, so friction acts left on the top block and right on the bottom block, by Newton's third law.
Write each block's velocity as a function of time and set them equal to find when relative motion stops.
Solve for the time and the common velocity.
Use the same time in each block's displacement equation to find how far each one moved.

final_answer.value: (a) t = 7/6 s ≈ 1.17 s; (b) common velocity = 4 m/s, in the direction the 1 kg block first moved; (c) the 2 kg block displaces 7/12 m ≈ 0.58 m and the 1 kg block displaces 77/6 m ≈ 12.83 m, both in the direction the 1 kg block first moved

common_mistakes.text: Using the combined weight of both blocks for friction instead of only the top block's weight gives friction = 18 N and a wrong stopping time of 7/9 s ≈ 0.78 s.
Taking the bottom block's initial speed as +18 m/s, the same direction as the top block, instead of −18 m/s, gives a negative, impossible time of −5/6 s.

question.text: A ladder of length 4 m and mass 25 kg leans with its top end touching a smooth (frictionless) wall and its bottom end resting on rough ground, making an angle of 60° with the horizontal ground. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the smallest value the coefficient of friction between the ladder and the ground must have so the ladder does not slip.
conditions: ladder length = 4 m
ladder mass = 25 kg
upper end rests against a smooth (frictionless) wall
lower end rests on rough ground
ladder inclined at 60° to the horizontal
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Take torque about the foot of the ladder to find the wall's push, then use horizontal equilibrium to find the friction needed to balance it.

steps.text: The wall is smooth, so it pushes the ladder horizontally with a normal force N. The ground gives a vertical normal force equal to the ladder's weight and a horizontal friction force f.
Take torques about the foot of the ladder. The weight acts at the midpoint and the wall's push acts at the top.
Solve for the wall's push N.
Horizontal equilibrium requires the ground friction to equal the wall's push, so the minimum coefficient of friction is this ratio to the weight.
Substitute θ = 60° and compute.

common_mistakes.text: Using the full length L instead of L/2 as the moment arm of the weight gives μ = 1/tanθ = 0.58, double the correct value.
Using sinθ in place of tanθ in the final ratio gives μ = 1/(2 sin60°) = 0.58.

question.text: Picture two vertical walls facing each other with an open gap between them; inside that gap, ball A rests on the floor of the gap and leans against the left-hand wall, while a smaller ball B sits on top of ball A and leans against the right-hand wall. There is no friction anywhere in this arrangement. Sketch a separate free-body diagram for each ball.
conditions: ball A rests on the floor and touches the left wall
ball B rests on top of ball A and touches the right wall
no friction anywhere (walls, floor, or between the balls)

figure.description: Two vertical walls face each other with a gap between them. Inside the gap, the larger ball, A, sits on the floor of the gap and touches the left wall. A smaller ball, B, rests on top of ball A and touches the right wall.

solution.approach: List each contact of the two spheres and draw one normal force per contact, since friction is absent everywhere; the sphere-sphere force acts along the line joining their centres.

steps.text: Sphere A touches the ground, the left wall, and sphere B, and also has its own weight.
steps.equation: sphere A: weight W_A (down, at centre) + N_ground (up) + N_wall_left (horizontal, away from the left wall) + N_B (from sphere B, along the line joining the two centres)

steps.text: Sphere B does not touch the ground, so it only touches the right wall and sphere A, besides its own weight.
steps.equation: sphere B: weight W_B (down, at centre) + N_wall_right (horizontal, away from the right wall) + N_A (reaction to N_B, along the same centre-to-centre line, pushing B away from A)
steps.why_this_step: With no friction anywhere, every contact force must be perpendicular to the two touching surfaces, and for two spheres that direction is the line joining their centres.

final_answer.value: Sphere A: its weight, the ground's normal reaction, the left wall's normal reaction, and sphere B's normal reaction along the centre-to-centre line. Sphere B: its weight, the right wall's normal reaction, and sphere A's normal reaction along the same centre-to-centre line (equal and opposite to the force A feels from B); sphere B has no ground contact.

common_mistakes.text: Drawing sphere B's normal reaction from A as purely vertical or horizontal instead of along the line joining the two centres.
Giving sphere B a ground contact force, missing that only sphere A touches the ground in the figure.

question.text: In the pulley system pictured (block 1 hanging from the fixed pulley, blocks 2 and 3 from the two ends of the string over the movable pulley), at one instant blocks 1 and 2 are each moving upward at a speed of 1 m/s. Determine the velocity of block 3 at this same instant.
conditions: fixed pulley at top with block 1 hanging from it
movable pulley hangs below the fixed pulley, with blocks 2 and 3 hanging from its two ends
block 1 moves upward at 1 m/s at the given instant
block 2 moves upward at 1 m/s at the given instant

figure.description: A fixed pulley is mounted at the top, attached to a rigid support. A string runs over this fixed pulley: block 1 hangs from one end (the left side), and the other end connects to the axle of a second, movable pulley that hangs below it. A second string runs over this movable pulley, with block 2 hanging from its left end and block 3 hanging from its right end.

solution.approach: Use the string-length constraint twice, once at the fixed pulley and once at the movable pulley, to relate the three velocities.

steps.text: Take downward as positive for every velocity. Block 1 moves upward at 1 m/s, so its downward velocity is −1 m/s.
The fixed-pulley string constraint makes the movable pulley's downward velocity the negative of block 1's downward velocity.

Block 2 moves upward at 1 m/s, so its downward velocity is −1 m/s. The movable-pulley constraint makes the sum of the downward velocities of blocks 2 and 3 equal to twice the pulley's downward velocity.
Substitute the known values and solve for v₃.

final_answer.value: 3 m/s downward

common_mistakes.text: Taking the movable pulley's downward velocity equal to block 1's downward velocity, instead of its negative, gives v₃ = 1 m/s upward instead of 3 m/s downward.

question.text: Three blocks A, B and C, each of mass 2 kg, are connected by strings over a fixed frictionless pulley. Block A hangs alone from one side of the pulley. On the other side, block B hangs directly from the string over the pulley, and block C hangs below B, joined to B by a separate string. What is the tension in the string that connects B and C?
conditions: pulley is fixed and frictionless
A hangs alone on one side
B and C hang in series (B above C) on the other side, joined by a separate string
each block has mass 2 kg

figure.description: A fixed frictionless pulley is mounted on a ceiling. A string passes over the pulley. On the left side, block A (2 kg) hangs alone from the string. On the right side, block B (2 kg) hangs from the string over the pulley, and block C (2 kg) hangs below B, connected to B by its own separate string.

solution.approach: Find the system's acceleration from the unequal masses on each side, then apply Newton's second law to block C alone to get the tension between B and C.

steps.text: One side of the pulley carries A alone (2 kg); the other carries B and C together (2+2 = 4 kg).
Find the common acceleration from the excess weight on the heavier side, divided by the total mass.
Isolate block C alone: its own weight acts down, and the tension in the string above it (to B) acts up, while it accelerates downward with the system.
Solve for T using m_C = 2 kg.
This rounds to the printed option.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the system stays in equilibrium since 'three equal weights' sounds balanced, ignoring that four kilograms pull against two, giving T = m_C g = 2(9.8) = 19.6 N.
Correctly finding the system's acceleration a ≈ 3.27 m/s² but stopping there and reporting this number itself as the tension, skipping Newton's second law for block C alone.

question.text: A 5 m ladder leans against a frictionless (smooth) vertical wall. Call the corner where wall meets ground O, the ladder's top end touching the wall A, and its bottom end resting on the ground B, with AO = 4 m (the vertical rise) and OB = 3 m (the horizontal base). The ground has friction coefficient μ with the ladder. What is the least value μ can have so the ladder does not slip?
conditions: wall is smooth (frictionless)
ground has friction coefficient μ with the ladder
ladder length AB = 5 m
vertical rise AO = 4 m
horizontal base OB = 3 m

figure.description: A right-angle triangle formed by a vertical wall and the horizontal ground meeting at point O. The ladder AB is the sloping side, running from point A (up on the wall) down to point B (on the ground). AB = 5 m, AO (the vertical rise from O up to A) = 4 m, OB (the horizontal run from O out to B) = 3 m.

solution.approach: Balance forces on the ladder and take torques about its foot to find the wall's push, which must equal the floor's friction, then compare that to the ladder's weight.

steps.text: The wall is smooth, so it can only push the ladder sideways, away from the wall, at the top point A. The floor pushes up on the ladder at its foot B and also supplies friction, sideways, to stop the foot from sliding out.
steps.equation: wall force: horizontal N_w at A; floor forces: vertical N_g and horizontal friction f at B

steps.text: Balance forces vertically and horizontally. Vertically, the floor alone carries the ladder's weight. Horizontally, the wall's push must be matched by friction at the floor.
steps.equation: N_g = W (weight of ladder), f = N_w

steps.text: Take torques about the foot B, using the ladder's weight acting at its midpoint and the wall's push acting at the top A, using the given distances AO = 4 m and OB = 3 m.

Since friction must supply this same push, and the maximum friction available is μ times the floor's normal force, the smallest coefficient of friction that keeps the ladder from slipping is this ratio.

common_mistakes.text: Swapping the vertical height and horizontal base of the ladder's foot in the torque equation, using 3 m as the height and 4 m as the base, gives μ_min = 2/3.

question.text: A uniform rod AB has weight w. Its lower end A sits on rough, horizontal ground, while its upper end B leans on a smooth, vertical wall. In its equilibrium position, the rod is tilted at 30° to the ground. Find:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: The friction force at A.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: The normal reaction at A.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: The normal reaction at B.

conditions: rod AB is uniform, of weight w
end A rests on rough horizontal ground
end B leans on a smooth vertical wall
rod is in equilibrium, tilted at 30° to the ground

figure.description: A rod AB with end A resting on horizontal ground (along the X-axis) and end B leaning against a vertical wall (along the Y-axis), the ground and wall meeting at corner O. The rod makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal ground at A.

solution.approach: Balance vertical forces for the normal reaction at A, then take moments about A to find the wall's push, then balance horizontal forces for friction.

steps.text: The wall is smooth, so it can only push the rod horizontally at B. The ground is rough, so at A it pushes up (normal reaction N_A) and can resist sliding (friction f_A).
steps.equation: forces: N_A ↑, f_A →, N_B ← or →, w ↓ at the midpoint

steps.text: The only vertical forces are N_A (up) and the weight w (down), so they balance directly.
Take moments about A. Let the rod have length L. A is at (L cos30°, 0) and B is at (0, L sin30°); the weight acts at the midpoint. Setting the sum of moments to zero and solving for N_B.
The only horizontal forces are friction f_A and the wall's push N_B, so they balance.
steps.why_this_step: With only two horizontal forces on the rod, one must equal the other for equilibrium.

final_answer.value: (a) friction at A = 0.87w, (b) normal reaction at A = w, (c) normal reaction at B = 0.87w

common_mistakes.text: Taking the weight's moment arm as the full rod length L instead of the half-length to the midpoint, which doubles the answer for the wall's push.
Assuming friction is zero because the rod looks like it is only leaning, forgetting the ground must supply a horizontal force to balance the wall's push.

question.text: A 200 kg block rests on a frictionless horizontal floor. A light rope and a frictionless pulley are arranged as in the figure so that the block can be pulled toward a wall. What horizontal force F must be applied to the rope's free end so that the block accelerates at 1 m/s²?
conditions: floor is frictionless
pulley is frictionless and fixed to the wall
rope pulled horizontally toward the wall
block accelerates toward the pulley at 1 m/s²

figure.description: A vertical wall stands at the left; the 200 kg block sits on the floor to the right of it. A light pulley is joined to the block's left face by a short rigid link at the pulley's axle, so the pulley moves with the block. One end of the rope is anchored to the wall near floor level; the rope runs horizontally to the right, passes under and around the pulley, and its free end comes back off the top of the pulley running horizontally to the LEFT, toward the wall. The force F pulls this free end to the left, parallel to the anchored strand. The block accelerates to the left at 1 m/s².

solution.approach: Relate the rope's free end to the block through the pulley fixed to the block, then apply Newton's second law to the block using both rope tensions.

steps.text: Let x be the distance of the block, and the pulley fixed to it, from the wall, decreasing as the block moves toward the wall. The rope's wall-anchored strand has this same length x.

Since the pulley is fixed to the block, both strands, the one to the wall and the one to the free end, shorten together as the block moves; the free end must be pulled in twice as fast as the block moves.
The rope is light and the pulley is frictionless, so the tension is the same, T, all along the rope, and it equals the force F the free end is pulled with.
Both strands pull the pulley, and so the block, toward the wall with tension T each. Apply Newton's second law to the block.
Substitute T = F and solve for F.
Put in the numbers.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the pulley as if only one strand pulls the block and writing F = Ma directly, missing the second strand's contribution, gives 200 N.
Doubling instead of halving, writing F = 2Ma from the two strands instead of 2F = Ma, gives 400 N.

question.text: A block of mass m rests on an inclined plane. For the surface of this incline, the angle of repose is 45°. Work out the friction force on the block, the net force acting on it, and its acceleration, when the incline's angle θ is set to (a) 30°, (b) 45°, and (c) 60°.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the friction force, the net force, and the acceleration of the block when θ = 30°.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the friction force, the net force, and the acceleration of the block when θ = 45°.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the friction force, the net force, and the acceleration of the block when θ = 60°.

conditions: block of mass m placed on an inclined plane
angle of repose of the incline surface = 45°
incline angle θ is evaluated separately at 30°, 45°, 60°

figure.description: A block of mass m sits on the sloped surface of an inclined plane that rises from a horizontal base; the incline makes an angle θ with the horizontal, measured at the base of the slope. The angle of repose of this surface is 45°, and θ is then set to 30°, 45°, and 60° in turn.

solution.approach: Compare each angle to the 45° angle of repose, where μ = tan45° = 1, to decide if the block stays still or slides, then apply the matching friction law.

steps.text: The angle of repose is 45°, so the coefficient of friction equals tan45°.
For θ = 30°, which is less than the angle of repose, the block stays at rest: static friction exactly balances the weight component along the incline.
steps.equation: friction = mg sin30° = 0.5mg up the incline; net force = 0; a = 0

steps.text: For θ = 45°, equal to the angle of repose, the block is on the verge of sliding but still stays at rest.
steps.equation: friction = mg sin45° = mg/√2 ≈ 0.707mg up the incline; net force = 0; a = 0

steps.text: For θ = 60°, greater than the angle of repose, the block slides down, so kinetic friction now acts up the incline.
steps.equation: friction = μmg cos60° = 0.5mg up the incline

steps.text: Find the net force and acceleration for θ = 60° from the weight component along the incline minus the kinetic friction.
steps.equation: net force = mg sin60° − 0.5mg = mg(√3−1)/2 ≈ 0.366mg down the incline; a = g(√3−1)/2 ≈ 3.66 m/s² down the incline (using g = 10 m/s²)

final_answer.value: (a) θ=30°: friction = 0.5mg up the incline, net force = 0, a = 0. (b) θ=45°: friction ≈ 0.707mg up the incline, net force = 0, a = 0. (c) θ=60°: friction = 0.5mg up the incline, net force ≈ 0.366mg down the incline, a ≈ 3.66 m/s² down the incline

common_mistakes.text: Applying kinetic friction at θ = 30°, below the angle of repose, gives a negative net force of size 0.366mg (3.66 m/s² with g = 10), showing the block cannot actually be sliding there.

question.text: Two pulleys are fixed to the ceiling, one on the left and one on the right. A spring balance is connected horizontally between two strings. The left string goes from one end of the spring balance, over the left pulley, and down to a hanging block of mass 5 kg. The right string goes from the other end of the spring balance, over the right pulley, and down to a hanging block of mass 10 kg. What does the spring balance read?
conditions: both pulleys are fixed to the ceiling
spring balance is connected horizontally between the two strings
left string carries a 5 kg block
right string carries a 10 kg block

figure.description: Two pulleys are fixed to the ceiling, one on the left and one on the right, spaced apart. A spring balance connects the two strings horizontally between the pulleys. The left string passes over the left pulley and hangs down to a 5 kg block. The right string passes over the right pulley and hangs down to a 10 kg block.

solution.approach: Recognize the spring balance sits inline with one continuous string over two pulleys joining unequal masses, so it reads the standard Atwood tension, not either weight alone.

steps.text: One continuous string runs from the 5 kg mass, over the left pulley, through the spring balance, over the right pulley, to the 10 kg mass, so the balance reads the tension that string carries throughout.
The pulleys only redirect the string; since 10 kg ≠ 5 kg the masses are free to accelerate, so this is an Atwood pair and the reading is the standard Atwood tension.
Substitute m₁ = 5 kg, m₂ = 10 kg, g = 10 m/s² (the value that makes the given options come out as round numbers).
Compare this with the printed options 50 N, 100 N and 150 N — it matches none of them.

final_answer.value: None of the above

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the balance directly reads the heavier hanging weight, 10 kg × 10 m/s² = 100 N, without accounting for the system's acceleration.
Assuming the balance reads the combined weight of both masses as if the system were static, (5+10) kg × 10 m/s² = 150 N.

question.text: The diagonal string shown in the figure below carries a tension of 60 N.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out the size of the horizontal forces F₁ and F₂ needed to keep the whole system fixed in the position drawn.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out the weight of the block that hangs from the system.

conditions: tension in the diagonal string = 60 N
diagonal string makes a 45° angle with the horizontal
F₁ acts horizontally at the upper point A
F₂ acts horizontally at the lower point B
block hangs vertically below point B
system is held fixed (in equilibrium)

figure.description: A horizontal ceiling runs along the top. A short vertical link hangs from the ceiling down to point A. At A, force F₁ points horizontally to the left. From A, a diagonal string runs down and to the right to point B, making a 45° angle with the horizontal (measured at A between a horizontal reference line and the diagonal string). At B, force F₂ points horizontally to the right, and directly below B a block of weight W hangs on a vertical string.

solution.approach: At each end of the diagonal string, the horizontal force balances the string's horizontal part, and at B the string's vertical part supports the hanging weight.

steps.text: At point A, the diagonal string pulls toward B; F1 balances the horizontal part of this pull.
At point B, the diagonal string pulls toward A; F2 balances the horizontal part of this pull.
The weight hanging from B is supported by the vertical part of the string's tension.

common_mistakes.text: Taking F1 and F2 equal to the full string tension of 60 N, without resolving the 45° angle, ignores that only part of the tension acts horizontally.

question.text: A man of mass m stands on a platform that also has mass m. He holds two ropes, each of which passes over a pulley fixed to the ceiling and then attaches to the platform he is standing on, as shown in the figure. He pulls down on each rope with a force equal to half of his own weight. What is the resulting upward acceleration of the man (and platform)?
conditions: man's mass = m
platform's mass = m (equal to the man's mass)
man pulls on each of two ropes with a force equal to half his own weight
each rope passes over a fixed pulley and its other end is attached to the platform

figure.description: A rigid bar fixed to the ceiling holds four pulleys in a row. The man stands in the middle of a platform, both hands raised overhead to hold the two innermost ropes. On each side, one rope starts tied to an edge of the platform, runs upward and passes over the outer pulley on that side, runs horizontally along the ceiling to the neighboring inner pulley, then runs back down to the man's hand on that side. So each of the man's two hands pulls one continuous rope whose other end is fixed to the platform he stands on.

solution.approach: Each rope carries one tension throughout its length; add the upward pull on the platform and on the man's hands, then compare it to their total weight.

steps.text: Each rope has one tension throughout, equal to the force the man pulls with, which is half his weight.
Two ropes each pull up on the platform at one end and up on the man's hands at the other end, giving four upward pulls of size T in total.
The total weight of the man and the platform together is also 2mg.
The upward pull equals the total weight, so the net force, and the acceleration, is zero.

final_answer.value: zero

common_mistakes.text: Counting all four upward pulls, 2mg, but comparing them to the man's own weight mg alone, forgetting the platform's mass, gives a net force mg on mass m and an acceleration of g.

question.text: Two balls, A and B, are the same size and are released from the same point at the same time, falling under gravity. Ball A has a greater mass than ball B. The air resistance on each ball is equal. Which ball lands first, if either?

options.1: both the balls reach the ground simultaneously

conditions: A and B are the same size
mass of A is greater than mass of B
air resistance on A equals air resistance on B
both dropped from the same point

solution.approach: Write Newton's second law for each ball with the same air-resistance force but different mass, and compare their net downward accelerations.

steps.text: Both balls feel the same downward gravity and the same upward air-resistance force, since they are the same size.
steps.equation: m_A a_A = m_A g − F_air, m_B a_B = m_B g − F_air

steps.text: Solve each equation for the net downward acceleration.
steps.equation: a_A = g − F_air/m_A, a_B = g − F_air/m_B

steps.text: Since the mass of A is greater, the same F_air divided by the larger mass subtracts less from g.
The heavier ball A has the larger net downward acceleration, so starting together from the same point it falls faster and reaches the ground first.

final_answer.value: the ball A reaches earlier

common_mistakes.text: Applying the no-air rule that all falling bodies land together regardless of mass, missing that the given equal air-resistance force actually slows the lighter ball more.

question.text: A conveyor belt runs at a steady 6 m/s. A small block, initially at rest, is placed gently onto the moving belt. The friction coefficient between block and belt is μ = 0.3. Taking g = 10 m/s², work out:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: how much time passes before the block and the belt move at the same speed (no more sliding between them)

parts.label: b
parts.asks: how far the block travels (its displacement) up to that moment

conditions: belt moves at a constant 6 m/s
block starts at rest when dropped on the belt
friction coefficient between block and belt is 0.3
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A conveyor belt loops around two rollers, its top surface moving in one direction and its lower return stretch labeled with a speed of 6 m/s in the opposite direction. A small block is shown just above the belt, about to be placed on its top surface.

solution.approach: The block starts at rest while the belt surface under it moves at 6 m/s, so kinetic friction accelerates the block until its speed matches the belt.

steps.text: The block is slower than the belt, so kinetic friction acts forward on the block, along the belt's direction of motion.
Compute the block's acceleration.
The block speeds up from rest until it matches the belt's speed of 6 m/s; find that time.
Find the block's displacement in that time using s = ½at².

final_answer.value: (a) t = 2 s, (b) displacement of the block = 6 m

common_mistakes.text: Using the belt's displacement (v×t = 12 m) instead of the block's own displacement, which is asked for.
Forgetting that the mass cancels in a = μg and instead trying to use an unstated mass value.

question.text: A string 0.5 m long has one end fixed at point A, and its other end tied to a small object weighing 8 N. A horizontal force F pulls the object sideways until it lies 0.3 m away from the vertical line through A. Determine the string's tension T and the magnitude of the pulling force F.
conditions: string length AC = 0.5 m
horizontal displacement of the object from the vertical through A (distance BC) = 0.3 m
weight of object = 8 N
force F is horizontal

figure.description: Point A is fixed at the top of a vertical support. A string runs from A down to point C, where the object hangs. B lies on the vertical line through A at the same height as C. The horizontal distance BC is 0.3 m. At C, three forces act: the string tension T pulling up and toward A, the weight of the object (8 N) acting straight down, and the horizontal force F acting away from the vertical line (to the right).

solution.approach: The string, its vertical drop, and the horizontal pull form a right triangle; use it to find the string's angle, then balance vertical and horizontal forces.

steps.text: The string AC = 0.5 m is the hypotenuse; the horizontal offset BC = 0.3 m is one side. Find the vertical side AB by Pythagoras.
This gives the angle θ the string makes with the vertical: sin θ = 0.3/0.5 = 0.6 and cos θ = 0.4/0.5 = 0.8.
Vertically, the string's tension balances the weight of the object.
Horizontally, the applied force balances the horizontal part of the tension.
steps.why_this_step: The object is in equilibrium under three forces: weight, tension and F, so each direction balances separately.

final_answer.value: T = 10 N, F = 6 N

common_mistakes.text: Swapping sine and cosine, using T sinθ = 8 for the vertical balance, which gives T = 13.3 N instead of 10 N.
Finding the vertical drop AB as 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2 m by simple subtraction instead of using Pythagoras.

question.text: Three pulleys are connected one below another in a chain: the topmost is fixed to a ceiling, and two lighter pulleys hang below it in series, as shown in the figure. Using string-constraint equations, determine how the acceleration of block 2 is related to the acceleration of block 1.
conditions: three pulleys connected one below another in a vertical chain
the topmost pulley is fixed to the ceiling; point 1 and the two lower pulleys are free to move
block 2 hangs from the string over the lowest (innermost) pulley
every string length stays constant

figure.description: A large pulley P₁ is fixed to the ceiling. Below it hang two smaller movable pulleys, P₂ (medium) and P₃ (small), one below the other, and at the bottom sits block 1 (a wide base block); block 2 hangs beside the chain. Three light strings are used. String S₁ passes over P₁: its left end goes straight down to block 1 and its right end goes straight down to the axle of P₂. String S₂ passes over P₂: its left end goes straight down to block 1 and its right end goes straight down to the axle of P₃. String S₃ passes over P₃: its left end goes straight down to block 1 and its right end hangs straight down to block 2. So three string ends are tied to block 1 (one from each pulley) and block 2 hangs from S₃ only. All strings are vertical; pulleys and strings are massless and frictionless. Measure the downward positions of block 1 (x₁), the axle of P₂ (x₃), the axle of P₃ (x₄) and block 2 (x₂) from a fixed horizontal line through P₁; a₁ and a₂ are the accelerations of blocks 1 and 2.

solution.approach: Write the constant-length equation for each of the three strings in turn, then combine the three to connect block 1 and block 2 directly.

steps.text: The string over the top fixed pulley P₁ runs from block 1 to the axle of pulley P₂ (position x₃), so their distances from the reference line add to a constant.
The string S₂ over pulley P₂ (axle at x₃) runs from block 1 to the axle of pulley P₃ (at x₄), both measured relative to P₂'s own position.
The string S₃ over pulley P₃ (axle at x₄) runs from block 1 to block 2, both measured relative to P₃'s own position.
From the first equation, a₃ = −a₁. Put this into the second equation.
Put a₄ = −3a₁ into the third equation and solve for a₂.
steps.why_this_step: Each movable pulley moves with the string above it, and the string over it doubles that motion for the next level while block 1 adds its own; the factors grow 1, 3, 7, so block 2 accelerates seven times as fast as block 1.

final_answer.value: a₂ = −7a₁ (block 2's acceleration is 7 times block 1's acceleration, in the opposite direction)

common_mistakes.text: Writing only the top string's constraint (x₁ + x₃ = constant) and treating everything below P₁ as one body moving with pulley P₂, which gives |a₂| = |a₁|; each movable pulley adds its own constraint.

question.text: Block A, of mass 4 kg, rests on the ground, where the coefficient of friction between the block and the ground equals 0.8. A horizontal external push of 30 N, directed parallel to the ground, is applied to the block. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the total force the ground exerts back on the block.
conditions: block A mass = 4 kg
coefficient of friction between block and ground = 0.8
external force = 30 N applied parallel to ground
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Check whether the block moves; it does not, so friction equals the applied force, and the ground's push combines the normal force and friction at a right angle.

steps.text: Find the normal force and the largest friction the ground can supply.
Compare the applied force with the largest friction.
steps.equation: 30 N < 32 N, so the block stays still

steps.text: Since the block stays still, the friction force equals the applied force.
The ground pushes with the normal force and the friction force together, at a right angle to each other, so add them as a right triangle.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the ground's push as only the normal force and forgetting the friction force gives 40 N.
Taking the ground's push as only the friction force and forgetting the normal force gives 30 N.

question.text: Assertion: Suppose the vector sum of every force acting on a rigid body is zero. Then the body must be either at complete rest, or moving in a straight line with a velocity that never changes; there is no other possible motion. Reason: A velocity that does not change over time implies the linear acceleration equals zero.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: the body under discussion is rigid
net (resultant) force on the body is zero

solution.approach: Check whether zero net force truly rules out every other motion for a rigid body, then check the reason's kinematic claim on its own.

steps.text: Zero net force fixes only the motion of the center of mass: it must move at constant velocity, which may or may not be zero.

A rigid body can still rotate about its center of mass while the net force stays zero, if a net torque acts on it. Rotation is something else that can happen, so the assertion's claim that nothing else can happen is false.
Check the reason on its own: constant velocity means the velocity does not change with time, so its time derivative, the acceleration, is zero.
The reason is a correct kinematic statement by itself, but the assertion is false, so the reason cannot be its explanation. This matches: Assertion false, Reason true.

final_answer.value: (d) The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming zero net force fully determines a rigid body's motion, missing that it can still rotate, leads to marking the Assertion true and picking option (a).

question.text: A vertical chain, from top to bottom, consists of a 5 kg block, then a uniform rope of mass 4 kg, then a 7 kg block, with the rope connecting the two blocks. An upward force F of 200 N is applied at the very top of the 5 kg block. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², answer the following.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the acceleration of the system.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the tension at the top of the rope.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the tension at the mid-point of the rope.

conditions: top block mass = 5 kg
bottom block mass = 7 kg
rope connecting them is uniform, mass = 4 kg (not massless)
upward force F = 200 N applied at the top
g = 9.8 m/s²

figure.description: From top to bottom in a vertical line: an upward force F = 200 N pulls a 5 kg block; a uniform rope of mass 4 kg hangs below the 5 kg block; a 7 kg block hangs at the bottom of the rope.

solution.approach: Find the acceleration of the whole chain from the net upward force, then cut the rope at each point and apply Newton's second law to everything hanging below that cut.

steps.text: The total mass of the top block, rope and bottom block is 16 kg. Apply Newton's second law to the whole system under the applied force and total weight.
Compute the acceleration.
For the tension at the top of the rope, apply Newton's second law to everything below that point: the rope plus the 7 kg block, total 11 kg.
Compute this tension.
For the tension at the mid-point of the rope, the hanging mass below that cut is the 7 kg block plus half the rope's mass.

common_mistakes.text: Using g alone instead of g + a for the tension cuts gives 107.8 N and 88.2 N, ignoring the system's own acceleration.
Forgetting to include half the rope's mass below the mid-point gives 7 × 12.5 = 87.5 N there instead of 112.5 N.

concept_tags: tension in a rope with distributed mass

question.text: A wedge has two sloped faces meeting at a top vertex fitted with a frictionless pulley. The left face rises at 60° and the right face rises at 30°. Block A (1 kg) and block B (3 kg) lie one above the other on the 60° face, joined to each other by a string; block B is also joined by a string running over the pulley to block C (2 kg), which lies on the 30° face. Ignore friction everywhere, and take g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the common acceleration of blocks A, B and C.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the tension carried by each connecting string.

conditions: friction neglected on both inclined faces
pulley is frictionless
the string over the pulley connects block B to block C
blocks A and B are on the 60° face, block C is on the 30° face
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A double-sloped wedge has a frictionless pulley fixed at its top vertex. Its left face makes 60° with the horizontal and its right face makes 30° with the horizontal. On the 60° face, block A (lower down the slope) is tied to block B (higher up the slope) by a string. Block B is further connected, by a string running over the pulley, to block C, which rests on the 30° face. Blocks A and B slide down the 60° face while block C is drawn up the 30° face.

solution.approach: Blocks A and B move together down the 60° face while C is pulled up the 30° face at the same speed, so treat A+B as one mass against C.

steps.text: A and B (1 kg + 3 kg = 4 kg) slide down the 60° incline; C (2 kg) is pulled up the 30° incline; all three share one acceleration a.
Put in the masses and angles with g = 10 m/s².
Solve for a.
For block C alone, the string tension T_BC pulls it up the 30° incline against its weight component.
steps.equation: T_BC − mC g sin30° = mC a

steps.text: Put in mC = 2 kg, a = 4.11 m/s² and solve.
For block A alone, its weight component pulls it down the 60° incline while the string to B (tension T_AB) holds it back.
steps.equation: mA g sin60° − T_AB = mA a

steps.text: Put in mA = 1 kg, a = 4.11 m/s² and solve.
steps.why_this_step: Block A is at the bottom of the A–B pair, so only its own weight component and the string to B act on it along the incline.

final_answer.value: (a) a = 4.11 m/s², (b) T_AB = 4.55 N (string between A and B), T_BC = 18.2 N (string over the pulley to C)

common_mistakes.text: Leaving out block C's weight component on the 30° side and taking a = (mA+mB)g sin60°/(mA+mB+mC) = 5.77 m/s².

question.text: A 2 kg block lies on a smooth horizontal tabletop. A light, inextensible string runs from this block horizontally to a smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table, then turns downward to a 4 kg block hanging freely. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string.
conditions: all surfaces (table and pulley) are smooth
string is massless and does not stretch
the 2 kg block moves horizontally while the 4 kg block moves vertically with the same acceleration
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A 2 kg block rests on a smooth horizontal tabletop. A string connects it horizontally to a smooth pulley fixed at the corner of the table; the string then runs vertically down from the pulley to a 4 kg block hanging in the air. The 2 kg block accelerates horizontally toward the pulley, and the 4 kg block accelerates downward, both with the same magnitude a.

solution.approach: The hanging 4 kg block pulls the whole system, while the 2 kg block on the smooth table only adds mass, not weight, to resist it.

steps.text: Only the hanging block's weight drives the system; both blocks share the same acceleration through the taut string.
Put in m₂ = 2 kg, m₄ = 4 kg, g = 10 m/s².
For the 2 kg block on the table, the tension is the only horizontal force.
Put in m₂ = 2 kg and a = 20/3 m/s².
steps.why_this_step: The table is smooth, so no friction opposes the tension on the 2 kg block.

common_mistakes.text: Treating the hanging block as if it falls freely and taking a = g = 10 m/s², ignoring the 2 kg block it must also move.
Treating the hanging block as not accelerating and taking T = m₄g = 40 N.

question.text: A system of three blocks — 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg — is connected by pulleys as shown in the figure and let go from rest.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out how fast each block speeds up.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out the pulling force carried by each string.

conditions: the system starts from rest
a fixed pulley is mounted on the ceiling; a second, massless, movable pulley hangs from the string that also holds the 1 kg block
the 2 kg and 3 kg blocks hang from the two ends of the string that passes over the movable pulley

figure.description: A fixed pulley is mounted on the ceiling. A string over this fixed pulley carries tension 2T: one end holds a 1 kg block; the other end supports a second, massless, movable pulley. A separate string, carrying tension T, passes over this movable pulley: one end holds a 2 kg block and the other end holds a 3 kg block. The whole arrangement starts at rest and is then released.

solution.approach: Write Newton's second law for each of the three blocks, use the massless movable pulley to fix the tension ratio, then use the string-length constraint to link the three accelerations.

steps.text: The string over the fixed pulley has tension 2T throughout; taking downward as positive, for the 1 kg block gravity acts down and 2T acts up.
The string over the movable pulley P has tension T on each side, since pulley P is massless the string tied to its axle must carry exactly 2T to balance the two T's pulling down on it.
For the 2 kg and 3 kg blocks, gravity acts down and T acts up on each.
The main string's constant length links block 1's motion to pulley P's motion; the secondary string's constant length (measured from P) links blocks 2 and 3 to P.
Write a₂ and a₃ in terms of T from the block equations, add them, and set the sum equal to −2a₁ = −2(10−2T).
Collect terms and solve for T.
steps.why_this_step: This is the only tension value consistent with all three blocks' equations and the pulley's string constraint together.

steps.text: Put T back to get every acceleration.
steps.equation: a₁ = 10−2T = −6.55 m/s² (i.e. 6.55 m/s² upward), a₂ = 5.86 m/s² down, a₃ = 7.24 m/s² down

final_answer.value: T = 8.28 N (2T = 16.55 N); the 1 kg block accelerates upward at 6.55 m/s²; the 2 kg block accelerates downward at 5.86 m/s²; the 3 kg block accelerates downward at 7.24 m/s².

question.text: A 1 kg block and a 2 kg block are joined by a light, inextensible string that runs over a smooth, frictionless pulley. Besides its own weight, the 1 kg block has an extra downward pull of F = 20 N applied to it. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the magnitude of the acceleration common to both blocks.
conditions: masses are unequal: 1 kg and 2 kg
string is inextensible and light
pulley is smooth (frictionless)
extra force F = 20 N applied downward on the 1 kg block
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A pulley is fixed to a rigid ceiling support. A string runs over the pulley, connecting two blocks. On the left, the string holds a 1 kg block; an additional downward-pointing force, labelled F, acts on this 1 kg block. On the right, the string holds a 2 kg block, with no other applied force.

solution.approach: Write Newton's second law for each block along the string, then add the two equations to eliminate the tension.

steps.text: For the 1 kg block, its own weight and the applied force F both act downward, opposed by the string tension T.
For the 2 kg block, its weight acts downward and the tension pulls it upward, and it moves the same distance as the 1 kg block since the string is inextensible.
Add the two equations to eliminate T, using g = 10 m/s² and F = 20 N.
Solve for a.

final_answer.value: a = 10/3 m/s² ≈ 3.33 m/s² (the 1 kg block accelerates down, the 2 kg block accelerates up)

common_mistakes.text: Treating the 1 kg block as free under F alone, ignoring the string and the 2 kg block, giving a = F/1 = 20 m/s².
Leaving out the 1 kg block's own weight and keeping only F, then adding the two equations to get 0 = 3a, a wrong zero acceleration.

question.text: Inside a train carriage a 1 kg plumb bob hangs on a string from the ceiling. The train is climbing a slope of 30° at constant velocity. Take g = 10 m/s². Through what angle is the string tilted away from the normal to the ceiling, and what tension does it carry?
conditions: plumb bob mass = 1 kg
bob hung from the ceiling of a train compartment by a string
train moves at constant velocity (zero acceleration)
train moves on an inclined plane of angle 30°
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so no pseudo force acts on the bob and it hangs exactly vertical under gravity and tension alone.

steps.text: The train moves at constant velocity, so its acceleration is zero and no pseudo force acts on the bob in the train's frame.
With no horizontal force, the string hangs vertically downward, and the tension balances the bob's weight.
The ceiling is parallel to the 30° incline, so the normal to the ceiling is tilted 30° away from the true vertical.
steps.equation: normal to ceiling is 30° from vertical

steps.text: Since the string is exactly vertical, the angle between the string and the normal to the ceiling equals the incline angle.

final_answer.value: angle = 30°, T = 10 N

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the string must hang perpendicular to the tilted floor (aligned with the incline's normal) gives an angle of 0°, ignoring that constant velocity means no pseudo force at all.
Adding a pseudo force along the slope even though velocity is constant tilts the string from vertical and changes the tension; with zero acceleration there is none, so T = 10 N.

question.text: A box car begins at rest (v = 0) and holds a steady acceleration of 5 m/s² along its own line of travel, î (take g = 10 m/s²). Across the car's rough floor, a 2 kg object is given an initial push of 10 m/s along this same î direction; the coefficient of sliding (kinetic) friction between the object and the floor is 0.3, while their coefficient of static friction is known to be above 0.5. Work out how the object moves relative to the car.
conditions: floor has sliding friction coefficient 0.3
floor's static friction coefficient is greater than 0.5
car starts from rest, v = 0
car's acceleration is constant at 5 m/s² along î
object's initial speed is 10 m/s along the same î direction
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: While the object slides relative to the car, kinetic friction decelerates it; find when its velocity matches the car's, then check that static friction can then keep them moving together.

steps.text: While there is relative sliding, kinetic friction acts on the object, opposing the sliding. Its ground-frame deceleration follows from this friction alone.
Write the velocities of the object and the car and set them equal to find when the sliding stops.
Solve for the time and the common speed reached.
Check whether static friction can then keep the object moving with the car, which needs a force equal to ma_car; compare this to the maximum static friction available.

Since μₛ is given greater than 0.5, static friction is enough, so after t = 1.25 s the object moves with the car with no further sliding, having drifted 6.25 m forward relative to the car during the sliding phase.

final_answer.value: the object slides forward relative to the car for 1.25 s, drifting 6.25 m forward relative to it, reaches the car's speed of 6.25 m/s, and then moves with the car with no further relative sliding

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the object slides backward relative to the car once the speeds match, since the car keeps accelerating, and missing that static friction is strong enough to hold it with the car.
Using μₛ instead of μₖ to find the initial deceleration during the sliding phase gives the wrong deceleration, since kinetic friction (not static) governs while there is relative motion.

question.text: A uniform horizontal rod OA, of mass 4 kg and length 2 m, is hinged to a wall at end O. A massless string AB supports end A, where B is a point on the wall above O; the string meets the rod at A making an angle of 60° with the rod. Taking g = 10 m/s², work out the following.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine the tension in the string AB.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine the net force the hinge exerts on the rod at O.

conditions: rod OA is horizontal and uniform, mass 4 kg, length 2 m
hinged to a vertical wall at O
string AB attached at A, wall point B above O
string AB makes 60° with the rod at A
string is massless
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A vertical wall on the left with a rod OA hinged at O, extending horizontally to the right to end A, length 2 m. A string runs from A up to a point B on the wall, above O, making a 60° angle with the rod at A.

solution.approach: Take torques about the hinge to find the string tension, then balance forces on the rod to find the hinge force.

steps.text: The rod's weight acts at its center, 1 m from the hinge; the string's vertical part acts at the far end, 2 m from the hinge.
Solve for the tension.
Balance the horizontal and vertical forces on the rod to find the two parts of the hinge force.
steps.equation: H_x = T cos60° ≈ 11.55 N, H_y = mg − T sin60° = 20 N

steps.text: Combine the two parts to get the size of the net hinge force.

final_answer.value: (a) T ≈ 23.09 N, (b) net hinge force ≈ 23.09 N

common_mistakes.text: Using the rod's full length, 2 m, as the weight's distance from the hinge instead of 1 m gives T ≈ 46.19 N, twice the correct value.

question.text: Four forces F₁, F₂, F₃ and F₄ act at a single point O, as drawn in a force diagram. Write the x-component and the y-component of each of the four forces, measured along the ox and oy axes shown in the figure.
conditions: F₁ = 4 N, 30° above the horizontal ox line
F₂ = 4 N, 60° from the vertical dashed line, on the left side
F₃ = 6 N, directed straight down (negative oy)
F₄ = 4 N, directed along positive ox
all four forces act at the same point O

figure.description: Four force vectors are drawn from a common point O. A horizontal reference line runs through O; ox points to the right along it and oy points straight up. F₁ = 4 N points up and to the right, at 30° above the +x direction. F₂ = 4 N points up and to the left, at 60° above the −x direction (the 60° is measured from the leftward horizontal, so F₂ is 30° from the +y direction). F₄ = 4 N points horizontally to the right, along +x. F₃ = 6 N points straight down along −y.

solution.approach: Resolve each force along ox and oy using the angle it makes with the axes shown in the figure.

steps.text: F₁ = 4 N is at 30° above ox, so resolve it along ox and oy.
F₂ = 4 N is at 60° above the −ox direction (30° from oy), so its ox-component is negative and its oy-component is positive.
F₃ = 6 N points straight down along −oy, so it has no ox-component.
F₄ = 4 N points along +ox, so it has no oy-component.
Collect all four results as the final set of components.

common_mistakes.text: Measuring F₂'s 60° from oy instead of from the −ox direction, giving F₂ₓ = −4sin60° = −2√3 N and F₂ᵧ = 4cos60° = 2 N instead of the correct −2 N and 2√3 N.
Giving F₃ a positive oy-component instead of negative, missing that the arrow points downward.

question.text: A block of mass 2 kg is held against a vertical wall by a horizontal force F = 20 N pushing it into the wall, as pictured. The static friction coefficient between the block and the wall is μₛ = 0.8, and the kinetic friction coefficient is μₖ = 0.6. Taking g = 10 m/s², work out the block's acceleration and the friction force that acts on it.
conditions: the 20 N force is horizontal, directed into the wall
static friction coefficient between block and wall μₛ = 0.8
kinetic friction coefficient between block and wall μₖ = 0.6
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A 2 kg block is pressed against a vertical wall by a horizontal force F = 20 N pointing toward the wall. The wall provides friction on the block with μₛ = 0.8 (static) and μₖ = 0.6 (kinetic).

solution.approach: The push force sets the normal force against the wall; compare the block's weight to the maximum static friction that normal force can supply to see whether the block slides.

steps.text: The block does not accelerate into the wall, so the wall's normal reaction equals the push.
Find the maximum static friction available and compare it with the block's weight.
steps.equation: f(s,max) = μₛN = 0.8 × 20 = 16 N, weight = mg = 2 × 10 = 20 N

steps.text: Since the weight (20 N) exceeds the maximum static friction (16 N), the block slides down, so kinetic friction applies instead, directed upward.
Apply Newton's second law along the vertical, weight down and kinetic friction up.

final_answer.value: The block slides down with acceleration 4 m/s²; the friction acting on it is kinetic friction, 12 N, directed upward.

common_mistakes.text: Using the static friction limit (16 N) as the actual friction force even after checking that the block slides, giving a = 2 m/s² instead of 4 m/s².
Not checking whether the block slides at all and assuming it stays at rest because the wall is rough.

question.text: A round ball of weight w touches a smooth, vertical wall at a single point on its surface, labelled A. A cord runs from a second point on the ball, labelled B, up to a point on the wall, labelled C, and this cord holds the ball in place. Produce a free-body force diagram for the ball, showing every force acting on it.
conditions: ball touches the wall at point A
wall is smooth (frictionless) and vertical
a cord connects point B on the ball to point C on the wall
ball's weight is w

figure.description: A vertical wall stands on the left, smooth (frictionless). A ball touches this wall at one point, A, on its surface. A cord runs from a second point on the ball's surface, B (near the top of the ball, on the side away from A), up to the wall, attaching at point C, which is above and to the side of A. The cord holds the ball against gravity.

solution.approach: The sphere feels its weight, the wall's normal reaction, and the string's tension; since the first two act through the centre, the string's line must too.

steps.text: The sphere's weight acts at its centre, downward.
The wall is smooth, so it can only push perpendicular to itself at the contact point A; for a sphere this direction always points along the radius, so its line of action passes through the centre.
steps.equation: N (horizontal, away from the wall, its line passing through the centre)

steps.text: The string pulls at point B with tension T, directed from B toward C.

Since the weight and the normal reaction both pass through the centre, they create no turning effect about it; for the sphere to be in rotational equilibrium the string's line, extended, must also pass through the centre.
steps.equation: line BC extended passes through the centre O
steps.why_this_step: With only three forces on a rigid body in equilibrium, all three lines of action must meet at one point, or two of them being through the centre forces the third to pass through it as well.

final_answer.value: Three forces act on the sphere: its weight W downward at the centre, the wall's normal reaction N horizontal at A (its line through the centre), and the string's tension T along BC at B, whose line — because the other two pass through the centre — must also pass through the centre.

common_mistakes.text: Drawing the tension only along the visible segment BC without recognising that its line of action, extended, must pass through the sphere's centre for equilibrium.
Drawing friction from the wall on the sphere, even though the wall is stated to be smooth.

question.text: A square ABCD has side length 2 m, with O at its centre. Four forces act along the sides of the square, as described below. Determine the moment each force produces about each of the following axes, both perpendicular to the square's plane:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: A line through corner A.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: A line through the centre O.

conditions: square ABCD has side 2 m
O is the centre of the square
4 N force acts along side DC, from D to C
3 N force acts along side DA, from D to A
5 N force acts along side CB, from C to B
2 N force acts along side AB, from A to B

figure.description: A square ABCD of side 2 m: D at the top-left corner, C at the top-right corner, A at the bottom-left corner, B at the bottom-right corner, and O at the centre. A 4 N force acts along the top side, directed from C toward D (leftward). A 3 N force acts along the left side, directed from A toward D (upward). A 5 N force acts along the right side, directed from C toward B (downward). A 2 N force acts along the bottom side, directed from A toward B (rightward).

solution.approach: Set up coordinates for the square, then find each force's moment as force times perpendicular distance to the axis, signed by rotation sense, and add for the net moment.

steps.text: Place the square's corners at A(0,0), B(2,0), C(2,2), D(0,2) and the centre at O(1,1), with distances in metres.
A force whose line of action passes through the axis point has zero moment about that point, since its perpendicular distance to the axis is zero.
steps.equation: about A: the 3 N force runs along DA and the 2 N force runs along AB, and both these sides pass through A
steps.why_this_step: Both DA and AB have A as one endpoint, so a force acting along either side acts directly through A.

steps.text: The 4 N force (line DC) and 5 N force (line CB) each lie a perpendicular distance of 2 m from A, so their moments about A have magnitude force times 2 m, with sign set by the turning sense they produce.
steps.equation: moment(4N) about A = 4 N × 2 m = 8 N·m, anticlockwise; moment(5N) about A = 5 N × 2 m = 10 N·m, clockwise

steps.text: Adding the four signed moments about A gives the net moment there.
steps.equation: About A: 4 N force = 8 N·m (anticlockwise), 3 N force = 0, 5 N force = 10 N·m (clockwise), 2 N force = 0; net = 8 − 10 = −2 N·m, i.e. 2 N·m clockwise

steps.text: Every side of the square lies a perpendicular distance of 1 m from the centre O, half the side length, so each force's moment about O is its magnitude times 1 m, signed by rotation sense.
steps.equation: About O: 4 N force = 4 N·m (anticlockwise), 3 N force = 3 N·m (clockwise), 5 N force = 5 N·m (clockwise), 2 N force = 2 N·m (anticlockwise)

steps.text: Adding the four signed moments about O gives the net moment there, which comes out equal to the net moment about A.
steps.equation: About O: net = 4 − 3 − 5 + 2 = −2 N·m, i.e. 2 N·m clockwise
steps.why_this_step: The two net values agree here because the square's net force happens to act along the line joining A and O.

final_answer.value: (a) About A: 4 N force (along DC) = 8 N·m anticlockwise; 3 N force (along DA) = 0; 5 N force (along CB) = 10 N·m clockwise; 2 N force (along AB) = 0; net moment about A = 2 N·m clockwise. (b) About O: 4 N force = 4 N·m anticlockwise; 3 N force = 3 N·m clockwise; 5 N force = 5 N·m clockwise; 2 N force = 2 N·m anticlockwise; net moment about O = 2 N·m clockwise.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting a force through the axis has zero moment: treating the 3 N force along DA as 2 m from A gives 6 N·m instead of 0.
Using the distance from O to a corner (√2 m) instead of to the side (1 m) gives moments of about 5.7, 4.2, 7.1 and 2.8 N·m instead of 4, 3, 5 and 2 N·m.

question.text: Assertion: Looking at the arrangement shown, the friction force that block B exerts on block A will always point toward the right, in every case. Reason: A friction force always acts against the relative sliding (or tendency to slide) between the two touching surfaces.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: block A rests on top of block B
ground beneath B is smooth (frictionless)
F₁ acts on A, directed to the left
F₂ acts on B, directed to the right

figure.description: Block A sits on top of block B, and block B rests on the ground below it. The ground under B is smooth (frictionless), so there is no friction between B and the ground. A force F₁ is applied directly to block A, pointing horizontally to the left. A force F₂ is applied directly to block B, pointing horizontally to the right. Friction can act between A and B at their contact surface.

solution.approach: Solve for the friction on A from B in terms of arbitrary masses and forces, and show it always comes out positive (rightward) no matter the values.

steps.text: Let m₁ be the mass of A and m₂ the mass of B. Without friction, F₁ alone would push A left and F₂ alone would push B right, so A tends to slip left relative to B.
steps.equation: F₁ on A (left), F₂ on B (right)

steps.text: The ground under B is smooth, so the only horizontal forces on the whole system are F₁ and F₂; find their common acceleration.
Write Newton's second law for A alone, with F₁ acting left and the unknown friction f from B acting right (positive direction).
Substitute the common acceleration and solve for f.
Every term here is a positive mass or force, so f is always positive — friction on A from B is always rightward, for any values of F₁, F₂, m₁, m₂.
This rightward friction is exactly the force opposing A's tendency to slip left relative to B, so the Reason correctly explains the Assertion.
steps.equation: Assertion true, Reason true and explains it

final_answer.value: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the friction direction depends on whether F₁ or F₂ is larger and so could point either way, which makes the Assertion look false while still taking the Reason as a true general law.

question.text: A triangular wedge of mass m₂ = 4 kg rests on a frictionless horizontal floor; its sloping face makes 30° with the floor. A small block of mass m₁ = 1 kg sits on that frictionless slope. A light string tied to the wedge passes over a light pulley fixed at the edge of the floor and hangs down to a block of mass M. Find the mass M for which the small block m₁ does not slide relative to the wedge.
conditions: m₁ = 1 kg, the small block resting on the incline
m₂ = 4 kg, the triangular wedge resting on the floor
incline angle = 30°
all surfaces frictionless
string and pulley are light (massless)
M is the mass of the block hanging from the string over the pulley

figure.description: A triangular wedge of mass m2 = 4 kg rests on a horizontal floor. The wedge's vertical face is on the left. Its sloping face runs from the top of that vertical face down to the right, meeting the floor at the wedge's bottom-right tip; the angle between the sloping face and the floor, marked at this bottom-right tip, is 30 degrees. A small block of mass m1 = 1 kg rests on the sloping face, about halfway along it. No string is attached to m1. A small pulley is fixed at the right-hand end of the floor surface, just beyond the bottom-right tip of the wedge, at floor level. A light string is tied to the wedge at its bottom-right tip, runs the very short horizontal distance to the pulley, passes over the pulley, and then hangs straight down past the edge of the floor to a block of mass M, which hangs freely in the air below the level of the floor. Nothing else touches M. All surfaces are frictionless; the string and pulley are light.

solution.approach: Find the one horizontal acceleration of the wedge that keeps m1 from sliding on its frictionless slope, then use that acceleration to find the hanging mass M that produces it.

steps.text: Since the string ties M to the wedge itself (not to m1), the wedge and m1 move together as one horizontal unit with a common acceleration; the string over the pulley makes M's downward acceleration equal to this same value.
steps.equation: a(wedge) = a(m1, horizontal) = a(M, downward) = A
steps.why_this_step: This is the constraint relation linking every acceleration in the problem, fixed before any force equation is written.

steps.text: For m1 not to slide on the frictionless slope, the normal force alone must supply its horizontal acceleration A while also balancing its weight vertically.
steps.equation: N cosθ = m1 g,  N sinθ = m1 A

steps.text: Divide the two equations to eliminate N and solve for A.
steps.equation: A = g tanθ = g tan30° = 10/√3 ≈ 5.77 m/s²

steps.text: Write Newton's second law for the wedge-plus-m1 system moving horizontally under the string tension T.
Write Newton's second law for the hanging mass M, taking downward as positive.
Substitute T = (m1+m2)A and solve for M.

common_mistakes.text: Using A = g sinθ (the acceleration formula for a block sliding down a fixed frictionless incline) instead of A = g tanθ, giving M = 5 kg instead of the correct ≈ 6.83 kg.

question.text: A rigid support S holds two blocks in a vertical line using two inextensible wires, each 1 m long: the upper wire (negligible mass) hangs from S to a 2.9 kg block, and the lower wire (uniformly distributed mass 0.2 kg) hangs from that 2.9 kg block down to a 1.9 kg block below it. The entire system — blocks, wires and support — accelerates upward at 0.2 m/s². Taking g = 9.8 m/s², answer the following.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the tension at the midpoint of the lower wire.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the tension at the midpoint of the upper wire.

conditions: support S is rigid
two inextensible wires, each of length 1 m
upper wire has negligible mass, connects S to the 2.9 kg block
lower wire has uniformly distributed mass 0.2 kg, connects the 2.9 kg block to the 1.9 kg block
the whole system accelerates upward at 0.2 m/s²
g = 9.8 m/s²

figure.description: A horizontal rigid support S at the top. From S, an upper (massless) wire hangs down to a 2.9 kg block. From that 2.9 kg block, a lower wire of mass 0.2 kg hangs down further to a 1.9 kg block at the bottom.

solution.approach: Cut the wire at each midpoint and apply Newton's second law to everything hanging below that cut, using the system's own upward acceleration.

steps.text: For the lower wire midpoint, the hanging mass below the cut is the 1.9 kg block plus half the lower wire's mass.
Apply Newton's second law to this hanging mass, which accelerates upward at 0.2 m/s² along with the whole system.
This gives the tension at the lower wire's midpoint.
For the upper wire midpoint, the upper wire is massless, so the mass below the cut is the 2.9 kg block plus the entire lower wire plus the 1.9 kg block.
Apply Newton's second law to this total hanging mass with the same upward acceleration.

common_mistakes.text: Using g alone instead of g + a gives 19.6 N and 49 N, ignoring that the whole system accelerates upward.
Forgetting to include half the lower wire's mass below the lower midpoint gives 1.9 × 10 = 19 N there instead of 20 N.

concept_tags: tension in a wire with distributed mass

question.text: A body sliding down a rough inclined plane set at 45° takes twice as long to reach the bottom as the same body sliding down a smooth (frictionless) 45° inclined plane of the same length. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the body and the rough plane?
conditions: angle of incline is 45° in both cases
time on the rough plane is twice the time on the smooth plane
same plane length in both cases

solution.approach: Write the acceleration on the smooth and rough 45° inclines, use the given time ratio to relate them, and solve for the coefficient of kinetic friction.

steps.text: On the smooth 45° incline, the block's acceleration equals the gravity component along the incline, with nothing else acting.
On the rough 45° incline, kinetic friction subtracts from this.
Both blocks start from rest and cover the same incline length L, and time for a fixed distance from rest goes as the inverse square root of the acceleration.
The rough time is twice the smooth time, so squaring this ratio gives the rough acceleration as one quarter of the smooth acceleration.
Substitute and solve for μ at θ = 45°, where sin45° = cos45° so they cancel.

question.text: A block of mass m rests on a horizontal, rough surface whose angle of friction is φ. Someone pulls the block using a force F directed at an angle θ above the horizontal. What is the smallest value F can take and still move the block?
conditions: surface is rough with angle of friction φ
force F applied at angle θ above the horizontal
block starts at rest

solution.approach: Write the horizontal and vertical force balance for the block at the point motion begins, then rewrite the result using the angle of friction instead of the coefficient of friction.

steps.text: The pull F at angle θ has a horizontal part that drives the block forward and a vertical part that supports part of the block's weight, reducing the normal force from the surface.
At the point the block starts to move, the horizontal pull equals the maximum friction, which is the coefficient of friction times the normal force.
steps.equation: F cosθ = μN = μ(mg − F sinθ)

steps.text: Collect the F terms and solve for F.
steps.equation: F(cosθ + μ sinθ) = μmg ⇒ F = μmg/(cosθ + μ sinθ)

steps.text: Replace μ with tanφ, since the angle of friction φ is defined by tanφ = μ, and simplify using the cosine addition formula.
steps.equation: F = mg sinφ/(cosθ cosφ + sinθ sinφ) = mg sinφ / cos(θ − φ)

final_answer.value: mg sinφ / cos(θ − φ)

common_mistakes.text: Minimising over the pull angle as well, which gives the overall least pull mg sinφ (reached only at θ = φ), when the question fixes θ and asks for the least F at that angle.
Swapping sinφ and cosφ in the numerator gives mg cosφ / cos(θ − φ).

question.text: A block of mass m rests on the smooth inclined face (angle θ) of a wedge of mass M, which itself sits on a smooth horizontal floor. A horizontal force F is applied to the wedge, pushing the wedge and block together.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the value of F for which the block does not slide relative to the wedge.

conditions: all surfaces are smooth (frictionless): floor–wedge and wedge–block
the block must stay fixed in position relative to the wedge, moving together as one rigid system

figure.description: A wedge of mass M rests on a smooth horizontal floor; its inclined face rises at angle θ to the horizontal on the right side. A block of mass m sits on this incline. A horizontal force F is applied to the wedge at its vertical face, pushing the wedge (and, through the incline, the block) sideways.

solution.approach: For the block to stay still relative to the wedge, both must share one horizontal acceleration, and on a smooth incline that fixes the acceleration at g tanθ.

steps.text: Since the block does not slide on the wedge, the wedge and block move together with one common horizontal acceleration a.
On the block, only its weight mg (down) and the normal force N (perpendicular to the smooth incline) act. Its vertical acceleration is zero, and its horizontal acceleration is a.
steps.equation: N cosθ = mg, N sinθ = ma

steps.text: Divide the two equations to remove N.
steps.why_this_step: This is the one acceleration value at which the incline's normal force alone can hold the block in place without sliding, on a frictionless surface.

steps.text: Put a = g tanθ into the system equation and solve for F.

final_answer.value: F = (M+m) g tanθ

common_mistakes.text: Leaving out the wedge's mass and writing F = m g tanθ, using only the block's mass.
Inverting the trig ratio and writing F = (M+m) g / tanθ instead of (M+m) g tanθ.

question.text: A 2 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor, and a horizontal force F = 2t newtons (t in seconds) is applied to it, with g = 10 m/s². The floor gives two separate friction coefficients: static μₛ = 0.6 and kinetic μₖ = 0.4.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Sketch how the block's acceleration changes with time.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out the friction force on the block at t = 2 s and at t = 8 s.

conditions: block mass = 2 kg
applied force F = 2t newtons, t in seconds
g = 10 m/s²
static friction coefficient μₛ = 0.6
kinetic friction coefficient μₖ = 0.4
block on a rough horizontal floor

solution.approach: Find the time when the applied force reaches the maximum static friction, then use kinetic friction for the sliding phase after that time.

steps.text: Find the maximum static friction and the time at which the applied force reaches it.
steps.equation: f(max static) = μₛmg = 0.6×2×10 = 12 N; F = 2t = 12 N at t = 6 s

steps.text: For t < 6 s the block stays still, so friction equals the applied force.
For t > 6 s the block slides, so kinetic friction takes its constant value and the net force gives the acceleration.
At t = 2 s the block is still in the static phase.
At t = 8 s the block is in the sliding phase.

final_answer.value: (a) a = 0 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6 s, then a = t − 4 for t > 6 s, a straight line starting at (6 s, 2 m/s²) with slope 1; (b) friction = 4 N at t = 2 s, friction = 8 N at t = 8 s

common_mistakes.text: Using the static coefficient 0.6 instead of the kinetic coefficient 0.4 for the sliding phase gives friction = 12 N at t = 8 s and a = 2 m/s² instead of 4 m/s².
Forgetting to divide the net force by the mass gives a = 2t − 8 directly, so a = 8 m/s² at t = 8 s instead of the correct 4 m/s².

question.text: Inside a box car that starts from rest (v = 0) and keeps a steady acceleration of 5 m/s² along î, its own forward direction (take g = 10 m/s²), a 2 kg object is released on the car's flat, frictionless floor. At that instant the object already carries a sideways speed of 10 m/s along k̂, the horizontal direction at right angles to î in the floor plane (ĵ stays vertical, pointing up).

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Explain what path the object follows as seen by a passenger riding inside the car.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Explain what path the object follows as seen by an observer standing on the ground outside.

conditions: car floor has no friction
car starts from rest, v = 0
car keeps a constant acceleration of 5 m/s² along î
object's initial speed is 10 m/s along k̂, sideways to the car's direction of travel
g = 10 m/s²
î, ĵ, k̂ form a right-handed set: î along the car's acceleration, ĵ vertical, k̂ horizontal and transverse

figure.description: A rectangular car body sits on wheels on the ground. Inside it, three axes are drawn from a point: î points horizontally in the direction the car speeds up (forward), ĵ points straight up, and k̂ points horizontally out of that vertical plane, at right angles to î (sideways to the car's motion). Outside the car, an arrow marked a = 5 m/s² î shows its acceleration, and v = 0 marks its starting speed.

solution.approach: In the ground frame the frictionless floor exerts no force, so the object travels straight; the car's own acceleration bends this into a curved path relative to the car.

steps.text: In the ground frame, the frictionless floor gives the object no horizontal force in any direction, so it keeps its initial transverse velocity forever, moving in a straight line at constant speed.
steps.equation: ground frame: straight line at constant 10 m/s along k̂, no motion along î

steps.text: In the car's frame, the object starts with zero velocity along î (the car's direction of travel) but still feels the backward pseudo force from the car's forward acceleration, so its position along î grows backward starting from rest.
Along k̂, the car's acceleration does not affect the object's transverse motion, so it still moves at constant velocity in that direction relative to the car.
Combining these, the car's frame sees the object trace a parabola, curving backward relative to the car's forward direction as it moves along k̂.

final_answer.value: (a) in the car's frame the object traces a parabola, curving backward along î while moving at constant speed along k̂; (b) in the ground frame the object moves in a straight line at constant 10 m/s along k̂

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the object shares the car's acceleration along î in the ground frame gives a curved (parabolic) path in the ground frame, but the frictionless floor exerts no horizontal force on the object at all.

Describing the car frame motion as a straight line instead of a parabola misses that the pseudo force acts along î while the object's initial velocity is along k̂, a genuine two-dimensional combination.

question.text: Block A (1 kg) and block B (2 kg) start out side by side on a level floor, each tied to one end of a single cord that loops over a smooth, weightless pulley mounted above them; at the outset the cord has no slack and no tension. From time t = 0 onward, a force F = 20t newtons (with t measured in seconds) pulls the pulley straight upward. Taking g = 10 m/s², answer the following, noting that A lifts off the floor before B does.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the speed of block A at the moment block B leaves the floor.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find how high the pulley has moved upward by that same moment.

conditions: A has mass 1 kg, B has mass 2 kg
both blocks start on the floor side by side with the cord just taut and untensioned
the pulley is smooth and weightless
F = 20t newtons pulls the pulley upward starting at t = 0
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A pulley hangs freely above the floor; force F = 20t pulls straight up on its axle. A single cord passes over the pulley, one end running straight down to block A and the other straight down to block B. Blocks A and B begin resting side by side on the floor, each directly under its own side of the pulley.

solution.approach: The massless pulley fixes the string tension as F/2 always; find when each block leaves the floor, then apply Newton's second law and integrate for velocity and the pulley's rise.

steps.text: Since the pulley is massless, the upward force F is balanced by the two downward string tensions at every instant.
Each block leaves the floor once the tension reaches its own weight. Block A (1 kg, lighter) needs less tension than block B (2 kg), so A leaves first.
steps.equation: T = m_A g: 10t = 10 → t = 1 s (A leaves);  T = m_B g: 10t = 20 → t = 2 s (B on the verge of leaving)

steps.text: Between t = 1 s and t = 2 s, B still rests on the floor, so apply Newton's second law to A alone with the growing tension.
steps.equation: T − m_A g = m_A a_A  →  a_A(t) = 10t − 10, for 1 s ≤ t ≤ 2 s

steps.text: A starts this phase from rest, so integrate the acceleration to get A's velocity.
