Integrate the velocity to get A's rise over this interval, then halve it: with B fixed on the floor, the string's fixed length means the pulley rises by only half of A's rise.
steps.equation: y_A = ∫₁² 5(t−1)² dt = 5/3 m; pulley's rise = y_A/2 = 5/6 m ≈ 0.83 m
steps.why_this_step: The total string length is constant; with B's end fixed at the floor, the pulley-to-A segment and the pulley's own height are linked so the pulley moves half as far as A.

final_answer.value: (a) velocity of A when B loses contact = 5 m/s. (b) height raised by the pulley up to that instant = 5/6 m ≈ 0.83 m

common_mistakes.text: Integrating a_A from t = 0 instead of t = 1 gives v_A(2) = 0 m/s, ignoring that A rests on the floor until the tension reaches its weight at t = 1 s.
Taking the pulley's rise equal to A's full rise of 5/3 m instead of half of it, by missing that B staying on the floor fixes one end of the string.

question.text: In the setup shown, block m₁ rests on the sloped face of a frictionless wedge, while a second block, m₂, hangs in the air and is η times as heavy as m₁; the wedge's slope makes an angle θ with the ground. Every pulley and every string in the system is taken to be massless, and no surface exposes any friction. Work out the acceleration of block m₂.
conditions: m₂ has η times the mass of m₁
incline (wedge) makes angle θ with the horizontal
all pulleys and strings are massless
no friction anywhere in the system

figure.description: A wedge rests on the ground. Its sloped face rises from the lower-left corner, where it makes angle θ with the ground, up to the top-right corner of the wedge; its right face is vertical. A small pulley is fixed at the top-right corner of the wedge. Block m₁ rests on the sloped face. A cord is tied to block m₁, runs up the slope parallel to the incline, passes over the top of the fixed corner pulley, and drops vertically down just outside the vertical face to the axle of a second, smaller pulley. This second pulley is not fixed to anything; it hangs in the air beside the vertical face, held up only by that cord. A second cord passes over the top of this hanging pulley, and both of its segments run downward: the left segment goes straight down to a small bracket fixed to the wedge at the foot of the vertical face, at ground level; the right segment goes straight down to block m₂, which hangs freely in the air to the right of the wedge. Block m₂ has mass η times m₁. All pulleys and cords are massless, and every surface is frictionless.

solution.approach: Get the string-length constraint linking m1's motion up the incline to m2's fall, then combine it with Newton's second law for m1, the movable pulley, and m2.

steps.text: The cord from m1 goes over the fixed corner pulley down to the movable pulley; the second cord passes over the top of the hanging pulley; one segment runs down to the fixed bracket and the other runs down to m2.
steps.equation: cord 1: m1 to fixed pulley to movable pulley; cord 2: fixed bracket to movable pulley to m2

steps.text: If m1 moves a distance x up the incline, the movable pulley must move down by x (cord 1 is fixed length), and then both segments of cord 2 shorten or lengthen by that same x, so m2 must move down by 2x.
steps.why_this_step: This is the constraint relation: it links every acceleration in the system before any force equation is written.

steps.text: The hanging pulley is massless, so the single upward pull T₁ from cord 1 at its axle must balance the two downward pulls T₂ from the segments of cord 2.
Write Newton's second law for m1 along the frictionless incline, taking up the slope as positive.
steps.equation: T1 − m1 g sinθ = m1 a1

steps.text: Write Newton's second law for m2, taking downward as positive.
Substitute T1 = 2T2 and m2 = ηm1 into both equations and eliminate T2 to solve for a1.
steps.equation: T2 = ηm1(g − 2a1); T1 = m1(a1 + g sinθ) = 2T2 gives a1(1 + 4η) = g(2η − sinθ)

steps.text: So a1 = g(2η − sinθ)/(1 + 4η), and m2's acceleration is twice that.
steps.equation: a2 = 2g(2η − sinθ)/(1 + 4η), directed downward when 2η > sinθ; upward when 2η < sinθ

final_answer.value: a2 = 2g(2η − sinθ)/(1 + 4η), directed downward when 2η > sinθ; when 2η < sinθ the expression is negative and m₂ accelerates upward (the acceleration of the mass m2 = ηm1)

common_mistakes.text: Missing the movable-pulley factor of 2 in the constraint and taking a2 = a1, which gives a1(1 + 2η) = g(2η − sinθ), the wrong denominator (1 + 2η) instead of (1 + 4η).

question.text: In the arrangement shown, block A has mass 4 kg and block B has mass 5 kg. Find the acceleration of each block.
conditions: upper pulley fixed to the ceiling
lower pulley is movable
block A (4 kg) hangs from the right side of the string over the fixed pulley
block B (5 kg) hangs from the string over the movable pulley
one end of the movable-pulley's string is anchored near the fixed pulley's support

figure.description: A pulley P₁ is fixed to the ceiling. A single light string passes over P₁: its right end hangs straight down to block A (4 kg). Its left end goes down, passes UNDER a small movable pulley P₂ (wrapping round its lower half) and comes back up to be tied to the fixed support of P₁, so P₂ hangs in a loop of that string with two vertical strands above it. Block B (5 kg) hangs directly from the axle of P₂ by a short string. Pulleys and strings are light and frictionless. When B moves down by x, A moves up by 2x.

solution.approach: A hangs from one strand; the movable pulley (holding B) has two strands, so aA = 2aB, opposite in direction; apply Newton's second law to each block.

steps.text: Take downward as positive for each block separately. The movable-pulley string constraint gives aA = −2aB.
Write Newton's second law for A (4 kg), held by a single strand of tension T.
Write Newton's second law for B (5 kg), held by two strands of tension T at the movable pulley.
Solve the three equations together.
aA is positive, so A accelerates downward at 20/7 m/s²; aB is negative, so B accelerates upward at 10/7 m/s², half the magnitude of aA, as the constraint requires.
steps.equation: A: 20/7 m/s² ≈ 2.9 m/s² down, B: 10/7 m/s² ≈ 1.4 m/s² up

final_answer.value: A (4 kg) accelerates at 20/7 m/s² ≈ 2.9 m/s² downward, and B (5 kg) accelerates at 10/7 m/s² ≈ 1.4 m/s² upward.

common_mistakes.text: Treating both blocks as hanging from a single strand of the same tension and using the plain Atwood formula (g(mA−mB)/(mA+mB)), which ignores the movable pulley.
Using only one strand of tension in the 5 kg block's equation instead of two, giving the wrong magnitude for both accelerations.

question.text: To push a body up a rough incline right at the point where it just starts to move takes exactly twice the force that would just stop that same body from sliding down the incline. Given the friction coefficient μ between body and incline, and θ as the incline's angle with the horizontal, what is tan θ in terms of μ?
conditions: force to just move the body up the incline = twice the force to just prevent it sliding down
coefficient of friction between body and incline = μ
θ is the incline's angle with the horizontal

solution.approach: Write the force needed to push the block up the incline and the force needed to barely hold it from sliding down, then use the given ratio between them.

steps.text: To push the block up, gravity's pull down the incline and friction (which now opposes the upward push) both work against the applied force.
To barely stop the block sliding down, friction acts up the incline at its full value and helps hold the block, so the needed applied force is smaller.
Use the given condition that F_up is twice F_hold, then divide through by mg cosθ and solve for tanθ.

final_answer.value: 3μ

common_mistakes.text: Leaving friction out of F_hold, treating it as mg sinθ alone, gives sinθ + μcosθ = 2sinθ, so tanθ = μ.
Leaving friction out of F_up, treating it as mg sinθ alone, gives sinθ = 2(sinθ − μcosθ), so tanθ = 2μ.

question.text: Lined up in contact with each other on a smooth horizontal surface, from left to right, are three blocks: a 1 kg block, a 4 kg block, and a 2 kg block. A 120 N push acts on the 1 kg block from its left side, directed rightward into the row. A 50 N push acts on the 2 kg block from its right side, directed leftward into the row.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the acceleration of the three-block system.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the size of the normal contact force between the 1 kg block and the 4 kg block.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the net force acting on the 2 kg block.

conditions: surface is smooth (frictionless)
blocks are in contact, in order 1 kg, 4 kg, 2 kg from left to right
120 N applied to the 1 kg block from the left, pushing rightward
50 N applied to the 2 kg block from the right, pushing leftward

figure.description: On a smooth horizontal surface, three blocks touch each other in a row: 1 kg on the left, 4 kg in the middle, 2 kg on the right. A horizontal force of 120 N is applied to the outer (left) face of the 1 kg block, pointing right, into the row. A horizontal force of 50 N is applied to the outer (right) face of the 2 kg block, pointing left, into the row.

solution.approach: Treat all three blocks as one system to find the common acceleration, then isolate one block at a time using Newton's second law.

steps.text: Find the net external force and total mass of the system.
The system acceleration is the net force divided by the total mass.
steps.equation: a = 70/7 = 10 m/s², rightward, in the direction of the 120 N force

steps.text: Isolate the 1 kg block: the 120 N force acts forward, and the 4 kg block pushes back on it with the contact normal force N.
steps.why_this_step: The 1 kg block only touches the 120 N force and the 4 kg block, so its own equation isolates N directly.

steps.text: The net force on the 2 kg block equals its mass times the common acceleration.

final_answer.value: (a) a = 10 m/s²; (b) N = 110 N; (c) net force on the 2 kg block = 20 N

common_mistakes.text: Adding 120 N and 50 N instead of subtracting, since both forces push toward the middle of the row, giving a = 170/7 ≈ 24.3 m/s².
Using the far side (4 kg + 2 kg) but forgetting the 50 N force acting there, giving N = 6×10 = 60 N instead of 110 N.

question.text: On a horizontal road with friction present, the coefficient of friction between a car's tyres and the road is μ = 0.4. The car starts at rest, speeds up, then slows back down to rest, and in doing so covers a total distance of 400 m. Work out the shortest possible time in which this 400 m distance can be covered.
conditions: horizontal rough road
car starts from rest
car ends at rest
total distance covered = 400 m

solution.approach: Use the maximum friction-limited acceleration to speed up for half the distance, then the same maximum deceleration to stop over the other half, and add the two times.

steps.text: The road's friction limits both the car's acceleration and its braking deceleration to the same maximum value.

To cover the distance in the least time while starting and ending at rest, the car speeds up at this maximum rate for the first half of the distance, then brakes at the same maximum rate for the second half.
Find the time for the first half using distance equals half of acceleration times time squared.
By symmetry the braking half takes the same time, so add the two.

common_mistakes.text: Using the full 400 m in a single accelerating phase, instead of splitting it into two halves, gives 400 = ½×4×t², so t = √200 ≈ 14.1 s, which ignores that the car must stop.
Finding the correct time for one half, 10 s, and forgetting to double it for the braking half reports 10 s as the final answer, missing half the trip.

question.text: A rough wedge has its sloped face tilted at 60° to the horizontal. A block of mass 6 kg sits on this slope, with the static friction coefficient between block and slope μs = 0.6 and the kinetic friction coefficient μk = 0.4. A force F is applied to the block, directed up along the slope's surface. Taking g = 10 m/s², work out the size of F needed in each of these situations:

parts.label: a
parts.asks: F keeps the block completely still on the slope.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: F makes the block slide down the slope at a steady (constant) speed.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: F makes the block move up the slope while speeding up at 4 m/s².

conditions: incline angle is 60°
static friction coefficient μs = 0.6
kinetic friction coefficient μk = 0.4
force F acts along the incline surface, directed up the slope
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A wedge stands with its slope rising from a 60° angle at the base. A 6 kg block rests on this slanted surface. A force F is applied to the block along the slope, pointing up and away from the base. The friction coefficients printed beside the incline are μs = 0.6 and μk = 0.4.

solution.approach: Write Newton's second law along the incline for each case, using static friction at its limit for the stationary range and kinetic friction, opposing motion, for the moving cases.

steps.text: The normal force is unaffected by F since F acts along the incline, so N = mg cos60°.

To keep the block stationary, F must lie between the value that barely stops it sliding down (friction at its maximum, acting up the slope) and the value that barely stops it sliding up (friction at its maximum, acting down the slope).
steps.equation: F_min = mg sin60° − μₛmg cos60°,  F_max = mg sin60° + μₛmg cos60°

steps.text: Compute both limits.
To move the block down at constant velocity, kinetic friction acts up the slope (opposing the downward slide) and the net force is zero.
To move the block up with acceleration 4 m/s², kinetic friction acts down the slope (opposing the upward slide), and Newton's second law along the incline gives F.

common_mistakes.text: Using kinetic friction instead of static friction for part (a) gives a narrower, incorrect range of 40.0 N to 64.0 N.
Reversing the direction of kinetic friction in part (c) (treating it as helping instead of opposing the upward motion) gives F ≈ 64.0 N instead of 88.0 N.

question.text: A weight of 10 N is to be split into two components: one directed parallel to a slope, and one directed perpendicular to it. The slope makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal. Find both components.
conditions: slope makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal

figure.description: An inclined slope rising to the right at 30° to the horizontal ground. A weight w = 10 N acts vertically downward at a point on the slope. It is split into w∥, directed along the slope surface toward its lower end, and w⊥, directed into the slope surface, perpendicular to it. The angle between the vertical weight and the perpendicular component is 30°, and the angle between the slope surface and the vertical is 60°.

solution.approach: Split the weight into a component along the slope and a component into the slope using the incline angle.

steps.text: The weight acts vertically downward. The angle between the weight and the perpendicular to the slope equals the slope angle, 30°.
The component along the slope (parallel to the surface) is the weight times the sine of the slope angle.
steps.equation: w∥ = w sin θ = 10 × sin 30° = 5 N

steps.text: The component into the slope (perpendicular to the surface) is the weight times the cosine of the slope angle.
steps.equation: w⊥ = w cos θ = 10 × cos 30° = 8.66 N
steps.why_this_step: The 30 deg angle lies between the weight and its perpendicular component, so the perpendicular component is the adjacent side, w cos30, and the along-slope component is the opposite side, w sin30.

final_answer.value: component parallel to the slope = 5 N (down the slope); component perpendicular to the slope = 8.66 N (into the slope)

common_mistakes.text: Swapping sine and cosine gives 8.66 N along the slope and 5 N perpendicular to it.

question.text: Two blocks lie one on top of the other on a frictionless floor: a 1 kg block sits on a 2 kg block. The friction coefficient between the two blocks themselves is μ = 0.4. The 1 kg block starts out moving at 2 m/s and the 2 kg block starts out moving at 8 m/s, both toward the same side, as pictured. Take g = 10 m/s² and answer the following.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the time after which the two blocks stop sliding relative to each other.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the common speed the two blocks share at that instant.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find how far each block, the 1 kg block and the 2 kg block, has travelled by that instant.

conditions: 1 kg block rests on top of a 2 kg block
the floor beneath the 2 kg block is frictionless (smooth)
coefficient of friction between the two blocks μ = 0.4
1 kg block starting speed 2 m/s
2 kg block starting speed 8 m/s
both blocks move in the same direction
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A 1 kg block sits on top of a 2 kg block, which itself rests on a frictionless (smooth) floor. The 1 kg block moves to the right at 2 m/s and the 2 kg block moves to the right at 8 m/s. Friction, with coefficient μ = 0.4, acts only between the 1 kg block and the 2 kg block; there is no friction between the 2 kg block and the floor.

solution.approach: The ground is smooth, so only friction between the two blocks acts; the faster bottom block drags the top one forward while it itself slows down.

steps.text: The bottom (2 kg) block moves faster (8 m/s) than the top (1 kg) block (2 m/s), so kinetic friction from the 1 kg block acts backward on the 2 kg block and forward on the 1 kg block.
Find each block's acceleration. The 1 kg block feels only this forward friction; the 2 kg block feels only the equal, opposite friction (the ground beneath it is smooth).
Set the two velocities equal to find when they reach a common speed.
Find the common velocity at that time.
Find each block's displacement in that 1 s using s = v₀t + ½at².

final_answer.value: (a) t = 1 s, (b) common velocity = 6 m/s, (c) displacement of 1 kg block = 4 m, displacement of 2 kg block = 7 m

common_mistakes.text: Applying friction to the 2 kg block from the ground as well, even though the ground is stated to be smooth, which changes its acceleration and the final time.
Swapping which block speeds up and which slows down, giving friction the wrong direction on each block.

question.text: A box, open at the top, moves with a downward acceleration a, as shown in the figure. A block of mass m sits on the floor inside this box. What value must a have so that the block presses on the box's floor with a force of mg/4?
conditions: box accelerates downward with acceleration a
block of mass m rests on the floor of the box

figure.description: A square box, open at the top, accelerates downward; a downward arrow labelled a is drawn just to the left of the box, outside it. Inside the box, a block (of mass m) rests on the box's floor.

solution.approach: In the ground frame, apply Newton's second law to the block along the vertical, using the given floor reaction to find the box's acceleration.

steps.text: The block accelerates downward with the box, so its weight minus the floor's normal push equals mass times acceleration.
Substitute the given floor reaction, N = mg/4.
Divide by m and solve for a.

final_answer.value: a = 3g/4, directed downward (≈ 7.5 m/s² for g = 10 m/s²)

common_mistakes.text: Writing the equation as N − mg = ma, treating the floor force as larger than the weight, which gives the wrong sign a = −3g/4.
Setting the acceleration equal to N/m directly, a = g/4, instead of first subtracting N from the weight.

question.text: A 6 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor where the static friction coefficient is μₛ = 0.6 and the kinetic friction coefficient is μₖ = 0.4. A horizontal force that increases with time, F = 4t newton (with t in seconds), acts on the block, as pictured. Taking g = 10 m/s², draw how the block's acceleration varies with time.
conditions: surface is rough
static friction coefficient μₛ = 0.6
kinetic friction coefficient μₖ = 0.4
applied force is horizontal and time-varying, F = 4t newton
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A 6 kg block rests on a rough horizontal surface with static friction coefficient μₛ = 0.6 and kinetic friction coefficient μₖ = 0.4. A horizontal force F = 4t (in newton, t in seconds) pushes the block to the right, increasing with time.

solution.approach: The block stays still until F = 4t exceeds the static limit; once moving, friction drops to the lower kinetic value, so the acceleration jumps upward.

steps.text: Find the maximum static friction, which the growing force must exceed before the block moves.
Find the time at which F first reaches this value; before that time the block does not move, so a = 0.
Once the block starts moving, kinetic friction takes over, and it is smaller than the static limit that was needed to start motion.
For t ≥ 9 s, apply Newton's second law with this smaller kinetic friction opposing F.
At t = 9 s this gives a jump: a = (36 − 24)/6 = 2 m/s², so the acceleration jumps from 0 to 2 m/s² at t = 9 s, then keeps rising with slope 2/3.
steps.equation: a = 0 for 0 ≤ t < 9 s; a jumps to 2 m/s² at t = 9 s and then a = (4t − 24)/6 m/s² for t ≥ 9 s

final_answer.value: a = 0 for 0 ≤ t < 9 s; at t = 9 s the acceleration jumps discontinuously to 2 m/s² (because kinetic friction, 24 N, is less than the static limit, 36 N, that was needed to start motion); for t ≥ 9 s, a = (4t − 24)/6 m/s², a straight line of slope 2/3 m/s³ starting from 2 m/s² at t = 9 s.

common_mistakes.text: Using the static friction value 36 N in the formula for t ≥ 9 s instead of the kinetic value 24 N, giving a = 0 at t = 9 s and missing the jump.
Missing the discontinuity and drawing the graph as one smooth straight line through a = 0 at t = 9 s, instead of a jump to a = 2 m/s².

question.text: Four forces meet at one point of a body and the body does not move, so it is in equilibrium. Two of the forces are known, 8 N and 4 N; the other two, F₁ and F₂, are not. Using the directions drawn in the figure, work out how large F₁ and F₂ are.
conditions: four forces are concurrent, acting through one point
object is in equilibrium

figure.description: Four forces act on an object at a single point O. One force of 8 N points horizontally to the right. A second force of 4 N points up and to the right, making a 60° angle with the 8 N force. A third force, F₁, points nearly straight up, making a further 30° angle with the 4 N force (so F₁ is 90° from the 8 N force). A fourth force, F₂, points down and to the left, making a 30° angle with the horizontal line extending to the left (opposite to the 8 N force).

solution.approach: Write each force by its angle from the 8 N force, then set the horizontal sum and the vertical sum each to zero.

steps.text: Measure every angle from the 8 N force. The 4 N force is at 60°. F₁ is a further 30° from the 4 N force, so F₁ is at 90°. F₂ is 30° below the line opposite the 8 N force, so F₂ is at 210°.
steps.equation: 8 N at 0°, 4 N at 60°, F₁ at 90°, F₂ at 210°

steps.text: For equilibrium the horizontal parts of all four forces add to zero.
steps.equation: 8 cos0° + 4 cos60° + F₁ cos90° + F₂ cos210° = 0

steps.text: cos90° = 0, so F₁ drops out of this equation. Solve for F₂.
For equilibrium the vertical parts of all four forces also add to zero.
steps.equation: 8 sin0° + 4 sin60° + F₁ sin90° + F₂ sin210° = 0

steps.text: Put in the values found so far and solve for F₁.
steps.why_this_step: sin210° = −0.5, so the F₂ term is −5.77, leaving F₁ = 5.77 − 3.46.

common_mistakes.text: Taking F₂'s angle from the horizontal as 30° instead of 210°, which flips the sign of its components and gives the wrong values.
Placing F₁ at 30° from the 8 N force instead of 90°, missing that the 30° is measured from the 4 N force, which is itself already at 60°.

question.text: Two fixed pulleys, A and B, are mounted on a rigid horizontal support. A single string runs over both pulleys; its two free ends, marked P and Q, are each pulled straight downward at the same constant speed U, as the figure shows. This action makes a mass M, hanging from the string midway between the two pulleys, rise steadily upward. At what speed does M move upward?
conditions: the string is unstretchable (inextensible)
both free ends P and Q move straight downward at the same constant speed U
pulleys A and B stay fixed in place
mass M hangs from the string, centered symmetrically between the two pulleys
each slanted string segment from a pulley down to M makes angle θ with the vertical, and θ changes as M rises

figure.description: A fixed horizontal support at the top holds two pulleys, A on the left and B on the right, a constant distance apart. Over pulley A, a string has one part hanging straight down to a free end P, and another part running diagonally down and inward to mass M, which hangs centered below, between the pulleys. Over pulley B, symmetrically, a string has one part hanging straight down to a free end Q, and another part running diagonally down and inward to the same mass M. Each diagonal segment makes angle θ with the vertical line drawn through the midpoint between A and B. Ends P and Q both move straight down at speed U.

solution.approach: Write the string's constant total length as the P-to-pulley part plus the pulley-to-M part, then differentiate to relate the speeds.

steps.text: The total length of each string (from P to pulley A, then A to mass M) stays constant, since the string is unstretchable.
As P moves down at speed U, the P-to-A part grows at rate U, so the A-to-M part must shrink at the same rate.
The rate at which the A-to-M segment shortens equals the component of M's upward velocity along that segment.
Equate the two expressions and solve for the speed of M.
steps.equation: U = v cosθ, so v = U/cosθ

final_answer.value: U/cosθ

common_mistakes.text: Multiplying by cosθ instead of dividing, and doubling for the two strings, gives 2U cosθ.
Doubling U/cosθ because two strings pull on M, instead of recognizing the same relation holds independently on each side, gives 2U/cosθ.
Multiplying by cosθ instead of dividing by it gives U cosθ.

concept_tags: rate of change of string length

question.text: For the arrangement pictured, work out how fast block M accelerates. Every surface in the picture is frictionless.
conditions: all surfaces are frictionless

figure.description: A fixed wedge has a sloped face rising from left (low) to right (high) at 30° to the horizontal. A block of mass M rests on the slope. A string tied to M runs up along the slope to a pulley fixed at the wedge's top corner, passes over it, then goes straight down, passes UNDER a second, movable pulley (wrapping round its lower half) and rises vertically to a fixed anchor on a horizontal support above. The block of mass 2M hangs directly from the axle of that movable pulley. So the movable pulley hangs in a loop of the single string, and 2M descends half as far as M moves along the slope. All surfaces, pulleys and the string are frictionless and light.

solution.approach: Link M's motion up the slope to 2M's fall through the single string over the movable pulley, then apply Newton's second law to M and to the pulley-plus-2M system.

steps.text: One string runs from M up the slope, over the fixed pulley at the top, straight down, under the movable pulley carrying 2M, and up to a fixed anchor above.

If 2M descends a distance x, both the segment above it going to the fixed pulley and the segment going to the fixed anchor shorten by x each, so 2x of string must come from M's side, meaning M moves 2x up the slope.
steps.why_this_step: This is the constraint relation, fixed purely by the string geometry, and it holds before any force equation is written.

steps.text: Write Newton's second law for M along the frictionless incline, taking up the slope as positive.
steps.equation: T − Mg sin30° = M aM = M(2a2M)

steps.text: Write Newton's second law for the 2M-plus-movable-pulley system, taking downward as positive; two string segments pull it up with tension T each.
From the second equation, T = Mg − M a2M. Substitute into the first equation and solve for a2M.
steps.equation: Mg − M a2M − Mg sin30° = 2M a2M → Mg(1 − sin30°) = 3M a2M → a2M = g(1 − sin30°)/3 = g/6

steps.text: Use aM = 2 a2M to get M's acceleration up the slope.
steps.equation: aM = 2(g/6) = g/3, directed up the incline

final_answer.value: acceleration of block M = g/3, directed up the incline (≈ 3.3 m/s² taking g = 10 m/s²)

common_mistakes.text: Writing the pulley-and-2M equation as 2T − 2Mg = 2M a2M instead of 2Mg − 2T = 2M a2M, which gives the wrong answer a = g instead of the correct g/3.

question.text: A ball of weight w and radius a rests against a smooth, vertical wall, touching it at one point on its surface. A string of length a, equal to the ball's radius, runs from a second point on the ball's surface to a point on the wall, holding the ball in place. Find the tension in this string.
conditions: ball's weight is w
ball's radius is a
wall is smooth and vertical
string length equals a (same as the radius)
string runs from a point on the ball's surface to a point on the wall

figure.description: A ball of radius a touches a smooth vertical wall at one point on its surface. A string of length a runs from a different point on the ball's surface up to a point on the wall, and this string holds the ball against gravity.

solution.approach: Since the weight and normal reaction pass through the sphere's centre, the string's line must too; this fixes its angle, and a force balance then gives the tension.

steps.text: Let O be the ball's centre, A where it touches the wall, B where the string ties to the ball, and C where the string ties to the wall. The weight and normal reaction pass through O, so for rotational equilibrium the string's line, extended, must also pass through O; hence O, B and C lie on one straight line.
B is on the sphere's surface, so OB equals the radius a; since the string has length a, C lies a further distance a beyond B along the same line.

C is a point on the wall, at the same perpendicular distance a from O as the contact point A (since the wall is a flat vertical plane), so in the right triangle formed by O, A and C, cos(angle AOC) = OA/OC.
steps.why_this_step: OA is horizontal (the radius to the wall contact point) and OC has length 2a, so this ratio fixes the string's direction from the horizontal.

steps.text: The string, along OC, makes 60° with the horizontal. Resolve forces on the sphere: weight w down, normal reaction N horizontal (away from the wall), tension T along OC toward the wall.
steps.equation: horizontal: N = T cos60°;  vertical: T sin60° = w

steps.text: Solve the vertical equation for the tension.

common_mistakes.text: Swapping the two angles of the right triangle and taking the string's angle from the horizontal as 30° instead of 60° gives the wrong T = w/sin30° = 2w.
Assuming the string is horizontal, like the wall's normal reaction, leaves no way to balance the sphere's weight vertically.

concept_tags: geometry of a sphere in contact

question.text: Assertion: To start sliding a block along a rough surface, the smallest possible applied force is required precisely when the force is applied at an angle θ equal to the angle of friction of that surface. Reason: The angle of friction has the same numerical value as the angle of repose.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: surface is rough
force F is applied at angle θ to the horizontal, as marked in the figure

figure.description: A block sits on a rough horizontal surface. A force F is applied to the block, directed up and away from the surface at angle θ measured from a horizontal reference line drawn at the top of the block (the dashed line runs horizontally from the block's top corner, and F points up and to the right, making angle θ with it).

solution.approach: Derive the force F(θ) needed to move the block and minimize it over θ, then separately check whether the angle-of-repose fact actually explains that minimum.

steps.text: Write the force balance for the block on the verge of sliding under a pull F at angle θ above the horizontal, with friction at its limiting value.
steps.equation: F cosθ = μN, N = mg − F sinθ

steps.text: Combine these into F as a function of θ alone.
F(θ) is smallest when cosθ + μ sinθ is largest, which calculus shows happens exactly when tanθ equals the coefficient ratio μ.
tanθ = μ is exactly the definition of the angle of friction λ, so the minimum force does occur at θ = λ, confirming the Assertion.
The angle of repose is the incline angle at which a block on that incline starts to slide under gravity alone, and this also works out to arctan μ — the Reason is true on its own.

This equality between angle of repose and angle of friction is a separate fact about a different setup (an incline) and is not what makes F(θ) minimum in this horizontal-pull problem, so the Reason is true but does not explain the Assertion.
steps.equation: Assertion true, Reason true, not the explanation

final_answer.value: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the Reason must be the explanation whenever both statements happen to be true, without checking that the repose-friction equality is not what produces the minimum in F(θ).

question.text: For the setup pictured, work out how the size of aA is related to the size of aB.
conditions: a rod A can only slide along its own fixed straight-line axis, guided through a fixed bracket
the rod stays in contact with a wedge's slanted surface, meeting it at a right angle (90°) at the contact point
the wedge's slanted surface makes a constant angle θ with the horizontal ground
B refers to the direction along the wedge's slanted surface

figure.description: A wedge (a right-triangular ramp) sits on the ground, its slanted face climbing from the ground at a fixed angle θ to the horizontal, up to a vertical right-hand edge. A straight rod, marked A, runs through a fixed guide bracket mounted above and to the left, so it can move only along its own straight axis. The rod's lower tip touches the wedge's slanted face, and right where they meet, the rod's axis is perpendicular to that slanted face (a 90° angle is marked there). B labels the slanted face itself, measured from that contact point up toward the top of the wedge.

solution.approach: The rod moves only along a line that is the normal to the incline, so its speed equals the component of the wedge's horizontal speed along that normal.

steps.text: The rod can move only along its guide's fixed line, which is the normal to the incline at the point where rod and wedge touch.
The incline's face makes angle θ with the horizontal, so its normal makes angle θ with the vertical, or (90° − θ) with the horizontal.
steps.equation: normal direction makes angle θ with the vertical

steps.text: For the rod's end to stay on the moving incline face, the rod's speed along the normal must equal the component of the wedge's horizontal speed along that same normal.
Simplify the component, and the same relation holds for acceleration.
steps.equation: vA = vB sinθ, so aA = aB sinθ

final_answer.value: aA = aB sinθ

common_mistakes.text: Using cosθ instead of sinθ gives aA = aB cosθ, mixing up the angle the incline makes with the horizontal and the angle its normal makes with the horizontal.

question.text: A 1 kg particle sits on a rough inclined plane that makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal ground. The particle is right at the point of sliding down. Determine the coefficient of friction acting between the particle and the incline.
conditions: particle mass is 1 kg
incline makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal
particle is on the verge of slipping (limiting friction condition)

figure.description: A ramp rises from left to right, making an angle of 30° with the horizontal ground at its base. A small block sits on the slope. The block feels a normal push N perpendicular to the slope surface, a friction force f pointing up along the slope, and its own weight split into two parts: one part pulling it down along the slope surface and the other pressing it into the slope surface.

solution.approach: At the point of slipping, the friction force reaches its maximum value and exactly balances the weight component along the incline.

steps.text: On the incline, the weight component along the surface pulls the particle down, and friction resists it, reaching its maximum since the particle is about to slip.
The common factor mg cancels from both sides, leaving a relation that depends only on the angle.
Put in θ = 30°.
steps.why_this_step: tan30° is the ratio of the weight's component along the slope, mg sin30°, to the normal force, mg cos30°; at the point of slipping the limiting friction μN equals mg sin30°, so this ratio is μ, whatever the particle's mass.

common_mistakes.text: Using sinθ instead of tanθ and taking μ = sin30° = 0.5.
Using cosθ instead of tanθ and taking μ = cos30° = 0.87.

question.text: Sliding down a smooth incline set at angle θ to the horizontal, a body reaches the bottom in time t. When that same incline is instead made rough, the body now needs 2t to get to the bottom. Find the coefficient of friction of that rough surface.
conditions: incline is smooth in the first case
the same incline is made rough in the second case
incline angle is unchanged, θ

solution.approach: Distance from rest grows as time squared, so doubling the time on the rough incline means the acceleration drops to a quarter; use that to find the friction coefficient.

steps.text: On the smooth incline, the body starts from rest and covers the length L in time t.
steps.equation: L = ½(g sinθ)t² ⇒ acceleration = g sinθ

steps.text: On the rough incline, the same length L is covered in time 2t. Since distance from rest goes as the square of time, doubling the time means the acceleration is one quarter of the smooth-incline value.
On the rough incline, friction reduces the acceleration below g sinθ by the friction term. Set this equal to the value found above and solve for μ.
steps.equation: g sinθ − μg cosθ = (g sinθ)/4 ⇒ μg cosθ = (3/4)g sinθ ⇒ μ = (3/4)tanθ

final_answer.value: (3/4) tanθ

common_mistakes.text: Assuming acceleration drops in direct proportion to time instead of its square, so a_rough = (g sinθ)/2, gives μ = (1/2)tanθ.

question.text: For the pulley arrangement shown in the figure, write the equation connecting the accelerations a₁, a₂ and a₃ of blocks 1, 2 and 3, using the string-length (constraint) method.
conditions: upper pulley is fixed to a rigid support
lower pulley is movable, suspended from the string that passes over the fixed pulley
block 1 hangs from the fixed-pulley string
blocks 2 and 3 hang from the two ends of the movable-pulley string

figure.description: A fixed pulley is mounted at the top, attached to a rigid support. A string runs over this fixed pulley: block 1 hangs from one end (the left side), and the other end connects to the axle of a second, movable pulley that hangs below it. A second string runs over this movable pulley, with block 2 hanging from its left end and block 3 hanging from its right end.

solution.approach: Write the total length of each string as constant, then differentiate twice to relate the accelerations of the three blocks.

steps.text: Let the fixed pulley be the reference. If block 1 moves down by x₁, the string over the fixed pulley shortens on the movable-pulley side by the same amount, so the movable pulley moves up by x₁.
Differentiate this length relation twice to relate the accelerations, taking downward as positive for all bodies.
For the movable pulley's own string, the sum of the two segments to blocks 2 and 3 stays constant as the pulley moves.
Differentiate this relation twice.
steps.why_this_step: The movable pulley's own displacement enters this length twice, once for each side of its string.

steps.text: Combine the two results by substituting a_p from the first relation.

final_answer.value: 2a₁ + a₂ + a₃ = 0, with all three accelerations measured downward as positive

common_mistakes.text: Treating the movable pulley as fixed and writing a₂ + a₃ = 0 directly, missing that the movable pulley itself accelerates when block 1 moves.
Writing a₁ + a₂ + a₃ = 0 instead of 2a₁ + a₂ + a₃ = 0, missing that the movable pulley's own motion enters its string's length twice, once for each side.

question.text: A small particle is put at rest on the inner surface of a hollow hemispherical bowl whose radius is R. Friction between particle and bowl has coefficient μ = 1/√3. Measured from the lowest point of the bowl, what is the greatest height at which the particle can stay at rest without sliding?
conditions: particle is at rest on the inner surface of the hemisphere
radius of the hemisphere is R
coefficient of friction is μ = 1/√3

solution.approach: The particle slips once the weight's component along the bowl's curved surface exceeds the maximum friction; that condition fixes the angle and hence the height.

steps.text: At the point where the particle rests, the surface makes angle θ with the horizontal, measured from the bottom of the bowl. Split the weight into a part along the surface and a part perpendicular to it.
steps.equation: along surface: mg sinθ, perpendicular: mg cosθ

steps.text: Balance forces perpendicular to the surface and along it: the normal force matches the perpendicular part of the weight, and friction matches the part along the surface.
steps.equation: N = mg cosθ, f = mg sinθ

steps.text: The particle stays still as long as the needed friction does not exceed the maximum friction available. The greatest height is reached exactly when friction reaches this maximum.
steps.equation: f = μN ⇒ mg sinθ = μ·mg cosθ ⇒ tanθ = μ

steps.text: Use μ = 1/√3 to get the angle, then find the height above the bottom of the bowl from the bowl's radius.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the height as R cosθ, the vertical drop from the sphere's centre to the particle, instead of R(1 − cosθ), the height measured from the bottom of the bowl, gives (√3/2)R.
Mixing up sinθ and cosθ while finding the height gives R sinθ = R/2 instead of R(1 − cosθ).

question.text: Three separate blocks — masses 3 kg, 2 kg and 1 kg — are lined up touching each other on a smooth flat surface, in that order. A horizontal push of 12 N is exerted on the 3 kg block.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Calculate the overall force acting on the 2 kg block.

conditions: smooth (frictionless) surface
three blocks touch in a row: 3 kg, then 2 kg, then 1 kg
12 N horizontal force applied on the 3 kg block

figure.description: Three blocks touch each other in a row on a horizontal frictionless surface: a 3 kg block, then a 2 kg block, then a 1 kg block, arranged left to right. A horizontal force of 12 N pushes on the outer (left) face of the 3 kg block, directed toward the other two blocks.

solution.approach: Find the common acceleration of all three blocks together, then apply Newton's second law to the 2 kg block alone.

steps.text: All three blocks touch and move together on the smooth surface, so treat them as one combined mass to find the acceleration.
This acceleration is the same for every block, including the 2 kg block in the middle.
The net force on the 2 kg block is its mass times this acceleration.
steps.why_this_step: Newton's second law gives the net force on a block directly from its own mass and the common acceleration, without needing to know the individual contact forces on it.

final_answer.value: 4 N

common_mistakes.text: Using only the 2 kg and 1 kg blocks' combined mass to find the acceleration, forgetting the 3 kg block is also part of the system being pushed.
Taking the net force on the 2 kg block as the full applied 12 N instead of scaling it down by mass.

question.text: A block sits motionless on a rough incline tilted at 30° from the horizontal. Between the block and the incline, the static friction coefficient equals 0.8, and the friction force acting on the block measures 10 N. Using g = 10 m/s², determine the block's mass, in kilograms.
conditions: block rests on the incline (static equilibrium)
incline angle = 30° from horizontal
coefficient of static friction = 0.8
friction force on the block = 10 N
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Since the block is not sliding, friction exactly balances the pull of gravity along the incline, so set that friction force equal to 10 N and solve for the mass.

steps.text: The block rests without sliding, so along the incline the only two forces are gravity's component down the slope and friction up the slope; these must balance.
Put in the given friction force, the angle, and g, then solve for the mass.
Check that this friction is within what the surface can supply, using the given coefficient of static friction.
steps.equation: μₛN = 0.8 × 2.0 × 10 × cos30° ≈ 13.9 N, which is more than 10 N, so the block can indeed stay still

common_mistakes.text: Using the friction formula μmg instead of the balance mg sinθ, ignoring that the incline reduces the normal force, gives m = 10/(0.8 × 10) = 1.25 kg.
Mixing up sinθ and cosθ in the balance equation gives m = 10/(10cos30°) ≈ 1.15 kg.

question.text: A frictionless inclined plane of length L, set at angle θ to the horizontal, stands inside a lift. The lift is moving downward but slowing down, with retardation a. A body starts from rest at the top of the incline and slides down its length. How much time does it take to slide down?
conditions: inclined plane is smooth (frictionless)
length of incline is L
angle of incline is θ
lift moves downward with retardation a
body starts from rest

solution.approach: Work in the lift's frame: its upward retardation adds a downward pseudo force, so the body slides down with effective gravity g + a instead of g.

steps.text: The lift moves down but is slowing down, so its acceleration points upward, with size a. In the lift's frame, this adds a pseudo force on the body, directed downward.
The effective downward pull on the body is now gravity plus the pseudo force, so the effective gravity is g + a.
The incline is smooth, so the only force along the incline is the component of the effective weight along it. Find the acceleration down the incline.
Use the equation for distance from rest to find the time to slide the full length L.
steps.equation: L = ½(g + a)sinθ · t² ⇒ t = √(2L / ((g + a) sinθ))

final_answer.value: √(2L / ((g + a) sin θ))

common_mistakes.text: Treating the lift's retardation as making the effective gravity smaller instead of larger gives g − a in place of g + a.
Ignoring the lift's motion entirely and using plain gravity gives the answer for a stationary lift, √(2L / (g sinθ)).

question.text: A rope with negligible weight runs over a frictionless pulley. On one end, a 20 kg monkey grips the rope tightly; tied to the other end is a hanging bundle of bananas that also weighs 20 kg. The monkey spots the bananas above and begins climbing up the rope toward them.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: While the monkey is climbing, do the bananas rise, fall, or stay where they are?

parts.label: b
parts.asks: While the monkey is climbing, does the space separating her from the bananas shrink, grow, or stay the same?

parts.label: c
parts.asks: If the monkey then lets go of the rope and falls freely, what then happens to the gap between her and the bananas as she falls?

parts.label: d
parts.asks: If, before hitting the ground, the monkey catches hold of the rope again to stop falling, what happens to the bananas at that moment?

conditions: rope is light (negligible mass)
pulley is frictionless
monkey's mass equals the bananas' mass: 20 kg each

solution.approach: The rope is light and the pulley is frictionless, so the tension is the same on both sides at every instant, and the monkey and the bunch have equal mass.

steps.text: Write Newton's second law for the monkey and for the bananas, taking upward as positive.
steps.equation: T − mg = m aₘ (monkey), T − mg = m a_b (bananas)

steps.text: Both equations use the same tension T and the same mass m (20 kg each), so the two equations are identical at every instant.
steps.why_this_step: A single string over a frictionless, massless pulley carries the same tension throughout, and equal masses under equal tension get equal acceleration.

steps.text: So aₘ = a_b always, whatever the monkey does. Starting from rest, this makes their velocity and displacement equal at every instant too.
(a) The monkey climbs upward, so aₘ is upward; since a_b = aₘ, the bananas also move up, rising by the same amount at the same time as the monkey.
(b) Since the monkey and the bananas share the same velocity at every instant (both start at rest with equal acceleration), the gap between them does not change.

(c) When the monkey lets go, her hand exerts no force on the rope, so T = 0 there; with T = 0 the bananas obey −mg = m a_b, i.e. a_b = −g, the same as the monkey's free-fall acceleration, so the constant-distance result of (b) continues unchanged while she falls.
steps.equation: T = 0, aₘ = a_b = −g, distance stays constant

steps.text: (d) When the monkey grips the rope again, the tension she generates to slow her fall is the same tension felt by the bananas, so the bananas decelerate exactly as she does; the bananas do the same thing the monkey does, and the gap between them stays the same throughout.
steps.equation: aₘ = a_b again, bananas slow down like the monkey does

final_answer.value: (a) Move up. (b) Distance remains constant. (c) Distance remains constant while she is falling. (d) The bananas do exactly what the monkey does (they also decelerate the same way), so the distance between them stays constant.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the bananas stay still because the monkey is doing the climbing, ignoring that the pulley makes the tension pull the bananas up too.
Thinking the gap closes because the monkey is climbing toward the bananas, forgetting the bananas rise by the same amount at the same time.

question.text: A wedge with a slope angled 37° above the horizontal (use sin 37° = 3/5) carries a small block of mass m resting on its slanted face. The wedge itself is driven so that it gains speed toward the right at a steady 3 m/s² (take g = 10 m/s²). What frictional force, acting between the block and the wedge's surface, is needed to keep the block from sliding down or up the slope while this happens?
conditions: incline angle is 37° from the horizontal
the wedge (incline) accelerates horizontally to the right at 3 m/s²
block does not slide relative to the incline
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A triangular wedge stands on level ground with its vertical face on the LEFT. Its sloped face runs from the top of that vertical face down to the right, meeting the ground at the wedge's bottom-right tip, where the 37° angle between slope and ground is marked; so the slope is high on the left and low on the right. A block of mass m rests on the sloped face. The whole wedge accelerates horizontally to the RIGHT (toward the low end of the slope) at 3 m/s², shown by an arrow beside the wedge.

solution.approach: In the wedge's accelerating frame the block is held by gravity, a leftward pseudo-force, the normal force and friction; resolve along the slope to isolate friction directly.

steps.text: Since the block does not slide relative to the incline, it shares the wedge's acceleration exactly.
steps.equation: a(block) = a(wedge) = 3 m/s², horizontal, to the right

steps.text: Work in the wedge's own frame, where the block is at rest under an added pseudo-force equal to its mass times the wedge's acceleration, directed opposite to that acceleration.
steps.equation: pseudo-force = m × 3 = 3m N, directed left, opposite the rightward acceleration

steps.text: Resolve gravity and the pseudo-force along the slope, which rises to the left at 37° to the horizontal, taking up-slope as positive.
steps.equation: gravity along slope = −m g sin37° = −6m N (down-slope); pseudo-force along slope = +m × 3 × cos37° = +2.4m N (up-slope)

steps.text: For the block to stay at rest in this frame, friction must balance the sum of these two along-slope components.
steps.equation: f = m g sin37° − m × 3 × cos37° = 6m − 2.4m = 3.6m N, directed up the slope

final_answer.value: f = 3.6m N, directed up the incline, where m is the block's mass in kg (equivalently f = 0.36mg).

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring that the incline itself is accelerating and treating it like a stationary incline gives friction as only the gravity component along the slope, m g sin37° = 6m N, instead of 3.6m N.
Adding the pseudo-force's along-slope component to gravity's instead of subtracting it gives m g sin37° + m × 3 × cos37° = 8.4m N instead of the correct 3.6m N.

question.text: A stick, labelled AB and having weight w₁, leans across a ball of weight w₂ as pictured; the ball also touches a vertical wall and the ground. The ground beneath is rough, but no friction acts at either the stick-and-ball contact or the ball-and-wall contact. Produce separate free-body force diagrams for the ball and for the stick. Also work out why no friction can act at the ball-ground contact.
conditions: rod AB has weight w₁
sphere has weight w₂
ground is rough
no friction between rod and sphere
no friction between sphere and wall
contact point C (rod-sphere) is closer to A than to B (AC < CB)

figure.description: A vertical wall (brick) stands on the left, meeting a horizontal, rough ground at a right angle. A rod runs from its upper end A, which is in the air just above the top of the wall and touches nothing, down to its lower end B resting on the ground off to the right, like the hypotenuse of a right triangle. A sphere sits in the corner between the wall and the ground, touching both, and also touching the underside of the rod at a point C on the rod; C lies closer to A than to B (AC < CB).

solution.approach: Draw one force per contact for rod and sphere; A touches nothing, and since the sphere's other contacts are frictionless, ground friction on it must be zero.

steps.text: The rod touches only the ground (at B, rough) and the sphere (at C, smooth); its end A near the wall touches nothing.
steps.equation: rod: weight w₁ (down, at its centre of gravity) + N_ground and f_ground (at B) + N_sphere (at C, perpendicular to the rod, since rod–sphere is frictionless)

steps.text: The sphere touches the wall, the ground, and the rod; the rod–sphere and sphere–wall contacts are frictionless, so those two forces act along the radius, straight through the sphere's centre.
steps.equation: sphere: weight w₂ (down, at the centre) + N_wall (horizontal, radial) + N_rod (reaction to the rod's N_sphere, radial)

steps.text: Since the sphere's weight, the wall's normal reaction, and the rod's normal reaction all pass through the sphere's centre, none of them can turn the sphere about that centre.
steps.equation: sum of moments about the sphere's centre from weight, N_wall, N_rod = 0

steps.text: If the ground exerted friction on the sphere, it would act tangentially at the ground contact, with a moment arm equal to the sphere's radius, and nothing else could balance that turning effect.
steps.equation: f_ground_on_sphere ≠ 0 would leave a net moment about the centre
steps.why_this_step: A body in equilibrium cannot have a leftover, unbalanced moment, so this friction must be zero.

steps.text: So the ground can only push the sphere perpendicular to itself; the sphere's forces are its weight, the wall's normal reaction, the rod's normal reaction, and the ground's normal reaction only.
steps.equation: sphere: weight w₂ + N_wall + N_rod + N_ground (no friction)

final_answer.value: Rod AB: its weight w₁ at its centre of gravity, the ground's normal reaction and friction at B, and the sphere's normal reaction at C (perpendicular to the rod); nothing acts at A, since it touches nothing. Sphere: its weight w₂ at the centre, the normal reactions from the wall and from the rod (both radial, passing through the centre), and the ground's normal reaction (also radial); the ground exerts no friction on the sphere, because the other three forces already pass through the centre and leave no turning effect for friction to balance.

common_mistakes.text: Drawing a force on the rod at end A even though A touches neither the wall nor anything else in the figure.
Drawing ground friction on the sphere by analogy with the rod's rough ground contact, without checking that the sphere's other forces already balance about its centre.

question.text: A 2 kg block sits on a ramp inclined at 37° to the horizontal. A 4 N force pushes the block up along the ramp's surface. Between the block and the ramp, the coefficients of friction are μₛ = 0.4 (static) and μₖ = 0.3 (kinetic).

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out the friction force acting on the block.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Decide whether the block starts moving, and if it does, work out its acceleration.

conditions: block rests on an incline of 37° to the horizontal
mass of block = 2 kg
4 N force applied along the incline surface, directed up the slope

figure.description: A 2 kg block rests on a ramp tilted at 37° to the horizontal, with friction coefficients μₛ = 0.4 and μₖ = 0.3 between the block and the ramp. A 4 N force pushes the block up the slope, along the ramp's surface.

solution.approach: Compare the weight component along the incline with the applied force and the maximum static friction to see if the block moves, then find kinetic friction and acceleration.

steps.text: Take g = 10 m/s², so W = 20 N. Resolve the weight along and perpendicular to the incline: W sin37° = 20×0.6 = 12 N down the slope and W cos37° = 20×0.8 = 16 N into the slope.
steps.equation: W sin37° = 12 N, W cos37° = 16 N

steps.text: The normal reaction equals the perpendicular component, since nothing else acts perpendicular to the incline.
Find the maximum static friction and compare it with the unbalanced force before friction is included.
steps.equation: f(max static) = μₛR = 0.4×16 = 6.4 N; unbalanced force = 12 − 4 = 8 N

steps.text: Since 8 N exceeds 6.4 N, friction cannot keep the block still, so it slides down and kinetic friction acts up the incline.
Find the acceleration from the net force along the incline.
steps.equation: a = (12 − 4 − 4.8)/2 = 1.6 m/s², directed down the incline

final_answer.value: (a) friction = 4.8 N, kinetic, acting up the incline; (b) the block moves down the incline with acceleration 1.6 m/s²

common_mistakes.text: Comparing only the weight component (12 N) with the maximum static friction, without subtracting the 4 N applied force, still concludes sliding but gives a = 3.6 m/s².
Adding the applied 4 N to the weight component instead of subtracting it gives an unbalanced force of 16 N and a = 5.6 m/s².

question.text: A rod of mass m is held between two frictionless walls that let it slide only along one fixed straight line; as it slides, it keeps touching the sloped face of a wedge of mass M at a constant right angle to that face, as the figure shows. Every contact surface here is smooth, with no friction anywhere. Compute the magnitude of the rod's acceleration, then compute the magnitude of the wedge's acceleration.
conditions: rod mass is m
wedge mass is M
rod is held between two smooth (frictionless) walls, sliding along one fixed straight line
rod stays perpendicular to the wedge's sloped surface at all times
every surface involved is frictionless
the wedge's sloped face makes angle α with the horizontal

figure.description: A wall fixed in space is mounted at an angle in the upper-left region. A rod is held in a channel between two smooth walls so it can only slide along this fixed line; it slides down-and-right or up-and-left along this direction. The rod's lower tip presses against the sloped face of a wedge sitting on the ground, whose base angle with the horizontal is α; the rod stays exactly perpendicular to this sloped face at all times. The wedge itself can slide horizontally.

solution.approach: Apply Newton's second law to the rod along its guide and to the wedge along the horizontal, then combine using a1 = a2 sinα, the rod-wedge acceleration constraint.

steps.text: The contact between rod and wedge is frictionless, so the contact force N acts along the rod's own axis, the common normal.
Along its guide, the rod feels this force N pushing it back and the component of its own weight pulling it toward the wedge.
The wedge feels the reaction to N, whose horizontal part is the only horizontal force on it.

The rod's tip must stay on the wedge face, so the rod's velocity relative to the wedge has no component perpendicular to the face. The rod moves along the face normal at speed v1 and the wedge moves horizontally at v2, whose component along that normal is v2 sinα; hence v1 = v2 sinα and a1 = a2 sinα.
Substitute N = M a2/sinα into the rod equation and use the constraint to write everything in terms of a2.
steps.equation: m a2 sinα = mg cosα − M a2/sinα

steps.text: Solve for the wedge's acceleration, then get the rod's acceleration from the constraint.
steps.equation: a2 = mg sinα cosα/(M + m sin²α); a1 = a2 sinα = mg sin²α cosα/(M + m sin²α)

final_answer.value: acceleration of the wedge a2 = mg sinα cosα/(M + m sin²α); acceleration of the rod along its guide a1 = mg sin²α cosα/(M + m sin²α)

common_mistakes.text: Using mg sinα instead of mg cosα for the weight component along the rod's guide gives a2 = mg sin²α/(M + m sin²α), a different formula.

question.text: A box car starts from rest (v = 0) and accelerates horizontally at a = 5 m/s² along the î direction. Take g = 10 m/s². Inside the car, on its frictionless floor, a 2 kg object is slid with an initial velocity of 10 m/s along î, measured relative to the car.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Describe the motion of the object relative to the car.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find when the object reaches its original position relative to the box car.

conditions: box car has initial velocity v = 0
box car acceleration a = 5 m/s², direction î
g = 10 m/s²
object mass = 2 kg
floor of the box car is frictionless
object's initial velocity relative to the car = 10 m/s, direction î

solution.approach: The floor is frictionless, so the object feels no horizontal force in the ground frame and keeps its initial velocity; subtract the car's motion to get its relative motion.

steps.text: In the ground frame the floor exerts no horizontal force on the object, so it keeps moving at its initial 10 m/s forever.
The car starts from rest and accelerates at 5 m/s², so its own position grows as a half-a-t-squared curve.
The object's position relative to the car is the difference of the two, giving its relative velocity by differentiating.
This means relative to the car the object moves forward, decelerating uniformly at 5 m/s², exactly like a ball thrown upward against gravity, until it momentarily stops relative to the car.
steps.equation: v_rel = 0 at t = 2 s, having moved 10 m forward relative to the car

steps.text: After that it reverses and speeds up backward relative to the car at the same constant 5 m/s². It returns to its starting position relative to the car when x_rel = 0 again.
steps.equation: 10t − 2.5t² = 0  ⟹  t = 4 s (moving at −10 m/s relative to the car at that instant)

final_answer.value: (a) relative to the car, the object moves forward, decelerates uniformly at 5 m/s², stops momentarily at t = 2 s after moving 10 m forward, then accelerates backward at 5 m/s²; (b) it returns to its original position relative to the car at t = 4 s

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the object also accelerates at 5 m/s² because the car does gives the wrong relative motion; the object feels no horizontal force at all since the floor is frictionless.
Taking the instant the object is momentarily at rest relative to the car (t = 2 s, 10 m ahead) as the return time, instead of x_rel = 0 at t = 4 s.

question.text: A 1 kg ball hangs motionlessly at point P, held there by two thin, weightless strings: one, OP, running up to a fixed point O, and another, RP, running horizontally to a wall anchor. At this position, string OP is inclined at θ = 45° to the vertical. String RP is then snipped, and the ball swings along a circular arc to a new point Q, where the remaining string (call it OQ) again makes a 45° angle with the vertical, on the far side. Taking g = 10 m/s², compute the tension in the string at position P (before RP was cut) and the tension in the string at position Q (once RP has been cut).
conditions: ball mass is 1 kg
the strings OP and RP are light (weightless)
ball is initially held at P by string OP (to fixed point O) and string RP (horizontal, to a wall anchor)
at P, string OP makes an angle of 45° with the vertical
string RP is cut, and the ball swings to point Q where string OQ also makes 45° with the vertical, on the opposite side
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A fixed support point O sits at the top. A ball hangs from O by a string; at its first position P, this string is tilted 45° from the vertical line through O, and a separate horizontal string ties the ball to a wall anchor, holding it at that tilt. A dashed curved path shows the ball's swing once the horizontal string is released, arcing down and across to a second position Q, symmetric to P, where the string from O is again tilted 45° from vertical but on the opposite side.

solution.approach: At P, balance the string OP against gravity and the horizontal string RP. At Q, the ball is momentarily at rest, so only the weight component along OQ acts.

steps.text: At P, resolve the ball's weight against the tension in OP and the horizontal tension in RP.
Solve the vertical equation for the tension in OP, using θ = 45° and g = 10 m/s².
After RP is cut, the ball swings on OP and rises to Q, which sits at the same height as P, so its speed there is zero.
steps.why_this_step: The swing is smooth, and P and Q lie at equal height above the lowest point of the arc.

steps.text: At Q the speed is zero, so the centripetal term is zero and only the weight component along OQ balances the tension.
The tensions are T(OP) = 10√2 N and T(OQ) = 5√2 N.
steps.equation: T(OP) ≈ 14.1 N, T(OQ) = mg cosθ = 10cos45° = 5√2 N ≈ 7.1 N

common_mistakes.text: Using T(OP) = mg cosθ, the formula that belongs to OQ, gives 5√2 N ≈ 7.1 N instead of 10√2 N ≈ 14.1 N.
Assuming the string tension stays the same after RP is cut gives T(OQ) = 10√2 N ≈ 14.1 N instead of 5√2 N ≈ 7.1 N.

question.text: A frame that moves at constant velocity is inertial, so the pseudo force needed in it is always zero. State whether this claim is true or false.

solution.approach: A frame moving with constant velocity has zero acceleration, and the pseudo force is proportional to the frame's acceleration.

steps.text: Recall the pseudo-force formula for a frame with acceleration a(frame).
A frame moving with constant velocity does not speed up, slow down, or change direction, so its acceleration is zero.
Substitute zero acceleration into the formula: the pseudo force is zero, so the statement is true.

final_answer.value: True

question.text: A block of mass 6 kg lies on a rough inclined surface, as pictured. Work out the applied force F, directed up along the slope, that is needed in each situation below. Take g = 10 m/s².

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the force so that the block remains at rest on the slope

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the force so that the block travels down the slope at a steady, unchanging speed

parts.label: c
parts.asks: the force so that the block travels up the slope while gaining speed at a rate of 4 m/s²

conditions: block mass is 6 kg
the incline makes a 60° angle with the horizontal
static friction coefficient μₛ = 0.6
kinetic friction coefficient μₖ = 0.4
g = 10 m/s²
the third case requires the block to speed up the slope at 4 m/s²

figure.description: A slope rises from left to right at 60° above the horizontal ground. A 6 kg block sits on this slope. A force F acts on the block along the slope's surface, pointing up and away from it, up the incline. Between the block and the slope, the static friction coefficient is 0.6 and the kinetic friction coefficient is 0.4.

solution.approach: Balance F, the weight component, and friction along the incline for each situation, using static friction where the block stays still and kinetic friction where it moves.

steps.text: Find the weight components along and perpendicular to the 60° incline.

For part (a), the block tends to slide down on its own since mg sinθ exceeds the maximum static friction, so F (up the slope) plus friction at its maximum keep it still; F can range between the case where friction helps most and where it opposes most.
steps.equation: F_min = mg sinθ − μₛ mg cosθ = 51.96 − 0.6×30 = 33.96 N

steps.text: The largest F before the block tends to slide up instead is found with friction now acting down the slope at its maximum.
steps.equation: F_max = mg sinθ + μₛ mg cosθ = 51.96 + 18 = 69.96 N

steps.text: For part (b), the block moves down at constant velocity, so kinetic friction acts up the slope and the net force is zero.
steps.equation: F = mg sinθ − μₖ mg cosθ = 51.96 − 0.4×30 = 39.96 N

steps.text: For part (c), the block moves up with acceleration 4 m/s², so kinetic friction now acts down the slope, opposing the upward motion.
steps.equation: F − mg sinθ − μₖ mg cosθ = ma

steps.text: Put in the numbers and solve for F.
steps.why_this_step: Moving up needs F to overcome both the weight component and friction, plus supply the extra force for the given acceleration.

final_answer.value: (a) F between 33.96 N and 69.96 N keeps the block stationary, (b) F = 39.96 N moves it down at constant velocity, (c) F = 87.96 N moves it up with acceleration 4 m/s².

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting that friction helps hold the block in part (a) and taking F = mg sinθ = 51.96 N alone, ignoring friction's contribution.
Using the static coefficient μₛ instead of the kinetic coefficient μₖ in part (b), giving F = 51.96 − 0.6×30 = 33.96 N.
Leaving out friction in part (c) and taking F = mg sinθ + ma = 51.96 + 24 = 75.96 N.

question.text: Block A (4 kg) and block C (20 kg) are joined by a string that runs over a pulley fixed at the left edge of a tabletop; block B (8 kg) and the same block C are joined by a second string running over another pulley fixed at the right edge of the tabletop, with C hanging between the two pulleys. Block A slides on a tabletop where the coefficient of friction is 0.2, whereas block B slides on a tabletop with no friction at all. Using g = 10 m/s², work out the common acceleration of the three blocks and the tension in each of the two strings.
conditions: A (4 kg) rests on a table with friction coefficient 0.2 against that table
B (8 kg) rests on a frictionless table
C (20 kg) hangs between two pulleys, one string to A and one string to B
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A horizontal tabletop has a rectangular opening cut through its middle. A small pulley is fixed at each of the two facing edges of this opening: a left pulley at the edge of the left part of the table and a right pulley at the edge of the right part. Block A (4 kg) rests on the left part of the tabletop, to the left of the opening. Block B (8 kg) rests on the right part of the tabletop, to the right of the opening. Block C (20 kg) hangs inside the opening, below table level, between the two pulleys. One string is tied to block A, runs horizontally to the right along the table to the left pulley, passes over the top of that pulley, and drops vertically down its inner (right) side to the top of block C. A second string is tied to block B, runs horizontally to the left along the table to the right pulley, passes over the top of that pulley, and drops vertically down its inner (left) side to the top of the same block C. So block C is held by two vertical string segments and, as it falls, block A slides right and block B slides left, both toward the opening. Call the tension in the string on A's side T₁ and in the string on B's side T₂. Block A's surface has coefficient of friction 0.2; block B's surface is frictionless.

solution.approach: Both strings end on the same falling block C, so A, B and C all share one acceleration magnitude; write Newton's second law for each block and solve together.

steps.text: Both strings drop onto block C from its two pulleys, so whatever distance A slides right and B slides left, C falls by exactly that much in the same time.
Block A rests on the rough surface, so friction opposes its motion toward the pulley.
Write Newton's second law for A along the table.
Block B moves on the frictionless surface, so only tension acts on it horizontally.
Write Newton's second law for the falling block C.
steps.equation: mC g − T1 − T2 = mC a → 200 − T1 − T2 = 20a

steps.text: Substitute T1 and T2 from the first two equations into C's equation and solve for a.
Use a = 6 m/s² to find the two tensions.

final_answer.value: a = 6 m/s²; T1 (string to A) = 32 N; T2 (string to B) = 48 N

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the friction on A and solving it as a plain three-block system, giving a = 6.25 m/s² instead of the correct 6 m/s².

question.text: Assertion: Suppose three forces F₁, F₂ and F₃ all act through one point, with F₁ making 30° with F₂ and 120° with F₃. Under these conditions the forces are unable to balance one another. Reason: For this to happen, at least one of the angles between the forces has to be greater than 180°.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: three forces act at a single common point (concurrent forces)

solution.approach: Three concurrent forces balance only when their directions surround the common point, so every angle between consecutive forces must stay under 180°; check whether that holds here.

steps.text: Three concurrent forces stay in equilibrium only when their directions surround the common point, so the three angles between consecutive forces, added all the way around, equal 360° and each one stays below 180°.
F2 is 30° from F1 and F3 is 120° from F1. The widest F2 and F3 can be apart, measured through F1, is the sum of these two angles.
Even in this widest case, all three forces lie inside a 150° arc, less than 180°. The angle needed to close the loop back to F1, on the other side, is 360° minus this arc.
steps.why_this_step: A group of vectors confined to an arc under 180° always has a component along one fixed direction, so a positive-weighted sum of them can never reach zero.

steps.text: Lami's theorem needs the sine of each of the three angles around the point to be positive, which requires every angle to stay under 180°. Here one angle is always at least 210°, so no set of positive force magnitudes can make F1, F2 and F3 balance.

So the three forces cannot be in equilibrium under the stated angles, making the Assertion true, and this happens exactly because one of the three angles around the point is always greater than 180°, so the Reason is true and correctly explains the Assertion.
steps.equation: Answer: option (a) — both true, Reason explains Assertion

final_answer.value: Both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Taking F3 as 120−30 = 90° from F2 and checking Lami's theorem with 30°, 90°, 120° gives every sine positive, which looks like a valid equilibrium and wrongly marks the Assertion false.
Correctly seeing the Assertion is true but checking the Reason only against 30°, 90° and 120°, none over 180°, and missing the real closing angle of 210°, wrongly marks the Reason false.

question.text: A smooth circular ring of radius a stands in a vertical plane with its centre at C. Two beads, each of mass m, sit on the ring: bead A at the topmost point (directly above C) and bead B at the point level with C on one side (so CB is horizontal), joined to each other by a string of length √2 a stretched along the chord AB. The beads are released from rest and can slide along the ring. Just after release, find the tension in the string and the acceleration of bead B.
conditions: ring is smooth (frictionless) and circular, radius a, fixed in a vertical plane
two beads of equal mass m, free to slide along the ring
string joining the beads has length √2 a, along chord AB
bead A is at the top of the ring (directly above centre C)
bead B is at the point on the ring level with C (CB horizontal)
beads released from rest

figure.description: Circle of radius a, centre C, vertical plane. Point A is the topmost point of the circle, directly above C. Point B is the leftmost point of the circle, at the same height as C, so CB is horizontal and CA is vertical. A straight string connects A and B (the chord), length √2 a.

solution.approach: Write each bead's tangential equation of motion on the ring, then use the fact that the string's length along AB cannot change at the first instant.

steps.text: At A, gravity points straight along the radius, so only the string's part along the ring's direction can start A moving.
At B, gravity points straight along the ring's own direction, while the string pulls partly against it.
Since the string cannot stretch, the two beads must move toward or away from each other along the string at matching rates; at the first instant this makes their along-the-ring accelerations equal.
Solve the two equations together for the tension and for the acceleration of B.

final_answer.value: T = mg/√2 ≈ 0.71mg, acceleration of B = g/2, directed along the ring, straight down

common_mistakes.text: Ignoring the string and treating B as a free bead on the ring gives an acceleration of g, missing that the string's pull reduces it to g/2.

question.text: A wedge with an incline angle θ is fixed to the floor of an elevator that moves upward with acceleration a. A block of mass m rests on the frictionless inclined surface of the wedge. Find the acceleration of the block relative to the wedge.
conditions: wedge is fixed to the elevator floor
elevator accelerates upward with acceleration a
wedge incline angle = θ
block mass = m
no friction between block and wedge surface

figure.description: An elevator box accelerates straight upward with acceleration a. Fixed to its floor is a wedge whose sloped surface rises from the floor at angle θ to the horizontal. A block of mass m sits on this sloped surface.

solution.approach: In the elevator's frame a downward pseudo force ma adds to gravity, giving an effective gravity (g + a) that pushes the block down the frictionless incline.

steps.text: In the elevator's own frame, a pseudo force ma acts downward on the block, opposite to the elevator's upward acceleration a.
This pseudo force adds to the block's true weight mg, giving an effective downward weight of m(g + a).
The incline is frictionless, so only the component of this effective weight along the incline accelerates the block relative to the wedge.
