This acceleration is directed down the incline, relative to the wedge.
steps.equation: a_rel = (g + a) sinθ, down the incline

final_answer.value: a_rel = (g + a) sinθ, directed down the incline

common_mistakes.text: Using g sinθ alone and ignoring the elevator's acceleration gives (g) sinθ, missing the added pseudo force from the upward-accelerating elevator.
Subtracting a from g instead of adding it gives (g − a) sinθ, treating the elevator's acceleration as reducing the effective weight instead of increasing it.

question.text: Three blocks of masses m₁ = 10 kg, m₂ = 20 kg and m₃ = 30 kg rest on a smooth horizontal table and are joined in a line by light, horizontal strings: one string of tension T₁ between m₁ and m₂, and another string of tension T₂ between m₂ and m₃. A horizontal pull of F = 60 N acts on m₃, directed away from m₂.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the tensions T₁ and T₂ in the two strings.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the tension T₂ immediately after the string between m₁ and m₂ suddenly breaks.

conditions: smooth horizontal table
blocks joined in a line by light strings
F = 60 N applied on m₃, directed away from m₂

figure.description: Three blocks m₁, m₂, m₃ sit in a row on a horizontal frictionless table, ordered left to right as m₁, m₂, m₃. A light string of tension T₁ joins m₁ to m₂, and a light string of tension T₂ joins m₂ to m₃. A horizontal force F acts on the right (outer) face of m₃, pulling the whole line to the right, away from m₂.

solution.approach: Use the whole system to find the acceleration, then isolate one block to find each tension; repeat with the reduced system after the string snaps.

steps.text: Find the acceleration of the three connected blocks under F.
T₁ pulls only m₁, so it equals m₁ times the common acceleration.
T₂ pulls the combined m₁ and m₂, so it equals their total mass times the acceleration.
After the string between m₁ and m₂ snaps, only m₂ and m₃ remain connected; find their new common acceleration.
T₂ now pulls only m₂, so it equals m₂ times the new acceleration.

final_answer.value: (a) T₁ = 10 N, T₂ = 30 N; (b) T₂ = 24 N after the string between m₁ and m₂ snaps

common_mistakes.text: Keeping the acceleration at 1 m/s² after the string snaps instead of recomputing it for the smaller connected mass, giving T₂ = 20×1 = 20 N instead of 24 N.
Computing T₁ as the force needed to accelerate m₂ and m₃ together instead of m₁ alone, giving T₁ = 50 N instead of 10 N.

question.text: Block A has a mass of 1 kg and block B has a mass of 2 kg. Block A's acceleration is (2î) m/s² and block B's acceleration is (−4ĵ) m/s², measured in the ground frame.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the pseudo force on block A, as measured in a reference frame attached to block B.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the pseudo force on block B, as measured in a reference frame attached to block A.

conditions: accelerations given as vectors using unit vectors î (x-direction) and ĵ (y-direction)

solution.approach: The pseudo force on an object, as seen from an accelerating frame, is minus the object's mass times the frame's own acceleration.

steps.text: Write the pseudo-force formula for an object of mass m viewed from a frame accelerating at a(frame).
For part (a), the frame is block B, so a(frame) = a(B) = (−4ĵ) m/s², and the object is block A with mass 1 kg.
For part (b), the frame is block A, so a(frame) = a(A) = (2î) m/s², and the object is block B with mass 2 kg.

final_answer.value: (a) 4ĵ N (4 N along +y); (b) −4î N (4 N along −x)

common_mistakes.text: Dropping the negative sign in the pseudo-force formula gives −4ĵ N on A and 4î N on B, both pointing the wrong way.

question.text: A worn plank leans against a round cylinder that lies on rough ground; the lower end of the plank also touches the rough ground directly, while the plank's other end rises up, resting on top of the cylinder. There is no friction between the plank and the cylinder, though friction exists at the ground contacts. Sketch separate free-body diagrams to display the following.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Show every force acting on the plank.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Show every force acting on the cylinder.

conditions: plank is rough; ground is rough
no friction between plank and cylinder
one end of the plank touches the ground directly
the rest of the plank rests on top of the cylinder, which also touches the ground

figure.description: A cylinder (circular cross-section) rests on the ground. A long plank leans up at an angle from the ground, passing over the top of the cylinder partway along its length, so the plank is supported at two points: one end resting directly on the ground, and the middle/upper part resting on top of the cylinder. Neither the plank nor the cylinder is fixed or attached to anything else.

solution.approach: A normal reaction at every contact, friction where the contact is rough, each weight at its centre; on a circular body a smooth contact's normal reaction passes through the centre.

steps.text: The plank touches the rough ground at its lower end and touches the smooth cylinder at one point partway along its length, so four forces act on it in total.
steps.equation: plank: weight, ground normal, ground friction, cylinder normal

steps.text: At the ground contact the surface is rough, so both a normal reaction and a friction force act there, along with the plank's weight at its centre of gravity.
steps.equation: N_ground (perpendicular to ground) + f_ground (along ground) + W_plank (down, at centre of gravity)

steps.text: At the cylinder contact there is no friction (given), so only a normal reaction acts there, perpendicular to the plank's own surface at that point.
steps.equation: N_cylinder (perpendicular to the plank, at the point of contact)
steps.why_this_step: A frictionless contact can only push perpendicular to the surfaces touching, never along them.

steps.text: The cylinder touches the rough ground and the smooth plank, and carries its own weight, so it feels four forces: weight, the plank's normal reaction, the ground's normal reaction, and the ground's friction.
steps.equation: cylinder: weight W_cylinder (down, at centre) + N_ground2 (from ground, vertical, through centre) + N_plank (reaction to N_cylinder, radial, through centre) + f_ground_cyl (from ground, horizontal, at the ground contact)
steps.why_this_step: The plank's normal push on the cylinder has a horizontal part along the ground, and the ground contact is rough, so a horizontal friction force is drawn there; whether it is zero is a separate question, since it is the only force with a moment about the centre.

final_answer.value: On the plank: its weight (at its centre of gravity), the ground's normal reaction (perpendicular to the ground) and friction (along the ground, toward the cylinder) at its lower end, and the cylinder's normal reaction perpendicular to the plank (at the contact point). On the cylinder: its weight at the centre, the normal reaction from the plank (perpendicular to the plank, through the centre), the ground's normal reaction (vertical, through the centre) and the ground's friction (horizontal, at the ground contact, directed toward the plank's lower end if it acts).

common_mistakes.text: Drawing a friction force between the plank and the cylinder, contradicting the statement that this contact is frictionless.
Leaving out the ground's friction on the cylinder, although the ground is rough and the plank's push on the cylinder has a horizontal part that makes it tend to move along the ground.

question.text: Three blocks of masses 6 kg, 4 kg and 10 kg touch each other in a line on a frictionless horizontal floor, arranged in that order from left to right. A horizontal force of 100 N pushes on the outer face of the 6 kg block, directed rightward toward the other blocks, and a horizontal force of 40 N pushes on the outer face of the 10 kg block, directed leftward toward the other blocks. All surfaces, including the floor, are smooth.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Find the acceleration of each of the three blocks.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Find the net force acting on the 6 kg block, on the 4 kg block, and on the 10 kg block.

parts.label: c
parts.asks: Find the contact force between the 4 kg block and the 10 kg block.

conditions: frictionless horizontal floor
all surfaces smooth
blocks arranged touching each other, 6 kg then 4 kg then 10 kg left to right
100 N applied on 6 kg block, directed rightward
40 N applied on 10 kg block, directed leftward

figure.description: Three blocks rest touching each other on a horizontal frictionless floor, arranged left to right as 6 kg, 4 kg, 10 kg, with no gaps between them. A 100 N horizontal force pushes on the left (outer) face of the 6 kg block, directed rightward into the row of blocks. A 40 N horizontal force pushes on the right (outer) face of the 10 kg block, directed leftward into the row of blocks. Every contact surface, block-to-block and block-to-floor, is frictionless.

solution.approach: Treat the three blocks as one system to find the common acceleration, then isolate the 10 kg block to find the contact force with the 4 kg block.

steps.text: Find the net force and total mass of the three-block system.
The common acceleration of all three blocks follows from the net force and total mass.
The net force on each block equals its own mass times this common acceleration.
steps.equation: 6 kg block: 18 N, 4 kg block: 12 N, 10 kg block: 30 N

steps.text: Isolate the 10 kg block: the contact push from the 4 kg block, N, minus the 40 N force gives its net force.

final_answer.value: (a) a = 3 m/s²; (b) net force: 18 N on the 6 kg block, 12 N on the 4 kg block, 30 N on the 10 kg block; (c) force between the 4 kg and 10 kg blocks = 70 N

common_mistakes.text: Adding 100 N and 40 N instead of subtracting them, since both arrows point toward the middle of the row, giving a = 140/20 = 7 m/s².
Taking the contact force between the 4 kg and 10 kg blocks as the 40 N applied force, ignoring the 10 kg block's own net force, giving N = 40 N.

question.text: A block of mass m sits on a smooth (frictionless) horizontal surface, and a time-dependent horizontal force F = at is applied to it, where a is a constant and t is time. A second, identical block of mass m rests on top of the first block, and the coefficient of friction between the two blocks is μ. Find the time at which the upper block first starts sliding relative to the lower block.
conditions: mass of each block = m
lower block rests on a smooth horizontal surface
upper block is identical, resting on the lower block
applied horizontal force F = at, on the lower block
coefficient of friction between the two blocks = μ

solution.approach: Find the common acceleration of the two blocks from the total applied force, then find when the friction needed to carry the top block reaches its largest possible value.

steps.text: Since the lower surface is smooth, the applied force accelerates both blocks together.
The upper block is carried along only by friction from the lower block, so the friction needed on it equals its mass times the common acceleration.
Sliding between the blocks begins when this needed friction reaches the largest friction the surface between them can supply.
Solve for the time.

final_answer.value: 2μmg/a

common_mistakes.text: Setting the full applied force F = at equal to the largest friction μmg, instead of the smaller friction actually needed to carry the top block, gives t = μmg/a.

question.text: A vertical assembly hangs together: a 2 kg block sits at the top and is pulled upward by a force F = 100 N. Below this block is a string of mass 2 kg, whose upper end is named A, whose lower end is named B, and whose exact midpoint is named C. A 4 kg block is tied to the string's lower end B. Work out the string tension at each of the points A, B and C.
conditions: string AB has its own mass, spread evenly along its length
an upward force F = 100 N acts on the 2 kg block at the top
a 4 kg block hangs from the string's lower end B
C is the exact midpoint of string AB

figure.description: A dashed outline encloses a vertical setup: at the top, a force of 100 N pulls upward, acting on a 2 kg block. Beneath that block hangs a string of mass 2 kg; its top end is A, its bottom end is B, and its midpoint is C. A 4 kg block hangs from end B. An upward arrow marks the acceleration a of the whole system.

solution.approach: Find the common upward acceleration of the whole system from the net force, then apply Newton's second law to whatever hangs below each labeled point.

steps.text: Find the acceleration of the whole system (top block, string, bottom block) from the net upward force.
Compute the acceleration.
The tension at A supports everything below A: the whole string and the bottom block.
The tension at C supports everything below C: half the string and the bottom block.
The tension at B supports only the bottom block below B, so T(A) = 75 N, T(C) = 62.5 N, T(B) = 50 N.

common_mistakes.text: Using the total system mass (8 kg) at every point instead of only the mass below each labeled point gives the same wrong tension, 100 N, everywhere.
Treating the string as massless drops its weight from the mass below A and C, giving T(A) = 50 N and T(C) = 50 N instead of 75 N and 62.5 N.

concept_tags: tension in a string with mass

question.text: A block of mass m stays motionless on a rough, wedge-shaped inclined surface, as pictured. Find the single net force that the wedge exerts on this block.
conditions: block of mass m rests without moving on a rough wedge
the wedge's sloped surface makes angle θ with the ground
block is in static equilibrium

figure.description: A triangular wedge rests on flat ground, its slanted face going up from left to right, with the base angle θ marked at the bottom-left where the slope meets the ground. A block m sits on this slanted face, somewhere partway up the slope.

solution.approach: Since the block is at rest, only two forces act on it overall, gravity and the wedge's contact force, so the contact force must exactly cancel gravity.

steps.text: Only two forces act on the block: its weight mg straight down, and the total contact force from the wedge, which is the normal force and friction combined into one force.
steps.equation: Forces on block: mg (down), R (from wedge)

steps.text: The block is at rest, so the net force on it is zero, meaning R must be equal and opposite to mg.
steps.why_this_step: With only two forces on the block, equilibrium forces them to be exactly equal and opposite, whatever the incline angle or the friction coefficient.

steps.text: So the wedge pushes on the block with a force of size mg, directed straight up.

final_answer.value: R = mg, directed vertically upward (independent of the angle θ)

common_mistakes.text: Taking the force from the wedge as only the normal force, R = mg cosθ, and leaving out the friction force needed to keep the block at rest.

question.text: Assertion: Two blocks of the same size and mass sit on a rough inclined plane. One of them is set moving up the slope with some initial speed, while the other is set moving down the slope with some initial speed. Given μ = 1/3 and an incline angle θ = 45°, the magnitudes of their accelerations come out in the ratio 2 : 1. Reason: This ratio should equal (1 + μ) over (1 − μ).

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: two identical blocks on a rough inclined plane
one block moving up the slope, the other moving down the slope
incline angle θ = 45°

solution.approach: Find the deceleration of the block moving up and the acceleration of the block moving down on the same rough incline, then compare them with the given μ and θ.

steps.text: For the block moving up the incline, both gravity and kinetic friction act down the incline, opposing the upward motion, so its deceleration is their sum.
For the block moving down the incline, kinetic friction acts up the incline, opposing the downward motion, so its acceleration is gravity's component minus friction.
Divide the two expressions and cancel g cosθ, then use tanθ = 1 at θ = 45°.
Substitute μ = 1/3 into the ratio.

final_answer.value: (a) Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion — the ratio is 2:1.

common_mistakes.text: Not checking that tanθ = 1 is exactly what turns the general ratio (tanθ+μ)/(tanθ−μ) into (1+μ)/(1−μ), a student might doubt the reason explains it and pick option (b) instead of (a).

question.text: In the pulley arrangement shown, find how the acceleration of block A is related to the acceleration of block B.
conditions: upper pulley is fixed to the ceiling
lower pulley is movable, suspended by the string that carries block A
string over the lower pulley carries block B on one end and is anchored near the fixed pulley on the other
strings and pulleys are treated as ideal (light and frictionless), consistent with the figure

figure.description: A pulley P₁ is fixed to the ceiling. One string runs over P₁: its left end goes straight down to block A, its right end goes down to the axle hanger of a second, movable pulley P₂ that hangs below P₁ and to the right of A. A second string runs over P₂: its left end also goes straight down to block A (so two strands rise from A, one to P₁ and one to P₂), and its right end hangs down to block B. Block B hangs higher than block A. All strings are vertical; pulleys and strings are light. Taking positions downward from the ceiling, string 1 gives y_A + y_P₂ = constant and string 2 gives (y_A − y_P₂) + (y_B − y_P₂) = constant.

solution.approach: Write both strings' fixed-length equations in terms of downward positions, then differentiate each twice to connect the accelerations of A and B.

steps.text: String 1 goes over the fixed pulley P1 from A to the movable pulley P2, so the sum of their depths below the ceiling stays fixed.
String 2 goes over the movable pulley P2, with both of its ends going down to A and to B, so the sum of their depths measured from P2 stays fixed.
steps.equation: (yA − yP2) + (yB − yP2) = constant, i.e. yA + yB − 2yP2 = constant

steps.text: Differentiate each length equation twice with respect to time to turn it into a relation between accelerations; this is the constraint relation, found before writing any force equation.
From the first relation, the movable pulley's acceleration is the negative of A's.
Substitute this into the second relation and solve for B's acceleration in terms of A's.

final_answer.value: aB = −3aA, i.e. B's acceleration is three times A's in magnitude and opposite in direction: when A accelerates downward, B accelerates upward by three times as much, and vice versa.

common_mistakes.text: Treating P2 as if it were fixed and using only the second string's length equation gives aB = −aA, missing the factor of 3 that comes from P2's own motion.

question.text: A uniform, smooth solid sphere of mass 50 kg is held in place by two smooth contact surfaces: an incline, named A, tilted at 30° to the horizontal, and a vertical wall, named B. Work out the contact force the sphere receives at A and the contact force it receives at B.
conditions: sphere is homogeneous (uniform) and smooth, mass 50 kg
incline A is smooth, at 30° to the horizontal
wall B is smooth and vertical
sphere touches both A and B at the same time

figure.description: A circular sphere is wedged between two surfaces. On its lower-left, a smooth incline named A rises at 30° to the horizontal (the incline meets a horizontal reference line at 30°, shown near the bottom-left). On its right, a smooth vertical wall named B touches the sphere; the wall has a horizontal ledge at the sphere's base.

solution.approach: The sphere is in equilibrium under its weight and two normal reactions; resolve both reactions along the vertical and horizontal directions.

steps.text: The incline's normal reaction Nₐ makes angle 30° with the vertical, since the incline makes 30° with the horizontal, and the wall's normal reaction N_B is horizontal.
steps.equation: Nₐ at 30° from vertical, N_B horizontal

steps.text: Balance the vertical direction: the vertical component of Nₐ supports the sphere's weight.
Take g = 10 m/s², so Mg = 50 × 10 = 500 N, and solve for Nₐ.
Balance the horizontal direction: the horizontal component of Nₐ is balanced by the wall's reaction N_B.

final_answer.value: Nₐ ≈ 577.35 N (contact force at the incline), N_B ≈ 288.68 N (contact force at the wall), taking g = 10 m/s²

common_mistakes.text: Taking the incline's normal reaction as making 30° with the horizontal instead of with the vertical, which swaps sine and cosine and gives Nₐ = 500/sin30° = 1000 N.
Forgetting that the wall's reaction is horizontal and instead resolving it at 30° like the incline reaction.

question.text: A man of mass m climbs down a rope hanging from an elevator's ceiling, and relative to the rope his downward motion is slowing at rate a. Meanwhile the elevator itself accelerates upward at rate a, measured relative to the ground. What is the tension in the rope?
conditions: rope hangs from the ceiling of the elevator
man's downward slide decelerates at rate a relative to the rope
elevator accelerates upward at rate a relative to the ground

solution.approach: Add the man's deceleration relative to the rope to the elevator's own acceleration to get his true acceleration relative to the ground, then apply Newton's second law to him.

steps.text: The man is sliding down but slowing down relative to the rope, so his acceleration relative to the rope points upward, with size a.
steps.equation: acceleration of man relative to rope = a, upward

steps.text: The elevator itself accelerates upward with size a relative to the ground.
steps.equation: acceleration of rope relative to ground = a, upward

steps.text: The man's acceleration relative to the ground is the sum of his acceleration relative to the rope and the rope's acceleration relative to the ground, since both point the same way.
steps.equation: acceleration of man relative to ground = a + a = 2a, upward

steps.text: Apply Newton's second law to the man: the rope tension acts upward on him, his weight acts downward, and their difference gives his mass times his upward acceleration.

final_answer.value: m(g + 2a)

common_mistakes.text: Adding only one of the two accelerations, either the man's motion relative to the rope or the elevator's own motion, but not both, gives T = m(g + a).

question.text: Two blocks, A (2 kg) on top and B (4 kg) below, are stacked on a smooth horizontal floor. A horizontal force is applied on the top block A, with magnitude in newtons F = 2t, where t is time in seconds. The coefficient of friction between A and B is μ = ½; the floor beneath B is frictionless. Using g = 10 m/s², sketch how the accelerations of A and of B individually change with time, with acceleration on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis.
conditions: mass of A = 2 kg
mass of B = 4 kg
A rests on top of B
B rests on a smooth (frictionless) horizontal floor
μ between A and B = ½
applied force F = 2t newtons (t in seconds), applied horizontally on A
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: Block A (2 kg) sits on top of block B (4 kg); B rests on a smooth horizontal floor. A horizontal force is applied to A, with magnitude F = 2t newtons where t is time in seconds.

solution.approach: Check whether the friction needed to move both blocks together stays within the maximum available friction; find when it is exceeded, then treat each block separately after that.

steps.text: While the blocks move together, both share the same acceleration from the total applied force.
The friction needed to accelerate block B at this common rate must not exceed the maximum available friction between A and B.
steps.equation: f(needed) = mB × a(common) = 4t/3; f(max) = μmAg = 0.5×2×10 = 10 N

steps.text: Find the time when the needed friction reaches the maximum, which is when the blocks start to slip on each other.
For t < 7.5 s, both blocks move together, reaching 2.5 m/s² at t = 7.5 s.
For t > 7.5 s, friction on B stays fixed at its maximum, so B's acceleration is constant while A speeds up under the growing force minus this fixed friction.

final_answer.value: For 0 ≤ t ≤ 7.5 s, a_A = a_B = t/3, both rising together from 0 to 2.5 m/s². For t > 7.5 s, a_B stays constant at 2.5 m/s², while a_A = t − 5 rises from 2.5 m/s² with slope 1 m/s² per second and is greater than a_B.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the blocks move together for all time without checking the friction limit gives a_A = a_B = t/3 throughout, missing the point where they slip.
Using the combined weight of both blocks instead of only block A's weight for the maximum friction gives f(max) = 30 N and a much later, wrong slip time of 22.5 s.

question.text: A wedge in the shape of a right triangle stands with its incline surface tilted 30° above the horizontal. A pulley is fixed at the top of the incline, and another pulley is fixed at the bottom of the incline, at the edge of the surface the wedge sits on. A 2 kg block rests on the incline. A string ties this block, runs up the slope, passes over the top pulley, and goes straight down the vertical face of the wedge to block A, which hangs freely. A second string ties the same 2 kg block, runs down the slope, passes over the bottom pulley, and hangs straight down over the edge to a second 2 kg block. Friction and the mass of the strings are both negligible. What mass must block A have for the whole system to stay at rest?
conditions: incline (wedge) makes 30° with the horizontal
pulley fixed at the top of the incline
pulley fixed at the bottom of the incline, at the table edge
2 kg block rests on the incline, tied to two strings
2 kg block hangs below the bottom pulley, off the edge
friction is negligible
mass of the strings is negligible
system is at rest (equilibrium)

figure.description: A wedge shaped like a right triangle sits on a horizontal surface. Its incline (hypotenuse) rises at 30° from the bottom-left to a pulley fixed at the top-right apex; its vertical right face runs straight down from that apex to the base. A 2 kg block rests on the incline. One string from this block runs up the slope, over the top pulley, then straight down the vertical face to block A, which hangs in the air on the right. A second pulley is fixed at the bottom-left, at the foot of the incline, right at the edge of the base surface. A second string from the same 2 kg block runs down the slope, around this bottom pulley, and then straight down past the edge to a second 2 kg block hanging below.

solution.approach: Write the along-incline equilibrium of the 2 kg block on the incline, using the tension found from each hanging block's own equilibrium.

steps.text: The 2 kg block hanging below the bottom pulley is in equilibrium, so the tension pulling the incline block down the slope equals its weight.
Block A hangs from the top pulley and is in equilibrium, so the tension pulling the incline block up the slope equals A's weight.
For the 2 kg block on the incline, balance the forces along the slope: the upward-pulling tension equals the downward-pulling tension plus the weight component along the slope.
Solve for mₐ.

final_answer.value: mₐ = 3 kg

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the weight component of the 2 kg block along the slope, giving mₐ = 2 kg instead of 3 kg.
Using the full weight of the 2 kg incline block instead of only its component along the slope, giving mₐ = 2 + 2 = 4 kg.

question.text: A block of mass M sits on a horizontal, frictionless table. A light string tied to it runs along the table to a small fixed pulley at the table's left end, comes back over the top of the block to a second fixed pulley at the table's right-hand corner, and hangs straight down to a second block of the same mass M. Both pulleys are light and frictionless. Work out how much each block accelerates and the tension the string carries.
conditions: pulley and string are massless (light)
table surface is frictionless (smooth)

figure.description: A block of mass M rests on a smooth horizontal table. A light string tied to the block runs LEFT along the table to a small fixed pulley mounted on a post at the table's left end, wraps around it, comes back to the right above the block, passes over a second fixed pulley at the table's right-hand corner, and hangs straight down to a second block of the same mass M. Both pulleys are fixed; when the hanging block descends a distance x, the table block moves left by the same distance x.

solution.approach: Both blocks have equal mass M, one on a frictionless table and one hanging, joined by a light string over two fixed pulleys; apply Newton's second law to each.

steps.text: Write Newton's second law for the hanging block M.
Write Newton's second law for the block M on the table.
Add the two equations; the mass M cancels out, leaving the acceleration in terms of g.
Find the tension using T = Ma.
steps.equation: T = Mg/2 (a = g/2 ≈ 5 m/s² and T = Mg/2, using g = 10 m/s²)

final_answer.value: a = g/2 (≈ 5 m/s² with g = 10 m/s²); T = Mg/2

common_mistakes.text: Treating the hanging block as if it falls freely, ignoring the inertia of the block on the table, gives a = g instead of g/2.

question.text: A ball weighing 1 kg is held motionless, suspended by two strings OA and OB, with the geometry described below. Taking g = 10 m/s², work out the tension carried by each of the strings OA and OB.
conditions: mass of ball = 1 kg
g = 10 m/s²
ball hangs in equilibrium from strings OA and OB
string OA makes a 30° angle with the horizontal at its upper fixed point A
string OB makes a 60° angle with the horizontal at its upper fixed point B
at O, string OA makes a 120° angle with the downward vertical, string OB makes a 150° angle with the downward vertical, and OA and OB make a 90° angle with each other

figure.description: Two fixed points A and B lie on a common horizontal line, A to the left and B to the right. Point O lies below and between them. String OA connects O to A, sloping up and to the left, and makes a 30° angle with the horizontal line at A. String OB connects O to B, sloping up and to the right, and makes a 60° angle with the horizontal line at B. The ball hangs directly below O on a vertical string, its weight w = 10 N pulling straight down. At O, going around: the angle from string OA to the downward vertical is 120°, the angle from the downward vertical to string OB is 150°, and the angle between OA and OB (measured the other way, over the top) is 90°.

solution.approach: Use the three marked angles at O between the two strings and the weight to apply Lami's theorem for three forces meeting at a point.

steps.text: Let T1 be the tension in OA and T2 the tension in OB. Write Lami's theorem using, for each force, the angle between the other two forces: T1 is opposite the 150° angle between OB and the weight, T2 opposite the 120° angle between OA and the weight.
Solve for T1 using w = 10 N.
Solve for T2.

common_mistakes.text: Treating string OA alone as if it supported the full weight vertically gives T1 = w/sin30° = 20 N, ignoring the pull from string OB.

question.text: Two identical particles, each of mass m, are joined by an inextensible string. The string is pulled at its midpoint by a steady force F. The entire arrangement rests on a frictionless horizontal surface. Find the acceleration with which each particle approaches the other.
conditions: string is inextensible
surface is smooth (frictionless)
force F is applied at the string's midpoint
particles are identical, each of mass m

figure.description: Two particles sit at the ends of a V formed by a single string that runs from one particle to a central point and then to the other particle. At that central point a constant, steady force F pulls horizontally, exactly along the line that bisects the V. Each half of the string makes a 30° angle with this bisecting line, so the two string halves together enclose a 60° angle.

solution.approach: Find the string tension from the force balance where F is applied, then use its component across the centreline to get each particle's acceleration toward the other.

steps.text: At the point where F is applied, the same tension T pulls back along each string segment, each at 30° to the centreline. Since this point carries no mass, these forces plus F must balance.
For one particle, only the string tension T acts on it, directed 30° from the centreline. The component of this tension across the centreline pulls the particle toward the other one.
Divide by the mass to get the acceleration of that particle toward the other one.

common_mistakes.text: Using the full 60° angle between the two string segments in place of the 30° angle each segment makes with the centreline gives (√3/2)(F/m).
Reporting the acceleration along the centreline (toward F) instead of across it toward the other particle gives T cos30°/m = F/(2m).

question.text: A string runs over a single fixed pulley; block 1 hangs from one end and block 2 hangs from the other end.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Using the constraint (string-length) method, work out how the acceleration of block 1 relates to the acceleration of block 2.

conditions: string passes over a single fixed pulley
block 1 and block 2 each hang from one end of the string
the total length of the string is constant

figure.description: A single fixed pulley is mounted at a fixed point. A string passes over it, with block 1 hanging from one end and block 2 hanging from the other end. Taking a fixed horizontal reference line at the level of the pulley, x₁ is the distance block 1 hangs below this line and x₂ is the distance block 2 hangs below this line; because the total string length is fixed, as one block moves down the other moves up by the same amount.

solution.approach: The string over the fixed pulley has a constant total length, so the two distances measured from the pulley must always add to that constant.

steps.text: The string runs from block 1 up to the pulley and down to block 2, so its total length is the sum of the two measured distances.
A length that stays constant has a rate of change of zero, so the sum of the two velocities dx₁/dt + dx₂/dt is zero, and the sum of the accelerations is zero too.
This gives the acceleration of block 1 equal in size to the acceleration of block 2, in the opposite sense.
steps.why_this_step: If block 1 moves down by a certain amount, block 2 must move up by the same amount to keep the string length fixed.

final_answer.value: a₁ = −a₂ (the two blocks have equal acceleration magnitude, and move in opposite directions — one down as much as the other goes up)

common_mistakes.text: Assuming both blocks move the same way and writing a₁ = a₂ instead of a₁ = −a₂.

question.text: A 4 kg block and a 2 kg block rest next to each other on a frictionless horizontal table, touching along one face. A push of 20 N acts sideways on the 4 kg block, directed toward the 2 kg block.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Work out how quickly the two blocks speed up together.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Work out the size of the push each block exerts on the other.

conditions: frictionless (smooth) horizontal surface
4 kg block and 2 kg block touch side by side
20 N horizontal force applied on the 4 kg block, directed toward the 2 kg block

figure.description: Two blocks touch each other on a flat, frictionless surface. Block A (4 kg) is on the left, block B (2 kg) is on the right, sharing a vertical contact face. A horizontal force of 20 N pushes block A to the right, toward block B.

solution.approach: Treat both blocks together to find the common acceleration, then apply Newton's second law to one block alone to find the push between them.

steps.text: Since the blocks stay in contact and the surface is smooth, both move together with the same acceleration. Treating them as one combined mass gives this acceleration, which is the acceleration of each block.
Look at the 2 kg block alone. The only horizontal force on it is the push N from the 4 kg block, so apply Newton's second law to it.
steps.why_this_step: The 2 kg block is not directly pushed by the 20 N force; it is pushed only by the block touching it.

final_answer.value: (a) acceleration of each block = 3.33 m/s², (b) normal reaction between the blocks = 6.67 N

common_mistakes.text: Dividing the 20 N force by the mass of the 4 kg block alone, giving 5 m/s² instead of treating both blocks together.
Taking the contact force as the full 20 N applied force instead of only the part needed to accelerate the 2 kg block.

question.text: A small ball of mass m hangs by a light string tied to the roof of a railway carriage. The carriage speeds up horizontally with a steady acceleration a, and the ball comes to rest at a fixed tilt relative to the vertical, as the figure shows. Work out this equilibrium tilt angle θ.
conditions: ball hangs from the roof of an accelerating railway carriage
carriage acceleration is horizontal with magnitude a
the ball is in equilibrium relative to the carriage, string tilted by angle θ from vertical

figure.description: A carriage rolling on wheels accelerates horizontally, shown by an arrow marked a pointing in the direction of motion. A ball hangs on a string from the carriage roof; a vertical dashed reference line drops straight down from the roof attachment, and the actual string leans away from this line by angle θ, with the ball sitting toward the rear of the carriage (the side opposite to the direction the arrow a points).

solution.approach: Inside the accelerating train, a backward pseudo force acts on the bob along with gravity, and the string settles along their combined direction.

steps.text: In the train's frame, the bob feels its weight mg straight down and a pseudo force ma directed backward, opposite to the train's acceleration a.
At equilibrium the string lies along the direction of the combined force, so the string tension balances both parts.
steps.equation: T sinθ = ma, T cosθ = mg

steps.text: Divide the two equations to remove T.
steps.why_this_step: The angle the string makes with the vertical depends only on the ratio of the pseudo force to gravity, not on the mass of the bob.

steps.text: Write θ using the inverse tangent.

final_answer.value: θ = tan⁻¹(a/g)

common_mistakes.text: Inverting the ratio and writing θ = tan⁻¹(g/a) instead of tan⁻¹(a/g).

question.text: A single string runs over a pulley that is fixed to a ceiling. On one side, the string carries a 2 kg block, and a second string hangs a 1 kg block below that 2 kg block; call the tension in this lower string T₃. On the other side, the string carries a 3 kg block, and a second string hangs a 4 kg block below that 3 kg block; call the tension in this lower string T₁. Call the tension in the main string over the pulley T₂. Taking g = 10 m/s², work out the system's acceleration and the tension values T₁, T₂ and T₃.
conditions: pulley is fixed to the ceiling
left side: 2 kg block above, 1 kg block below, joined by string T₃
right side: 3 kg block above, 4 kg block below, joined by string T₁
main string over the pulley has tension T₂
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A pulley is fixed to a ceiling. A single string passes over this pulley. On the left, this string is tied to a 2 kg block; a second string, T₃, hangs from the 2 kg block down to a 1 kg block below it. On the right, the string is tied to a 3 kg block; a second string, T₁, hangs from the 3 kg block down to a 4 kg block below it. The tension in the main string over the pulley, on either side, is called T₂.

solution.approach: Find the common acceleration from the total mass on each side of the pulley, then isolate each block in turn to find its own tension.

steps.text: Add the mass on each side of the fixed pulley.
The heavier right side descends; find the common acceleration from the whole system.
Find T₂, the main string tension, from the left side (2 kg + 1 kg) moving upward.
Find T₃, the tension between the 2 kg and 1 kg blocks, from the 1 kg block alone.
Find T₁, the tension between the 3 kg and 4 kg blocks, from the 4 kg block alone.

final_answer.value: a = 4 m/s²; T₁ = 24 N; T₂ = 42 N; T₃ = 14 N

common_mistakes.text: Using only the two blocks nearest the pulley (2 kg and 3 kg) for the acceleration instead of the full 3 kg and 7 kg sides, giving a = 2 m/s².
Finding T₃ as T₂ minus the 2 kg block's weight, forgetting its acceleration term, giving T₃ = 42−20 = 22 N instead of 14 N.

question.text: A plumb bob of mass 1 kg hangs by a string from the ceiling inside a train compartment. The train now moves up an inclined plane of angle 30° with acceleration a = g/2 (directed up the incline), instead of at constant velocity. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the angle the string makes with the normal to the ceiling, and find the tension in the string.
conditions: plumb bob mass = 1 kg
bob hung from the ceiling of a train compartment by a string
train moves on an inclined plane of angle 30°
train accelerates up the plane at a = g/2
g = 10 m/s²

solution.approach: Add a pseudo force down the incline to gravity in the train's frame, then find the direction and size of the net force, which the tension must match.

steps.text: In the train's frame, a pseudo force of magnitude ma acts on the bob directed down the incline, opposite to the train's acceleration.
steps.equation: a = g/2, pseudo force = m(g/2) down the incline

steps.text: Resolve gravity and the pseudo force into horizontal and vertical components and add them to get the net non-tension force on the bob.
The string tension balances this net force, so its magnitude equals the size of the net force.
Find the angle of this net force from the true vertical, then compare it with the 30° tilt of the ceiling's normal from the vertical to get the angle between the string and the normal to the ceiling.
steps.equation: angle from vertical ≈ 19.1°, ceiling normal is 30° from vertical on the other side

steps.text: Since the two tilts are on opposite sides of the vertical, the angle between the string and the normal to the ceiling is their sum.

common_mistakes.text: Adding the magnitudes of gravity and the pseudo force as scalars, T = mg + ma = 15 N, instead of adding them as vectors (60° apart), which gives T = 5√7 ≈ 13.2 N.
Taking the angle with the ceiling normal as 30° minus the tilt from vertical instead of the sum gives about 10.9° instead of 49.1°, missing that the tilts point to opposite sides of the vertical.

question.text: A block of mass m hangs from two strings: one runs horizontally to a fixed wall, and the other runs diagonally upward to a ceiling support, making angle θ with the horizontal. Sketch the free-body diagram of the block.
conditions: block is held by two strings
one string is horizontal, fixed to a wall
the other string runs diagonally up to a ceiling support at angle θ to the horizontal

figure.description: A block is connected by two strings: one horizontal string running to a fixed wall on one side, and another string running diagonally up to a ceiling support on the other side, making angle θ with the horizontal.

solution.approach: List every force on the block: its weight, and the tension in each of the two strings, each pulling along its own string.

steps.text: The block has weight mg, acting at its centre, pointing straight down.
One string runs horizontally to a fixed wall. It pulls the block horizontally, toward the wall, with tension T₁.
The other string runs up to a ceiling support at angle θ to the horizontal. It pulls the block along its own length, up and toward the ceiling support, with tension T₂.
steps.equation: T₂, at angle θ above horizontal
steps.why_this_step: A string can only pull along its own length, never sideways to it.

steps.text: The free body diagram of the block shows three forces: mg downward, T₁ horizontal toward the wall, and T₂ directed along the second string at angle θ above the horizontal.

final_answer.value: three forces act on the block: weight mg downward, tension T₁ horizontal (along the string to the wall), and tension T₂ directed along the string to the ceiling support, at angle θ above the horizontal

common_mistakes.text: Drawing T₂ as purely vertical, ignoring that it must point along the actual direction of that string, at angle θ.
Leaving out the weight mg from the diagram.

question.text: A rod is hinged to a wall at one end and held horizontal. Its mass is 2 kg and it is 4 m long. The other end of the rod is held up by a string that runs from a point on the wall above the hinge down to the rod's far end, meeting the rod at an angle of 37°. With the rod in equilibrium, find the force the hinge exerts on the rod — either as horizontal and vertical components, or as a single resultant — and find the tension in the string. Assume g = 10 m/s² throughout, with sin 37° equal to 3/5 and cos 37° equal to 4/5.
conditions: rod is hinged to a wall at one end
rod mass = 2 kg
rod length = 4 m
string runs from a point on the wall above the hinge to the far end of the rod, meeting it at 37°
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A rod is hinged to a vertical wall at its left end (the hinge) and lies horizontal. A string runs from a point on the wall above the hinge down to the right end of the rod, meeting the rod at an angle of 37°.

solution.approach: Take moments about the hinge to find the string tension, then balance horizontal and vertical forces to find the hinge force.

steps.text: The rod is horizontal, hinged at A, weight mg acting at its midpoint (2 m from A). The string pulls at B (4 m from A), at 37° to the rod, so its vertical part is T sin37°.
The string's horizontal part passes through the same height as the hinge, so it has no moment about A. Only its vertical part and the weight create moments about A.
Put in sin37° = 3/5 and solve for T.
Balance horizontal forces: the hinge's horizontal push balances the string's horizontal pull toward the wall.
Balance vertical forces: the hinge's vertical push, the string's vertical pull, and the weight together balance.
steps.why_this_step: The vertical part of the tension helps hold up the rod, so the hinge only needs to supply the rest of the weight.

final_answer.value: T = 16.67 N; hinge force components H_x = 13.33 N (horizontal), H_y = 10 N (vertical), resultant hinge force = 16.67 N

common_mistakes.text: Using the full rod length 4 m as the moment arm for the weight instead of the midpoint distance 2 m, which doubles the found tension to 33.33 N.
Swapping sin37° and cos37° when finding the hinge components, giving H_x = 10 N and H_y = 6.67 N.

question.text: A smooth (frictionless) horizontal wire carries a sliding ring A of mass 1 kg. A string runs from this ring, over a fixed pulley positioned below the wire, down to a hanging block B of mass 2 kg. The whole system starts from rest at the moment the string makes an angle θ = 60° with the wire. Work out the following.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: an equation relating the ring's speed to the block's speed, expressed in terms of θ

parts.label: b
parts.asks: an equation relating the ring's acceleration to the block's acceleration, evaluated right after release, when θ = 60°

parts.label: c
parts.asks: the string tension at that instant, together with the numerical value of each acceleration

conditions: the wire is smooth (frictionless)
ring A has mass 1 kg and slides along the wire
block B has mass 2 kg and hangs from the string
the system is released from rest
at the moment of release, the string makes an angle of 60° with the wire

figure.description: A fixed horizontal wire, smooth and frictionless, runs between two fixed points; a ring of mass 1 kg slides along it. A fixed pulley hangs a constant vertical distance below a point on the wire. A string of fixed length connects the ring, runs diagonally down to this fixed pulley, and then straight down to a block of mass 2 kg. The angle between the wire and the diagonal part of the string, measured at the ring, is θ. As the block falls, the ring slides along the wire toward the point directly above the pulley.

solution.approach: Differentiate the fixed length of string AQ in terms of the ring's horizontal distance to get vB = vA cosθ, then apply Newton's second law to both bodies.

steps.text: Let x be the ring's horizontal distance from the point on the wire above the pulley; the string length is AQ = √(x² + c²), with cosθ = x/AQ.
Differentiate AQ with respect to time; the rate AQ shortens equals the speed at which B descends, since the total string length is fixed.
steps.equation: d(AQ)/dt = (x/AQ)(dx/dt) = (cosθ)(−vA) = −vA cosθ, so vB = vA cosθ

steps.text: Differentiating again brings in a term from the changing angle, but that term is multiplied by vA, which is zero right after release from rest.
steps.equation: aB = aA cosθ − vA sinθ(dθ/dt), so aB = aA cosθ at release

steps.text: Apply Newton's second law: the string pulls the ring horizontally toward the point above the pulley, while gravity and tension act vertically on the block.
steps.equation: T cosθ = mA aA; mB g − T = mB aB

steps.text: Substitute aB = aA cosθ and θ = 60°, then solve for aA, aB and T.
steps.equation: aA = mB g cosθ/(mA + mB cos²θ) = 20/3 m/s² ≈ 6.67 m/s², aB = 10/3 m/s² ≈ 3.33 m/s², T = 40/3 N ≈ 13.3 N

final_answer.value: (a) vB = vA cosθ; (b) aB = aA cosθ at θ = 60°; (c) aA = 20/3 m/s² ≈ 6.67 m/s², aB = 10/3 m/s² ≈ 3.33 m/s², T = 40/3 N ≈ 13.3 N

common_mistakes.text: Using aB = aA cosθ at a later instant, when vA is no longer zero, forgets the −vA sinθ(dθ/dt) term; the simple relation holds only at the moment of release from rest.
Using sinθ instead of cosθ both in the ring's horizontal equation and in the constraint gives aA ≈ 6.93 m/s² instead of the correct 6.67 m/s².

question.text: A block that weighs 25 kg sits on a flat horizontal surface, and the coefficient of friction between the block and the surface is μ = 1/√3. Given 1 kgf = 9.8 N, what is the smallest possible force that can pull the block along the surface?
conditions: mass = 25 kg
coefficient of friction μ = 1/√3
1 kgf = 9.8 N
block dragged along a horizontal surface

solution.approach: The least force to drag a body is applied at an angle where tanθ = μ, giving F = μmg divided by √(1+μ²).

steps.text: Write the force needed to drag the body when it is pulled at an angle θ above the horizontal.
This force is smallest when the angle satisfies tanθ = μ.
Substitute this angle to get the simplified formula for the least force.
steps.why_this_step: At the angle where tanθ = μ, the denominator cosθ + μ sinθ simplifies to √(1+μ²).

steps.text: Put in the numbers, taking the weight directly in kgf since 1 kgf is the weight of 1 kg.

final_answer.value: 12.5 kgf

common_mistakes.text: Using the body's full weight as the force needed, as if pulling at an angle could not reduce it, gives 25 kgf.
Using the alternative form F_min = mg sinθ (tanθ = μ) but squaring the sine, mg sin²θ = 25 × 1/4 = 6.25 kgf, instead of mg sinθ = 12.5 kgf.
Pulling horizontally instead of at the angle that minimizes the force gives μmg = 14.4 kgf, which matches no listed option.

question.text: Block A (mass 2 kg) lies on top of block B (mass 8 kg), and B lies on a horizontal floor. Friction coefficients: 0.2 for the A–B contact and 0.5 for the B–floor contact. A horizontal force F = 25 N is applied to B. Find the friction force that acts between A and B.
conditions: mass of A = 2 kg
mass of B = 8 kg
block A rests on block B
block B rests on a horizontal floor
coefficient of friction between A and B = 0.2
coefficient of friction between B and floor = 0.5
horizontal force F = 25 N applied on block B

solution.approach: Check whether the applied force can move block B against the floor's friction; if the whole system stays still, block A needs no friction force to move with it.

steps.text: Find the largest friction the floor can supply on the two blocks together.
Compare this with the applied force.
steps.equation: F = 25 N < 50 N, so the blocks do not move

steps.text: Since block B does not accelerate, block A does not accelerate either, so block A needs no force from friction to move with it.
steps.equation: a = 0, friction on A from B = m_A × a = 0

final_answer.value: zero

common_mistakes.text: Taking the largest possible friction between A and B, μ_AB × m_A × g, as the actual friction gives 4 N, but A never needs that much force since the blocks stay still.

question.text: Block A rests on top of block B, which itself rests on top of block C, and block C sits on the ground below. Sketch separate free-body diagrams showing the forces acting on each of the three blocks, A, B and C.
conditions: block A rests on top of block B
block B rests on top of block C
block C rests on the ground

figure.description: Three rectangular blocks stacked vertically: block A on top, block B in the middle, block C at the bottom, with block C resting on a horizontal hatched ground surface.

solution.approach: Take each block on its own, and list its weight plus the contact push from whatever touches it above and below.

steps.text: Block A sits only on block B. Two forces act on A: its own weight W_A downward, and the normal reaction from B, N₁, upward.

Block B sits on block C and carries block A on top. Three forces act on B: its own weight W_B downward, the push from A on B (reaction to N₁, so it is N₁ downward), and the normal reaction from C, N₂, upward.
steps.why_this_step: By Newton's third law, if B pushes A up with N₁, A pushes B down with the same N₁.

steps.text: Block C sits on the ground and carries B (and, through B, A) on top. Three forces act on C: its own weight W_C downward, the push from B on C (reaction to N₂, so it is N₂ downward), and the normal reaction from the ground, N₃, upward.

final_answer.value: A: weight W_A down, reaction N₁ = W_A up from B. B: weight W_B down, reaction N₁ down (from A), reaction N₂ = W_A + W_B up from C. C: weight W_C down, reaction N₂ down (from B), ground reaction N₃ = W_A + W_B + W_C up.

common_mistakes.text: Giving block C's ground reaction as only W_C, forgetting it also carries the weight of A and B resting on top of it.
Leaving out the downward push that each upper block exerts on the block beneath it.

question.text: A monkey slides down a rope whose breaking strength is only 2/3 of the monkey's weight. What is the least downward acceleration with which the monkey must slide so that the rope does not break?
conditions: the rope's breaking strength is two-thirds of the monkey's weight

solution.approach: Write the rope tension while the monkey slides down with acceleration a, then find the smallest a that keeps this tension at or below the rope's breaking strength.

steps.text: If the monkey grips the rope and stays still, the tension equals its full weight, which is more than the rope's breaking strength, so the monkey must slide down to lower the tension.
Write Newton's second law for the monkey sliding down with acceleration a: weight acts down, tension acts up.
steps.equation: mg − T = ma ⇒ T = m(g − a)

steps.text: The rope survives only while its tension stays at or below the breaking strength.
Solve this inequality for the smallest acceleration that keeps the rope from breaking.

common_mistakes.text: Setting the tension to zero instead of to the breaking strength, giving a = g.
Using the fraction 2/3 directly as the coefficient of g without solving the inequality, giving a = 2g/3.

question.text: Assertion: A person walking on a rough road receives a friction force from the road that acts backward, against the walking direction. Reason: The motion of the walking person is produced by the force that the road exerts on the person.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
options.3: If Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: surface is rough
person is walking (in motion)

solution.approach: Identify which real force actually drives a walking person forward, using Newton's third law on the foot's push against the ground.

steps.text: While walking, a person's foot pushes backward on the ground through muscular effort.

By Newton's third law, the ground pushes back on the foot with an equal and opposite force — this reaction is the static friction from the ground, and it points forward, in the same direction as the person's motion.
steps.equation: friction on person = −(push on ground) ⇒ forward

steps.text: This makes the Assertion false: the friction is not opposite to the motion, it is what drives the motion forward.
Internal muscular forces alone cannot move the person's centre of mass; only an external force can, and that external force is exactly this forward friction from the road, so the Reason is true.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming friction always opposes motion, as with ordinary sliding friction, which makes the Assertion look true, while doubting that the road's force truly causes the motion, so the Reason is read as false.

question.text: A 4 kilogram block rests on a rough horizontal surface. A force that varies with time, F = kt, acts horizontally on it, where k = 2 N·s⁻¹. Given μ = 0.2, work out the friction acting between block and surface exactly when t = 2 s.
conditions: a time-varying horizontal force F = kt acts on the block
the surface is rough and horizontal

solution.approach: Find the applied force at t = 2 s and the maximum friction the surface can supply, then check that the applied force has not yet reached that maximum.

steps.text: Find the size of the applied force at t = 2 s.
Find the maximum friction force the surface can supply, using the normal force, which equals the block's weight on this horizontal plane.
Since the applied force, 4 N, is smaller than the maximum friction, 8 N, the block is still at rest, and friction matches the applied force to keep it still.

final_answer.value: 4 N

common_mistakes.text: Assuming friction is always at its maximum value once any force is applied, without checking whether the block has actually started moving, gives f = μmg = 8 N.

question.text: Three blocks with masses 4 kg, 2 kg and 1 kg, placed in that order, sit in a row on a frictionless surface. Two light strings that do not stretch join consecutive blocks — one between the 4 kg and 2 kg blocks, another between the 2 kg and 1 kg blocks. A horizontal pull of 14 N is applied to the 1 kg block, directed away from the other two blocks.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: Determine how fast each block accelerates.

parts.label: b
parts.asks: Determine the pulling force transmitted through each string.

conditions: frictionless (smooth) surface
two light, inextensible strings connect the blocks in series: 4 kg–2 kg–1 kg
14 N horizontal force pulls the 1 kg block away from the other two

figure.description: Three blocks lie in a row on a horizontal frictionless surface, left to right: 4 kg, then 2 kg, then 1 kg. A light inextensible string (tension T₂) connects the 4 kg and 2 kg blocks; another light inextensible string (tension T₁) connects the 2 kg and 1 kg blocks. A horizontal force of 14 N pulls the 1 kg block to the right, away from the other two blocks.

solution.approach: Find the common acceleration of the three-block system, then apply Newton's second law to each block in turn, starting from the pulled end, to find each string's tension.

steps.text: The pulling force F acts on the whole chain of three blocks through the strings, and the surface is smooth, so all three move with one common acceleration.
Look at the 1 kg block alone, the one being pulled. F acts forward on it, and T₁ (the string to the 2 kg block) pulls it back.
Look at the 4 kg block alone, the one farthest from the pull. Only T₂ (the string to the 2 kg block) acts on it, pulling it forward.
steps.why_this_step: The 4 kg block has no other horizontal force on it, so its whole forward force is the string tension pulling it along.

final_answer.value: (a) acceleration of each block = 2 m/s², (b) tension T₂ (between the 4 kg and 2 kg blocks) = 8 N, tension T₁ (between the 2 kg and 1 kg blocks) = 12 N

common_mistakes.text: Finding T₁ and T₂ as equal, missing that the string closer to the pulled block always carries more tension because it also has to move the blocks behind it.
Computing the acceleration using only the 1 kg block's mass, giving 14 m/s² instead of dividing by the total mass of the chain.

question.text: A rope, of mass M and length L, lies on a rough horizontal floor. A steady force drags it horizontally, with magnitude F = Mg, applied at one end and pointing along the rope's own length. Between rope and floor, the coefficient of kinetic friction is 1/2. Find the tension exactly at the rope's midpoint.
conditions: floor is rough
force is applied at one end of the rope, pointing along its length
coefficient of kinetic friction between rope and floor = 1/2
force magnitude F equals Mg

solution.approach: Find the rope's overall acceleration from the pull and the friction, then apply Newton's second law to the trailing half of the rope to find the tension at its midpoint.

steps.text: The whole rope has the pulling force F on one end and friction, spread evenly along its length, resisting the motion. Find the acceleration from the net force on the whole rope.
steps.equation: F − μMg = Ma, with F = Mg and μ = 1/2 ⇒ a = g(1 − μ) = g/2

steps.text: Look at the trailing half of the rope, the half farther from where F is pulled. The only forces on it are the tension T pulling it forward from the midpoint and friction on its own weight holding it back.
steps.equation: trailing half has mass M/2 and friction μ(M/2)g

steps.text: Apply Newton's second law to this half and solve for T.

final_answer.value: Mg/2

common_mistakes.text: Wrongly assuming all the friction acts only under the half being pulled, leaving none on the trailing half, gives T = (M/2)a = Mg/4.

question.text: A straight rod AB lies inside a spherical shell whose inner surface is rough. The shell rests on the ground below it. The rod's two ends, A and B, touch this rough inner surface at two different points. Draw a diagram of the rod on its own, showing all the forces that act on it.
conditions: rod AB rests inside a spherical shell
the shell's inner surface is rough where it touches the rod
the shell itself rests on the ground

figure.description: A circle represents the cross-section of a spherical shell resting on a horizontal ground below it. A straight rod lies inside the circle as a chord, touching the shell's rough inner surface at two points: end A near the bottom-left of the circle, close to where the shell meets the ground, and end B on the right side of the circle, above the mid-height.

solution.approach: At each contact point the rough shell gives a normal force toward its centre and a friction force along its surface, plus the rod's own weight.

steps.text: Mark the weight of the rod, Mg, acting vertically downward at its midpoint.
steps.equation: Mg ↓ at the midpoint of AB

steps.text: At end A, mark the normal reaction N(A) directed from A toward the centre of the shell, and a friction force f(A) tangent to the shell surface at A, since the shell is rough.
steps.equation: N(A) toward centre, f(A) tangent, both at A

steps.text: At end B, mark the normal reaction N(B) directed from B toward the centre of the shell, and a friction force f(B) tangent to the shell surface at B.
steps.equation: N(B) toward centre, f(B) tangent, both at B

steps.text: The free body diagram of the rod carries five forces in total.
steps.equation: Mg at the midpoint; N(A) and f(A) at A; N(B) and f(B) at B
steps.why_this_step: Each contact with a rough curved surface gives a normal part toward the centre and a friction part along the surface.

final_answer.value: Five forces act on the rod: weight Mg at its midpoint, normal reaction N(A) and friction f(A) at A, and normal reaction N(B) and friction f(B) at B, each normal force pointing toward the shell's centre and each friction force along the shell surface.

common_mistakes.text: Drawing only a normal force at A and B and leaving out friction, forgetting that the shell is stated to be rough.
Directing the normal forces along the rod instead of toward the shell's centre; a normal force from a curved surface always acts along the radius.

question.text: A 2 kg cube, 20 cm on each edge, is pressed flat against a rough vertical wall by a horizontal force F of 40 N that passes through the cube's centre, point C. Taking g = 10 m/s², find how far the wall's normal reaction acts from point C, measured perpendicular to F.
conditions: cube held stationary against a rough vertical wall
applied force F is horizontal, 40 N, and passes through the centre C
cube's side length is 20 cm
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A cube (drawn as a square in side view) is pressed against a vertical wall on its right-hand side by a horizontal force F applied at its left face, acting through the cube's centre C. The wall's surface is rough (frictional) and vertical.

solution.approach: Find the wall's normal force and the friction from equilibrium, then balance torques about C to find how far below C the wall's contact force must act.

steps.text: Since F passes through C and is horizontal, horizontal equilibrium gives the wall's normal reaction equal to F.
Vertical equilibrium requires friction from the wall to support the cube's weight.
Both F and the weight act through C, so they create no torque about C. The wall's normal force and friction act together at the contact point, a horizontal distance of half a side from C.
steps.equation: horizontal distance from C to wall face = 0.20/2 = 0.10 m

steps.text: Let the contact point be a distance h above C. Balance the torques of N and f about C.
Solve for h and take its magnitude as the perpendicular distance.
steps.equation: h = −(20×0.10)/40 = −0.05 m, so the distance is 0.05 m (below C)

final_answer.value: 0.05 m (5 cm), below the centre C

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting that F and the weight both pass through C, and so produce zero torque about C, leads to a wrong torque equation with extra terms in it.
Using the full side length instead of half the side for the horizontal distance from C to the wall face gives 0.10 m instead of 0.05 m.

question.text: A 2 kg block and a 4 kg block sit touching each other on a smooth incline that makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal; the 4 kg block is lower down the slope and the 2 kg block is higher up, in contact with it. Both blocks are let go from rest at the same instant. Find the normal force that acts between the two blocks.
conditions: incline is smooth (frictionless)
angle of incline is 30°
4 kg block is lower on the slope, 2 kg block is higher, touching each other
both blocks released from rest at the same time

figure.description: A wedge shaped like a right triangle has its sloped face rising at 30° from the horizontal, the angle marked where the slope meets the base. Two blocks touch each other on this sloped face, tilted to match the slope: a 4 kg block positioned lower down the slope, and a 2 kg block positioned higher up the slope, right above it.

solution.approach: With no applied force besides gravity and a frictionless incline, both blocks would accelerate at the same rate on their own, so they need no push from each other.

steps.text: On a smooth incline with no applied force, a block's acceleration along the slope depends only on gravity and the incline angle, not on its mass.
steps.equation: a = g sin30°, the same value for both blocks

steps.text: Since both blocks would accelerate at the same rate even if they were separate, no contact force is needed for them to move together.
The normal contact force between the two blocks is therefore zero.

final_answer.value: 0 N

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the heavier 4 kg block pushes on the lighter 2 kg block because it sits lower on the slope, missing that acceleration on a smooth incline does not depend on mass.
Computing a contact force from the mass difference, such as (4−2)g sin30° = 10 N; no such formula exists — a contact force appears only when the two blocks would accelerate at different rates.

question.text: Assertion: Suppose reference frames S₁ and S₂ are both non-inertial; then an observer in S₁ would find S₂ to be an inertial frame. Reason: A frame being in motion does not by itself make it non-inertial.

options.1: both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
options.2: both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
options.3: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
options.4: Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

conditions: S₁ and S₂ are both non-inertial frames
S₂ is viewed from S₁

solution.approach: Check whether the relative acceleration of S₂ with respect to S₁ must vanish merely because both are non-inertial, then judge the general truth of the Reason on its own.

steps.text: A frame is non-inertial only if it has some acceleration relative to an inertial (ground) frame; being non-inertial is about acceleration, not about motion in general.
Viewed from S₁, the relative acceleration of S₂ is the difference of their accelerations relative to the ground.
steps.equation: a(S₂ relative to S₁) = a(S₂) − a(S₁)

steps.text: This difference is zero only in the special case that S₁ and S₂ happen to share the same acceleration, which is not stated here, so in general S₂ stays non-inertial even when viewed from S₁ — the Assertion is false as a general claim.
steps.equation: a(S₂) − a(S₁) ≠ 0 in general ⇒ Assertion false

steps.text: The Reason is a true, separate statement: a frame moving at constant velocity is still inertial, so mere motion does not make a frame non-inertial — only acceleration does.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming that viewing one non-inertial frame from another non-inertial frame always cancels out the acceleration completely, making S₂ look inertial from S₁ in every case, and picking both statements true.

question.text: A student claims that in a non-inertial (accelerating) reference frame, the only way to analyse a mechanics problem is by bringing in a pseudo force. Decide whether this claim is correct or incorrect.
conditions: the reference frame under discussion is non-inertial (accelerating)

solution.approach: A problem set in a non-inertial frame can also be solved by working entirely in an inertial frame with only real forces, so pseudo force is not the only method.

steps.text: Every non-inertial-frame problem can be solved by switching to an inertial, ground frame and using Newton's second law with only real forces, never needing a pseudo force at all.
Pseudo force is added only as a convenience, so that Newton's second law appears to hold when the calculation is done directly inside the accelerating frame.
Since the ground-frame method with real forces alone always works, the claim that pseudo force is the only way to solve such problems is false.

final_answer.value: False

question.text: In the pulley system pictured, block 1 hangs from the fixed pulley and blocks 2 and 3 hang from the two ends of the string over the movable pulley. Block 3 accelerates downward at 6 m/s² and block 2 accelerates upward at 4 m/s². Determine the acceleration of block 1.
conditions: fixed pulley at top, block 1 hangs from it
movable pulley hangs below the fixed pulley, blocks 2 and 3 hang from its two ends

figure.description: A fixed pulley is mounted at the top, attached to a rigid support. A string runs over this fixed pulley: block 1 hangs from one end (the left side), and the other end connects to the axle of a second, movable pulley that hangs below it. A second string runs over this movable pulley, with block 2 hanging from its left end and block 3 hanging from its right end.

solution.approach: Use the movable-pulley constraint to find the pulley's acceleration from blocks 2 and 3, then use the fixed-pulley constraint to find block 1's acceleration.

steps.text: Take downward as positive. Block 3's acceleration is 6 m/s² downward and block 2's is 4 m/s² upward, so its downward value is −4 m/s².
The movable-pulley constraint makes the pulley's downward acceleration the average of the two.
The fixed-pulley constraint makes block 1's downward acceleration the negative of the movable pulley's.
A negative downward acceleration means block 1 actually accelerates upward.

final_answer.value: 1 m/s² upward

common_mistakes.text: Taking block 1's acceleration in the same direction as the movable pulley instead of the opposite direction gives 1 m/s² downward, the wrong direction.

question.text: A frictionless pulley is fixed to a ceiling. A light string that does not stretch passes over it: a 2 kg block hangs from one end. From the other end the string leads down to a 4 kg block; a second light string then connects the 4 kg block to a 6 kg block hanging below it. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the acceleration of the system and the tension in each of the two strings.
conditions: pulley is frictionless (smooth)
string is massless and does not stretch
the 4 kg and 6 kg blocks move down together while the 2 kg block moves up
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A single fixed pulley hangs from the ceiling. A string over the pulley holds a 2 kg block on one side, moving upward with acceleration a. On the other side, the string (tension T₁) runs down to a 4 kg block; a second string (tension T₂) hangs below the 4 kg block and connects it to a 6 kg block. The 4 kg and 6 kg blocks move downward together with acceleration a.

solution.approach: The 4 kg and 6 kg blocks move together as one 10 kg mass on the heavier side of the pulley, giving a plain two-mass pulley problem.

steps.text: The 2 kg block goes up and the combined 4 kg + 6 kg = 10 kg goes down with the same acceleration a.
Put in g = 10 m/s² and solve.
T₁ is the tension pulling the 2 kg block up, so apply Newton's second law to it.
Put in a = 20/3 m/s² and solve for T₁.
T₂ is the tension pulling the 6 kg block up from below the 4 kg block, so apply Newton's second law to the 6 kg block.
Put in a = 20/3 m/s² and solve for T₂.
steps.why_this_step: The 6 kg block feels only its own weight down and T₂ up, since nothing hangs below it.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the 4 kg block and taking the heavier side as only 6 kg, giving a = (6−2)×10/8 = 5 m/s².
Treating the 6 kg block as not accelerating and taking T₂ = 6g = 60 N.

question.text: A knot is held in place by three strings. String C runs horizontally from the knot to a wall. String B runs from the knot up to the ceiling, making a 30° angle with the vertical. String A hangs vertically down from the knot and supports a block of mass 10 kg. The whole system is in equilibrium. Which string has zero tension?
conditions: system is in equilibrium
string C is horizontal, tied to a wall
string B is tied to the ceiling, making a 30° angle with the ceiling
string A is vertical and supports the 10 kg block
mass of the block is 10 kg

figure.description: A vertical wall on the left and a horizontal ceiling meet at a corner. From a common knot below and to the right of the corner, string C runs horizontally to the left to the wall, string B runs up and to the right to the ceiling making a 30° angle with the vertical dashed line through the knot (so 60° with the ceiling), and string A hangs straight down from the knot, holding a 10 kg block at its bottom end.

solution.approach: Balance the knot vertically and horizontally to find all three string tensions, then check whether any of them actually comes out zero.

steps.text: At the knot, three strings pull: A straight down carrying the 10 kg block, B up to the ceiling at 30° from the vertical, and C straight toward the wall (horizontal).
Balance the vertical direction; only T(A) and the vertical part of T(B) act vertically.
Solve for T(B).
Balance the horizontal direction; only T(C) and the horizontal part of T(B) act horizontally.
All three tensions come out clearly positive, so none of the strings carries zero tension.

final_answer.value: None of the above

common_mistakes.text: Assuming a horizontal string like C carries no load since it does not hold up any weight directly, missing that it must balance the horizontal pull of the angled string B.

question.text: In the figure, three massless strings meet at a common knot. A horizontal string connects the knot to a fixed wall; the tension in this string is 30 N. A second string runs from the knot up to a fixed support, making a 45° angle with the vertical. A third string hangs straight down from the knot and supports a block of weight W. Find W.
conditions: all three strings are massless
tension in the horizontal string is 30 N
the inclined string makes a 45° angle with the vertical
the vertical string holds the block directly below the knot

figure.description: Three massless strings are tied together at one knot. A horizontal string runs from the knot to a fixed vertical wall. An inclined string runs from the same knot up to a fixed support, making a 45° angle with the vertical direction. A third string hangs straight down from the knot, with a block of weight W tied to its lower end.

solution.approach: At the knot, resolve the diagonal string's tension along the horizontal and vertical directions and balance each against the known tension and the hanging weight.

steps.text: At the knot, three strings pull: the diagonal string at 45° from the vertical, the horizontal string with tension 30 N, and the vertical string carrying weight W.
Balance the horizontal direction: the diagonal string's horizontal component equals the horizontal string's tension.
Solve for the diagonal string's tension T.
Balance the vertical direction: the diagonal string's vertical component supports the weight W.

final_answer.value: W = 30 N

common_mistakes.text: Resolving the 45° string's components the wrong way round (using cos45° for the horizontal part) still gives 30 N here only because sin45° = cos45°; at any other angle this swap gives a wrong W.
Setting W equal to the full diagonal tension T = 30√2 N ≈ 42.4 N, instead of only its vertical component.

question.text: In the arrangement shown, take g = 10 m/s² and find (a) the accelerations of the 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg blocks, and (b) the tensions T₁ and T₂.

parts.label: a
parts.asks: the acceleration of each of the 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg blocks

parts.label: b
parts.asks: the tensions T₁ and T₂

conditions: 1 kg block rests on a horizontal table
string from the 1 kg block passes over a pulley fixed at the table's edge
that string continues to a fixed ceiling pulley and then a movable pulley below it
2 kg block hangs from the movable pulley
3 kg block hangs below the 2 kg block, joined by tension T1
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A 1 kg block rests on a smooth horizontal table.
