A string of tension T₂ runs from the block to the right, over a small pulley fixed at the table's edge, then straight down, passes UNDER a movable pulley P₁ (wrapping around its lower half) and rises vertically to a fixed anchor on the ceiling; P₁ therefore hangs in the loop of the T₂ string. From the axle of P₁ a short vertical string hangs down to the axle of a second movable pulley P₂ directly below it. A string of tension T₁ passes over P₂: a 2 kg block hangs from its left end and a 3 kg block from its right end. All pulleys and strings are light and frictionless. When the 1 kg block moves right by x, P₁ and P₂ descend by x/2.

solution.approach: Use the two given string constraints to relate all four accelerations, note the two movable pulleys make T1 equal T2, then solve the three block equations together.

steps.text: The 1 kg block's string loops under the movable pulley P1, so P1 (and P2, joined rigidly below it) descend at half the 1 kg block's speed; this is given directly: when the 1 kg block moves x, P1 and P2 descend x/2.
steps.why_this_step: This is the first constraint relation, fixed by the string geometry, written before any force equation.

steps.text: The 2 kg and 3 kg blocks hang from a string over the movable pulley P2, so their accelerations add up to twice P2's own acceleration.
steps.why_this_step: This is the second constraint relation, from treating P2 as an ordinary pulley that itself accelerates at aP.

steps.text: P1 is massless: the two upward pulls of the T2 cord (looped under it) must balance the one downward pull of the short link to P2, and P2 is massless too: that link's pull upward must balance the two downward pulls of the T1 cord.
Write Newton's second law for the 1 kg block on the frictionless table.
Write Newton's second law for the 2 kg and the 3 kg blocks, taking downward as positive.
steps.equation: m2 g − T1 = m2 a2,   m3 g − T1 = m3 a3

steps.text: Using T1 = T2 = 2m1 aP, express a2 and a3 in terms of aP, substitute into a2 + a3 = 2aP, and solve.
Use aP to find the remaining accelerations and the common tension.

final_answer.value: acceleration of 1 kg block = 120/11 ≈ 10.9 m/s²; of 2 kg block = 50/11 ≈ 4.5 m/s² downward; of 3 kg block = 70/11 ≈ 6.4 m/s² downward; T1 = T2 = 120/11 ≈ 10.9 N

common_mistakes.text: Treating P2 as fixed and solving the 2 kg-3 kg pair as an ordinary Atwood machine, giving accelerations of 2 m/s² each way instead of the correct 4.5 and 6.4 m/s².

question.text: Two blocks are in contact with each other and are sliding down an incline that makes 30° with the horizontal. Between the 2.0 kg block and the incline surface, the friction coefficient is μ₁ = 0.20; between the 4.0 kg block and the incline surface, it is μ₂ = 0.30. The 2.0 kg block sits higher up the slope, pressing against the 4.0 kg block, which sits lower down. Using g = 10 m/s², work out the acceleration of the 2.0 kg block.
conditions: two blocks in contact on an incline of 30°
μ₁ = 0.20 between the 2.0 kg block and the incline
μ₂ = 0.30 between the 4.0 kg block and the incline
2.0 kg block positioned higher up the slope (behind), 4.0 kg block lower down (in front)
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: Two blocks touch each other on an incline of 30° to the horizontal: the 2.0 kg block sits higher up the slope, in contact with the 4.0 kg block which sits lower down; both slide down together.

solution.approach: The two blocks touch and slide down together with a common acceleration, so treat them as one system of total mass 6 kg with each block contributing its own friction.

steps.text: Write the weight component along the incline and the friction force for the combined system, using each block's own friction coefficient.
Substitute the given values: m₁ = 2.0 kg, μ₁ = 0.20, m₂ = 4.0 kg, μ₂ = 0.30, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s².
Solve for the common acceleration.
steps.why_this_step: Since μ₂ > μ₁, the 4.0 kg block in front resists more, so the 2.0 kg block behind pushes into it; this contact force does not change the combined system's acceleration because it is internal to the system.

final_answer.value: a ≈ 2.69 m/s², directed down the incline

common_mistakes.text: Using only the 2.0 kg block's own friction coefficient (0.20) for the whole system gives a ≈ 3.27 m/s², ignoring that the two blocks are pressed together and share the load.
Using only the 4.0 kg block's friction coefficient (0.30) for the whole system gives a ≈ 2.40 m/s², again ignoring that each block contributes its own friction.

question.text: A block of mass 2 kg sits on a rough horizontal floor whose friction coefficient is μ = 0.8. A horizontal force that grows with time, F = 2t newton (with t in seconds), pushes the block, as pictured. Using g = 10 m/s², sketch how the block's acceleration changes with time.
conditions: floor is rough
coefficient of friction μ = 0.8
applied force is horizontal and time-varying, F = 2t newton
g = 10 m/s²

figure.description: A 2 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor with friction coefficient μ = 0.8. A horizontal force F = 2t (F in newton, t in seconds) pushes the block to the right, increasing with time.

solution.approach: The block stays still until the growing force F = 2t exceeds the maximum friction, then it accelerates according to Newton's second law with that same friction opposing it.

steps.text: With only one μ given, the same value acts as both the static limit and the kinetic value once the block moves.
Find the time at which F first reaches this value; before that time the block does not move, so a = 0.
For t ≥ 8 s, the block slides, and kinetic friction (16 N, same value) opposes F; apply Newton's second law.
The full acceleration-time graph is flat at zero up to t = 8 s, then rises as a straight line of slope 1 starting from a = 0 at t = 8 s.
steps.equation: a = 0 for 0 ≤ t < 8 s; a = (t − 8) m/s² for t ≥ 8 s

final_answer.value: a = 0 for 0 ≤ t < 8 s; for t ≥ 8 s, a = (t − 8) m/s², a straight line starting at a = 0 when t = 8 s and rising with slope 1 m/s³ (no jump at t = 8 s, since the same μ gives the same friction immediately before and immediately after motion starts).

common_mistakes.text: Assuming motion starts at t = 0 and writing a = t − 8 for all t, giving a wrongly negative acceleration before t = 8 s.
Forgetting to subtract the friction force after motion starts and writing a = t (using F = 2t directly divided by mass without subtracting 16 N of friction).
